- Huldra: A seductive forest being with a cow's tail hidden under her skirts and a back hollow like a tree. She lures men to her mountain halls and can wed them, bringing luck, if her tail is hidden or dispelled. Betrayal brings terrible fury. A temptress of the woods and a possible bride.
- Sami noaidi: A drum shaman of the Sami people who journeys into the spirit world by beating a rune-painted drum and chanting joik. He heals, finds game, predicts weather and fights hostile spirits. Reindeer and bear spirits aid him. A potent spiritual guide for Arctic adventures, bridging worlds and negotiating with gods.
- Stallo: A Sami giant-ogre with great strength but little wit, who tries to kidnap and eat people, living in stone houses in the wilderness. Clever Sami heroes trick him into sunlight or boiling water. Some stallo have magical gear and wealthy hoards. A classic outwitted giant, used as a snowbound ogre.
- Gufihtar: Sami underground folk who dwell beneath hills and in the earth, living in their own bright communities with herds of invisible reindeer. They trade with mortals, lure children, and resent intrusion. Their hospitality is double-edged. A secretive fey society for tundra adventures and mysterious bargains.
- Rota: A Swedish water ghost haunting lakes and streams, often a woman in white who pulls the unwary under. She may be the spirit of a drowned maiden seeking company. Sightings foretell drownings and she hates iron. A mournful aquatic haunt for mist-covered ponds.
- Bäckahästen: A brook horse, a pale, shining steed that stands by streams and invites travellers to ride, then plunges into the water carrying them away to drown. Its hooves are reversed, a hint of danger. Quick-witted riders can slip a bridle on and make it work. A deceptive water-horse like the kelpie.
- Dutch klabautermann: A ship spirit who helps sailors by mending leaks and warning of storms, small and pipe-smoking in a sailor's cap. He is rarely seen, and only before the ship will sink. Insulting him or killing a crewmate drives him away. A cheerful maritime guardian and harbinger of fate.
- Flemish roodkapje: A witch-tale version of Little Red Riding Hood in Flemish folklore, in which the grandmother or wolf is a witch and the girl cleverly outwits her. The tale has darker undertones, with cannibalism and trickery. It is a story-driven villain and a cautionary character for dark fairy-tale adaptations.
- Alven: An elf of Low Countries and Scandinavian folk belief, shimmering and beautiful but mischievous, dancing in meadows on misty nights. They bring sickness with their breath, leave elf-circles in grass and trade favours with mortals. Offerings and respect appease them. A fey neighbour, helpful or perilous.
- Lindwurm of the north: A wingless dragon coiling through northern wilds, long and serpentine, hoarding gold in barrows. Its venom is lethal, and its blood can heal or poison. Heroes slay it with clever stabs from a pit. A classic legend monster, evoking Beowulf and Sigurd in frozen forests.
### Icelandic
- Huldufolk: The hidden folk of Iceland, a people who look human but live inside rocks, hills and lava fields, invisible to most eyes. They are courteous yet touchy, rewarding respect with luck and punishing trespass or vandalism of their stones with accidents, illness and failed machinery. Ideal as neutral quest-givers who guard sacred land.
- Yule Lads: Thirteen mischievous brothers who descend from the mountains one by one in the days before Christmas, each with a signature vice such as door-slamming, spoon-licking, sausage-snatching or window-peeping. They wear old wool and carry sacks. Playful pranksters as a rotating gang of minor antagonists with distinct tricks.
- Grýla: A monstrous mountain ogress with hooves, a tail, and a sack for stolen children, mother of the Yule Lads. She roams at midwinter hunting misbehaving youngsters to boil in her stew, ever hungry and cunning. A terrifying seasonal boss whose lair holds a cauldron, a cat, and countless captive souls.
- Yule Cat: A gigantic, glowing-eyed black cat that prowls the snowbound countryside on Christmas Eve, devouring anyone who has not received new clothes. It is a harsh enforcer of diligence and wool-work. As a creature it stalks villages silently, can be placated with a gift of clothing, and is dangerous to the idle.
- Draugr: A reanimated Norse corpse that guards its burial mound and treasure with unnatural strength, bloated size and a stench of decay. It can swell, shapeshift, curse the living and ride dreams. Defeated only by wrestling it down and beheading or burning it, making it a tough tomb-guardian encounter.
- Marbendill: An Icelandic merman, half man and half fish, who dwells beneath the northern seas and occasionally gets hauled up in fishing nets. Wise and prophetic, he may offer foresight or hard bargains in exchange for his freedom. A fine oracle character, valuable to sailors but resentful of captors.
- Nykur: A shape-shifting water horse that appears as a beautiful grey steed beside lakes and rivers, with hooves facing backwards. Anyone who mounts it is carried into the depths and drowned. It can be foiled by speaking its true name or by making the sign of the cross.
- Skoffin: A rare hybrid born of a fox and a cat, hunted by Icelanders for its deadly gaze. Its glare can kill instantly, so it is slain with careful ambush. In play it can be a glass-cannon predator, fast and cunning, whose stare is both its greatest weapon and its undoing.
- Sendling: A ghost summoned and sent by a sorcerer to torment an enemy, bound to its master's will by dark ritual. It follows a victim relentlessly, causing sickness, madness or death, growing stronger when fed with the caster's malice. It can be turned back upon its creator by a skilled counter-magician.
- Tilberi: A grotesque household creature made by a witch from a stolen rib and a communion wafer, sucking milk from neighbours' ewes and cows to feed its mistress. It resembles a lumpy grey-wool bundle on stubby legs. A comic yet nasty familiar, vulnerable if its owner is discovered and shamed.
- Lagarfljót worm: A colossal serpent said to lie in the glacial depths of Lake Lagarfljót in eastern Iceland, grown huge from a gold ring hidden beneath it. Its surfacing foretells disaster, flooding and famine. A perfect lake boss that sleeps for decades, then coils up to threaten shorelines and ferries.
- Fjörulalli: A lumbering shore monster of Icelandic coasts, appearing as a hulking, seaweed-draped brute that wanders tidal flats and hauls off those foolish enough to beachcomb at night. It is slow but tremendously strong, and weakened away from salt water. Good for coastal horror and shipwreck-salvage scenarios.
- Selma: A sea-wolf of Icelandic folklore, a seal-like beast with a canine head that haunts fjords and rocky skerries. Often tied to the tragic tale of Selma, a girl transformed into a seal who longs for the land. It can be hostile, sorrowful or protective, switching between predator and mourning kin.
### Romanian, Hungarian, Balkan
- Strigoi: A restless dead vampire of Romanian folklore that rises from an unquiet grave to drain blood and life from family and neighbours. Pale or ruddy, it may shapeshift into animals and spread plague. Staked, beheaded, or buried with garlic in its mouth to stop it, it makes a classic village-curse antagonist.
- Moroi: A living vampire of Romanian lore, a person born with a caul or cursed whose spirit leaves the body at night to feed on kin. By day the Moroi appears ordinary, even beloved, concealing a hunger. A subtle social-horror foe or tragic hero who struggles against inherited thirst.
- Pricolici: A werewolf-vampire hybrid, a wolfish ghoul that rises from the grave on moonlit nights to hunt villagers. It combines lycanthropic ferocity with undead resilience, rending flesh and drinking blood. Silver, burning, and fire-hardened stakes are its bane, making it a brutal late-game monster for gothic wildernesses.
- Vârcolac: A great wolf or wolf-like demon believed to swallow the sun or moon during eclipses, plunging the world into darkness. Sometimes also a restless undead that feeds on the living. It is best used as an apocalyptic omen creature whose appearance heralds doom unless villagers drive it off with noise and ritual.
- Zmeu: A dragon-man of Romanian fairy tales, a shapeshifting, flame-breathing ogre-king who abducts princesses and fights heroes with sorcery and brute strength. He can appear in human guise or as a winged serpent. A charismatic villain with a fortress, treasures and a weak point hidden in a magic object.
- Iele: Dancing fairies of Romanian folklore, beautiful and capricious women who gather in forests and fields at night to dance in enchanted circles. Those who see them may be struck mute, lame or mad, while those who join their dance are danced to death. They provide dangerous temptation and strange blessings.
- Muma Pădurii: The forest mother, a hideous hag who lurks in dark woods and preys on lost children, offering false shelter and bewitched food. Her appearance is warty and wild, her house hidden. She is a clever witch-trickster whom brave heroes can outwit, a gate-keeper of the wild.
- Solomonari: Weather wizards of Romania who studied at a mythical school run by the devil, riding dragons and wielding a magical book. They conjure hail, storms and rain, and can save or destroy a harvest. A powerful but mercenary spellcaster, best suited as a bribable ally or fearsome rival.
- Táltos: A Hungarian shaman born with extra teeth or fingers, chosen by spirits to heal, prophesy and wage spiritual battles. He fights rival táltos in animal forms, bull against stag, and flies in trances to the world tree. A heroic mystic who guards his people with visions and ritual drum.
- Liderc: A Hungarian will-o'-the-wisp, a flickering marsh light that lures travellers astray into bogs and rivers. It can also appear as a shape-shifting fiery being that visits people at night as a lover or chicken. A trickster hazard that rewards the wise and drowns the greedy.
- Lidérc: A shape-shifting spirit of Hungarian folklore that takes the form of a feathered creature, a lover or a sparkling flame, attaching itself to its host and bringing both wealth and ruin. It feeds on its owner's vitality, growing demanding. A seductive curse which requires an exorcism or clever trick to be rid of.
- Vukodlak: The Balkan werewolf and vampire, a cursed man who turns into a wolf or whose corpse rises as a bloodthirsty revenant. It stalks the mountain villages of the Balkans, tied to eclipses and unclean births. It can be destroyed by silver, hawthorn stake or decapitation, representing a fierce rural predator.
- Vila: A Balkan fairy, a beautiful, long-haired woman of mountains, clouds and lakes who is a protector or a perilous seductress. She can heal wounded heroes, grant gifts, or strike down those who offend her with arrows and curses. Vile when angered, she can serve as ally, mentor, or merciless foe.
- Drekavac: A screeching Balkan night creature of uncertain shape, often the ghost of an unbaptised child or a monstrous beast with a cry like a baby or hound. Its wails foretell death, and those who hear it sicken. It haunts cemeteries and crossroads, making an eerie omen enemy best fought with holy symbols.
- Zduhać: A storm guardian of Serbian and Montenegrin lore, a man born with a special spirit that leaves his body to battle storm demons in the sky. He fights hail-bringing witches and dragons to protect crops. A heroic weather warrior, vulnerable while his body sleeps in trance and defenceless.
- Kikimora (Slavic): A Slavic house spirit, often a small hag-like woman who lives behind the stove or in swamps, spinning at night. She torments untidy households with noises, tangled thread and nightmares, though a well-kept home earns her goodwill. A mischievous domestic sprite who can be bargained with or exorcised.
- Baba Roga: A horned crone of Balkan tales who prowls the forest and punishes wayward children, carrying them off in a sack to her hut. Gaunt, with iron teeth and a menacing voice, she tests trespassers with riddles and chores. A scary bogeywoman who can be outwitted by a clever, kindly child.
- Dahaka: An ancient three-headed dragon of ruin from Persian myth, born of the evil spirit and bound beneath Mount Damavand until the end of time. Six eyes burn, and it spews serpents and plague. A world-ending boss, whose eventual release threatens all creation and demands a legendary hero.
### Caucasus and Turkic
- Div: Giants of Persian and Caucasian legend, huge demonic ogres with horns, tusks and great strength, dwelling in mountain strongholds and ruins. They steal princesses, hoard treasure and war against heroes. Though brutal, they can be tricked by clever wits, making them ideal towering brutes in epic quests.
- Ejderha: The Turkic and Caucasian dragon, a vast serpentine beast with scales, wings and sometimes multiple heads that guards springs, caves and treasure. It demands tribute or maidens and hoards water in drought. A classic hero-slaying challenge, with weak points beneath its throat or in a magical sword.
- Aranyani: A forest goddess of wilderness and echoing sounds, mistress of the woodland who never sees a town. She is gentle, elusive and plentiful, feeding travellers who pass respectfully but luring the careless in circles with her echoes. An enigmatic nature spirit who rewards quiet reverence and punishes hunters.
- Shahmaran: A snake queen of Anatolian and Persian tales, half woman and half serpent, who lives in underground gardens and holds all the world's knowledge. Her blood cures any illness, but betrayal by humans brings tragedy. A wise, sorrowful sovereign who is both sought-after oracle and wronged victim.
- Al Karisi: A birth demon from Turkic and Central Asian folklore, a ghastly female spirit who attacks new mothers and infants, stealing the liver or lungs of the newborn. She is often clay-faced with long hair. Protective amulets, iron, and constant vigil keep her away, making her a menace in birth-themed horror.
- Simurgh: A gigantic benevolent bird of Persian myth, with the body of a peacock, the face of a human, and claws of a lion, who nests in the Tree of All Seeds. Ancient and wise, it heals wounds and guides heroes with feathers that summon aid. A mystical mentor and mighty ally.
- Kuyruklu: A fox spirit of Turkic folklore, a many-tailed, cunning creature that can take human guise to charm, deceive or aid. Each tail represents gained magic and age. Mischievous and shrewd, it can be a loyal companion or a treacherous seducer, depending on the respect shown and the bargain struck.
- Tepegöz: A Turkic cyclops with a single eye on his forehead and a flesh-hungry appetite, born of a shepherd and a jinn. He dwells in a cave and devours men by the dozen, with skin impervious to blades. A heroic trial-by-fire opponent, only vulnerable through his eye.
- Albasty: A nightmare woman of Turkic and Central Asian lore with long hair, pendulous breasts and clay-coloured skin, who sits on sleepers' chests and strangles them. She also attacks women in labour, stealing their breath and children. Iron, charms and fire ward her off, a pressing demon for dream-based horror.
- Asena: A mythic she-wolf, the ancestral mother of the Turkic peoples who nursed and saved a lone boy after his tribe was slaughtered, then bore ten half-wolf sons. Fierce, noble and maternal, she is a national totem symbol of strength, guidance and survival, perfect as a spirit guardian or tribal matriarch.
- Ergenekon: A legendary mountain valley, enclosed by iron cliffs, where the Turkic and Mongol peoples hid after defeat and were reborn. After four centuries they smelted the mountain open led by a grey wolf. A place of refuge, rebirth and revival, suited as a hidden homeland or lost-world setting.
- Hayk and Bel: The Armenian giant myth in which Hayk, the founding patriarch, defeats the tyrant Bel (Nimrod) with a bow at the Battle of Lake Van. The story establishes the nation's origin and ancestor-hero, with epic scale, archery and resistance to empire. A foundational tale for heroic leaders and arch-villains.
- Nart sagas: The heroic epics of the Nart warriors of the Caucasus, a proud clan of giants, sorcerers and blacksmith-heroes such as Sosruko, Batraz and Satanaya. They feature feasts, feuds, magic swords and clever tricksters who defy gods. Rich source material for warrior bands, mighty quests and tragic dooms.
- Gveleshapi: A serpent-dragon monster of Georgian folklore, a vast water-snake that lurks in rivers and lakes and rises to devour livestock and travellers, sometimes forging pacts with witches. It has a dreadful hiss and slime-covered body. It's a localized boss monster, defeated by cunning plans or a heroic dragon-slayer.
- Devs of the mountain: Ancient demonic giants dwelling in high peaks and remote caves, who rule over storms, avalanches and treasure. They are cruel and cunning, kidnap travellers, and war with heroes of old. Unlike simple brutes they are shrewd sorcerers, suiting a mountain fortress boss or a looming threat in the snowy pass.
- Kelpie of Caspian: A shape-shifting water horse of the Caspian shores, tempting weary riders to mount its dark glossy back before plunging into the depths to drown them. It may also take a handsome human form near the water's edge. A treacherous lakeside predator, bridled and tamed only with a magic bridle.
### Siberian and Central Asian
- Shaman of the Altai: A steppe mystic who drums into spirit realms, wearing a fringed, bell-hung coat and a feathered headdress to journey between worlds. He heals, divines, and mediates with ancestors and sky gods, battling hostile spirits for stolen souls. A versatile spiritual hero, healer, or morally ambiguous wanderer.
- Mongolian Khan spirit: The ghost of a ruling conqueror who guards the steppe, a mighty ancestral presence that rides on spectral horses at dusk with a phantom horde. He blesses the loyal and cuts down desecrators of sacred burial lands. A formidable spirit patron or warlord boss, bound to a hidden tomb.
- Almas: A wild man of Mongolia, a hairy, upright humanoid that roams remote mountains and deserts, shy and elusive but fiercely strong. Reported by herders, it leaves large footprints and avoids humans. A cryptid for survival expeditions, either a hostile giant or a gentle recluse that tests an explorer's compassion.
- Olgoi-khorkhoi: The Mongolian death worm, a bright-red, sausage-like creature said to lurk in the Gobi sands, spraying acid venom and killing by electrical shock at a distance. It emerges after rain. A fearsome desert ambusher that burrows beneath travellers, ideal for hazard-laden dune crossings and cryptid hunts.
- Erlik Khan: The lord of the underworld in Turkic and Mongol belief, a dark, bloated ruler who judges the dead from his black throne and torments sinners. Once the brother of creation, he now schemes against the sky. A grim, magnificent villain-god, offering bargains for souls and fearsome retribution.
- Umai: A mother goddess of Turkic and Mongolian religion who protects women, children and newborns, guiding souls into life. She is a tender yet powerful sky-borne spirit, invoked in childbirth and sacrifice. A benevolent divine patron whose favour heals, shelters and shields, and whose wrath is rare but cosmic.
- Yakut spirit: A forest lord of Yakut belief, a vast nature spirit who owns the taiga's game and rivers and must be pleased with offerings of fat and horsehair. Hunters seek its blessing; those who waste or disrespect nature face starvation. A moral guardian of the northern wilderness who can aid or ruin.
- Tungus shamans: Siberian spirit healers wearing antlers and bells, who dance and drum into trance to treat sickness, find lost souls and negotiate with spirits of the land. Their elaborate costumes carry magical power, and their journeys can be treacherous. Trusted community leaders, powerful allies, and potential rivals in spiritual duels.
- Manas: The Kyrgyz epic hero, a giant warrior-king who unites the tribes and fights Chinese and Kalmyk foes in a huge oral epic of over half a million lines. Mighty, generous and temperamental, he rides a magic horse and is guided by his wife Kanykei. A legendary champion and national icon.
- Ulgen: A benevolent sky god of Altaic belief, the creator of earth and humankind who dwells in the heavens and opposes the underworld lord Erlik. He rules a layered cosmos, receives horse sacrifices and sends shamans for guidance. A gracious and distant deity who answers earnest prayers with fortune.
- Reindeer spirits: Sacred herd guides leading souls across tundra, glowing antlered beings that emerge on auroral nights to carry shamans and the dead into the afterlife. They also protect herders from blizzards. Gentle yet otherworldly, these are perfect as mystical mounts, psychopomps, or sentinels of the frozen northern wastes.
- Ice-age mammoth ghost: A spectral, tusked giant roaming frozen plains, its great shaggy shape half-visible in snow-swirls and its trumpeting echoing from the permafrost. Locals believe it guards buried bones and punishes grave-robbers. A haunting, majestic apparition, either a wise ancient guardian or a stampeding, vengeful horror.
- Tengri: The eternal sky god of the Turkic and Mongol peoples, an all-encompassing power of heaven who grants rulers their mandate and watches over honour and oaths. He is distant, impartial and mighty, worshipped on mountaintops. A supreme deity whose blessings sanction conquerors and punish oathbreakers with storms and defeat.
- Amur tiger spirit: A forest guardian cat revered as a mountain lord, a huge golden-striped spirit that governs the taiga and judges hunters. Native peoples address it as grandfather and avoid killing it. It rewards respect with safe passage but hunts down the arrogant, making a noble, awe-inspiring protector or fearsome avenging beast.
### Indian regional and Tibetan
- Bhoot: A restless ghost in Indian belief, the spirit of someone who died violently or before their time, with backwards feet and no shadow. It haunts trees, crossroads and abandoned homes, causing fear, possession and misfortune. Exorcism, mantras, and finishing its unfinished business can set it free.
- Pishacha: A flesh-eating demon that haunts cremation grounds, a gaunt, ashen being with glowing eyes who feeds on corpses and possesses the weak-minded. It prowls at night, spreading disease and madness. Hindu mantras and sacred fire repel it, making it a gruesome graveyard foe for horror-themed adventures.
- Rakshasa: A powerful shapeshifting demon of Indian epics, with fangs, claws and sorcery, who disrupts rituals, devours humans and wages war against gods. Some are noble warriors, others mere monsters. They are strongest at night and can assume any form, offering varied antagonists from cunning schemers to towering demon-lords.
- Vetala: A vampiric spirit that inhabits corpses and haunts cemeteries, hanging upside-down from trees and asking riddles of those who carry its body. It can animate the dead and tell tales, trapping the unwary with unanswerable puzzles. A tricky, intelligent undead who tests wits as much as courage.
- Yaksha: A nature spirit of Indian myth, guardian of treasure and forests, who may be benevolent or mischievous. Male yakshas are stout and bearded servants of Kubera, while female yakshinis are lovely tree-spirits. They protect hidden hoards and grant boons or harm to the disrespectful.
- Naga: A divine serpent being of Indian, Buddhist and Southeast Asian lore, part human and part cobra, who guards underwater palaces, jewels and rain. Powerful and wise, nagas can bless or curse and are often at odds with Garuda. They make superb court intriguers, guardians or river-gods.
- Apsara: A graceful celestial dancer who enchants gods and mortals, born from the churning of the ocean and sent to distract sages from their austerities. Beautiful, musical and fickle, she moves through clouds and water. A seductive diplomat, divine emissary or temptress with both blessing and ruinous charm.
- Gandharva: A celestial musician of Indian myth, a skilled male spirit who plays in the courts of the gods and guards soma, the divine drink. Radiant and fond of music and love, he can inspire artists or enchant mortals with song. A talented bard-like figure who charms or protects.
- Kinnara: A half-bird, half-human celestial musician, often depicted as a couple devoted to each other, singing and playing instruments in Himalayan forests. They symbolize love and harmony, and appear on temple carvings. Gentle, shy creatures who offer blessings to the faithful and sorrow when separated, ideal for lyrical fantasy.
- Makara: An aquatic hybrid beast of Indian myth with the head of an elephant or crocodile and the body of a fish or serpent. It serves as the mount of the river goddess Ganga and the sea god Varuna. A mighty water guardian, often featured on temple gateways as a protective emblem.
- Jinn of Rajasthan: A desert fire spirit granting boons or playing tricks, born from smokeless flame and haunting dunes, ruined forts and wells. Some are friendly, others spiteful, appearing as whirlwinds or as humans. They honour bargains strictly, so wishes come with consequences, making them perfect for riddle-laden deals.
- Chudail: A witch ghost who walks backwards, with inverted feet, a beautiful face and a hideous true form, who lures men at night and drains their life. Usually the spirit of a woman who died in childbirth or in grief. Bound by iron and mantras, she is a deadly, tragic apparition.
- Mohini: An enchantress, the female avatar of Vishnu, who bewitches demons and gods with beauty to restore cosmic order, tricking them out of immortality nectar. Alluring and clever, she is a shapeshifting trickster whose charm is a weapon. A model for seductive diplomats, spies, or divine saviours in disguise.
- Garuda: The mighty eagle-faced king of birds and mount of Vishnu, golden-winged and blazing, sworn enemy of serpents. He stole the nectar of immortality to free his mother and consumes nagas. Swift and righteous, he serves as a celestial steed, protector, and fearsome war-spirit in the sky.
- Kumbhakarna: The sleeping giant brother of Ravana, a colossal rakshasa cursed to sleep for six months at a time, then wake ravenously hungry. Honourable despite his demon kin, he fights fiercely for his brother in the Ramayana war. A tragic gargantuan whose awakening is an event of towering destruction.
- Ravana: The ten-headed king of Lanka, a scholar, devotee of Shiva and great warrior who abducts Sita and wars with Rama. His ten heads reflect knowledge and ego, and he commands magic aerial chariots. A complex, charismatic antagonist: brilliant, proud, and doomed by his own desire.
- Hanuman: The monkey-god of strength and devotion, son of the wind, who leaps oceans, shrinks or grows at will, and carries a mountain to heal Lakshmana. Loyal servant of Rama, he is humble, clever and nearly invincible. An ideal heroic ally and champion, powered by faith and fearless loyalty.
- Tibetan yeti (Migoi): The wild snowman of the Himalayas, a towering, shaggy biped glimpsed on high passes with enormous footprints and a chilling whistle. Sherpas regard it with awe and fear, sometimes blaming it for stolen yaks. A cryptid for mountaineering stories, hostile or reclusive depending on how intruders behave.
- Rinpoche: A reincarnate lama of Tibetan Buddhism, recognised in childhood as the rebirth of a revered teacher, and trained to lead monasteries and guide disciples. Calm, learned and compassionate, he wields meditation, ritual and wisdom more than weapons. A revered mentor, spiritual leader, or political figure carrying the memory of past lives.
- Dharmapala: A wrathful protector of the Buddhist teachings, a fierce deity with fanged mouth, flaming hair and necklace of skulls who tramples ignorance and enemies of the dharma. Though terrifying, he is compassionate in purpose. A powerful divine guardian summoned by rituals to destroy obstacles and shield the faithful.
- Mahakala: A dark protector in Tibetan Buddhism, a black, multi-armed wrathful form of compassion that devours obstacles and demons, often shown with a flaying knife and skull cup. Revered in monasteries as a guardian of tradition and wealth. A fearsome ally for sacred sites, he rewards devotion and crushes sacrilege.
- Tulpa: A being created purely by concentrated thought and meditation in Tibetan mystical tradition, a manifest thought-form that can appear physical and act independently. It may grow beyond the creator's control, becoming a companion or menace. A fascinating concept for illusionists, mind-mages and tragic experiments in will.
- Thangka demon: A fierce painted guardian of temple scrolls, a vividly coloured fanged figure with bulging eyes who protects sacred images and teachings. In stories the painting may come to life against thieves and defilers. A decorative-turned-deadly sentinel that stands watch over monasteries and punishes those who disrespect the sacred.
- Himalayan ghost: A restless mountain wraith haunting passes and snow, the spirit of lost climbers, pilgrims or traders who froze or fell from the heights. It moans in the wind, lures travellers off the trail, and hides in whiteouts. Cold, pitiable and deadly, it suits survival horror in high altitude settings.
### Southeast Asia
- Phi (Thai ghost): The general Thai word for ghosts and spirits, from restless dead to nature wardens haunting trees, houses and crossroads. They appear as pale figures, lights or whispers. Offerings at spirit houses appease them, making them ideal omens, quest-givers or hazards in village settings.
- Krasue (Thai): A floating female head trailing glistening entrails, glowing faintly as she drifts through rice fields at night. She hungers for blood and filth, preying on livestock and newborns. Salt, thorny barriers and fishing nets repel her, and by day she hides as an ordinary woman.
- Nang Tani (banana tree ghost): A gentle but fearsome young woman's spirit dwelling in banana trees, often scented with jasmine and dressed in green. She may protect villagers who honour her, yet punishes anyone who fells her tree or disturbs her haunt. Offerings of cloth and flowers placate her.
- Mae Nak: A devoted wife who died in childbirth but refused to leave her husband, passing as living for years while her ghostly arm stretches impossibly long. Famed from Bangkok's Phra Khanong legend, she is tragic and terrifying, only subdued by exorcism or her husband's heartbreak.
- Phi Pop: A hungry possessing ghost that seizes a living host and devours the entrails of others, driving communities to expel the afflicted family. It spreads fear, suspicion and scapegoating. Monks, charms and exorcists can drive it out, making it a chilling social horror.
- Naga (Thai): A serpent being of rivers and the underworld, sometimes many-headed, guarding treasure and lending its form to temple stairways. It may grant rain and wealth to the pious or flood the land when offended. Capable of human disguise, it suits as ally, guardian or boss.
- Garuda (Thai): A mighty eagle-headed, golden-winged being who serves as the royal mount of Vishnu and a symbol of the Thai crown. Eternal enemy of nagas, he is swift, radiant and fierce. As a creature or patron he offers flight, divine authority and devastating dives.
- Nat spirits (Burmese): A pantheon of thirty-seven spirits, mostly heroes and royals who met violent deaths and were deified. Venerated at festivals with spirit mediums dancing in trance, they can bless or curse households. Slighted nats bring sickness, so they work well as capricious patrons.
- Weikza (Burmese): A Burmese magician-saint who has mastered alchemy, meditation and occult arts to prolong life and gain supernatural powers. Living in remote caves or flitting across the land, a weikza can fly, heal and vanish. They serve as mentors, enigmatic recluses or rivals seeking immortality.
- Zawgyi alchemist (Burmese): A wizened Burmese sorcerer who brews elixirs from mercury, herbs and minerals to attain eternal youth and magical power. Usually pictured in a tall hat with an alchemical flask, he can transmute metals and cure disease. Plots revolve around his secretive formulas and dangerous experiments.
- Ma Da (water ghost): A Vietnamese drowned spirit lurking in rivers and ponds, grasping at swimmers to pull them under so it may take their place and be reborn. Pallid and slimy, it clings to the shore. Rituals, offerings and fear of deep water keep villagers vigilant.
- Thanh Giong: A legendary Vietnamese boy hero who grew into a giant overnight, rode an iron horse and wielded an iron staff to crush invading Yin forces. After victory he flew to heaven. He represents national defence, miraculous growth and humble origins, suiting a champion archetype.
- Ma Lai (Vietnamese): A female head-and-entrails vampire spirit, kin to the Krasue, who detaches from her body to hunt at night for blood. By day she hides as a normal woman. Destroying or hiding her body kills her, giving investigators a clear weakness and a tense hunt.
- Tinh (fox spirit): A shape-shifting fox demon that turns into a beautiful woman to seduce, deceive and drain men, accumulating power across centuries. Cunning, vain and patient, it can be tricked by exposing its reflection or tail. A fine manipulative villain or tragic antiheroine.
- Aswang (Filipino): A notorious Filipino shapeshifter who appears as a gentle neighbor by day and a hungry predator by night, taking the form of a dog, pig or bat to devour the sick, pregnant and dead. Garlic, salt and holy objects ward it. Paranoia drives the stories.
- Manananggal (Filipino): A beautiful woman whose upper body separates at the waist to fly on bat-like wings, long tongue seeking sleeping pregnant women and foetuses. Sprinkling salt or ash on her severed lower half prevents her returning, killing her at dawn. Creepy, visual and hunter-friendly.
- Tikbalang (Filipino): A tall, lean horse-headed trickster of mountains and forests who leads travellers astray, disorienting them until they turn their clothes inside out. Fast and strong, it is sometimes tamed by plucking a magic hair from its mane. A mischievous guardian of wild places.
- Kapre (Filipino): A towering, hairy, dark-skinned tree giant who sits smoking an enormous cigar in the branches of old acacia or balete trees. Mostly benign, he plays tricks, leads walkers in circles and sometimes befriends humans. Gentle yet dangerous when angered, he guards ancient groves.
- Tiyanak (Filipino): A vengeful spirit of an unbaptized infant that mimics a crying baby in the jungle to lure kindly travellers, then reveals fangs and claws to devour them. Turning clothes inside out or presenting sacred items repels it. A haunting, tragic ambush monster.
- Engkanto (Filipino): An enchanting, beautiful, fair-skinned spirit of forest, mountain and sea who seduces mortals into their hidden realm, causing vanishings and mysterious illnesses. Capable of great kindness or cruelty, they court humans with gifts. Bargains and taboos define encounters, and returning victims are often changed.
- Diwata (Filipino): A radiant nature deity or fairy guardian of forests, mountains and rivers, who grants blessings or illness depending on respect shown. Often depicted as an ethereal woman with healing and weather powers. She can serve as a patron, quest-giver or fickle ally of heroes.
- Bakunawa (Filipino): A colossal sea-dragon serpent said to swallow the moon, causing eclipses, which people drive away by banging pots and drums. Originally having seven moons devoured, it embodies cosmic threat. A towering raid boss, with sky and ocean domains and ancient mythic scale.
- Sarimanok (Filipino): A legendary, brightly plumed rooster-bird of the Maranao people, carrying a fish in its beak and symbolizing good fortune, prosperity and power. Its feathers are ornate, resplendent and colourful. A sacred emblem, it might serve as a rare blessing, omen or prized treasure.
- Duwende (Filipino): A small, wizened dwarf-like spirit living in anthills, mounds and old houses, who bestows luck on those who respect it and sickness on those who trample its home. Wearing red or black, they are capricious and territorial. Offerings and polite phrases keep the peace.
- White Lady (Filipino): A ghostly woman in white, often killed by tragedy or violence, who haunts roads, bridges, schools and old houses in the Philippines. Appearing silently or weeping, she may lure drivers or warn of death. Urban-legend flavour makes her an easy hook for ghost stories.
- Pontianak (Indonesian and Malay): A vengeful vampire ghost of a woman who died in childbirth, announced by a sweet frangipani scent and a baby's cry. She hides in banana trees, tears out victims' stomachs with long nails, and is subdued by hammering a nail into her neck.
- Genderuwo (Indonesian and Malay): A large, hairy ape-like Javanese spirit living in old trees and abandoned buildings, capable of impersonating a husband to seduce wives. Strong, lustful and trickish, he frightens passers-by with stones and laughter. Charms, prayer and incense are common countermeasures.
- Kuntilanak (Indonesian and Malay): The Indonesian counterpart of the Pontianak, a long-haired woman in white, drifting through night trees with a laugh that gets quieter the nearer she is. She preys on pregnant women and men alone. A nail pushed into her neck tames her.
- Tuyul (Indonesian and Malay): A small, bald child-like spirit enslaved by a wealthy master to steal money from neighbors, who is repaid with milk or toys. Mischievous and loyal, it creeps into houses at night. Getting rid of it requires trapping it or exposing its owner.
- Leyak (Indonesian and Malay): A Balinese witch who flies at night as a disembodied head with trailing organs, dwelling in graveyards and feeding on newborns and corpses. By day she appears as an ordinary person. Fought by the Barong, she supplies a ready antagonist with dark magical reach.
- Barong (Indonesian and Malay): A lion-like protective spirit and king of good spirits in Balinese myth, with a shaggy mane and snapping jaws, performed by two dancers. He wages eternal war against Rangda and the forces of evil. A benevolent guardian, he embodies balance and communal protection.
- Rangda (Indonesian and Malay): The fearsome queen of witches and demons in Balinese mythology, with bulging eyes, a lolling fiery tongue, fangs and tangled hair. She commands leyaks and spreads plague, yet is also a fierce protector. Her duel with the Barong is eternal and unresolved.
- Penanggalan (Indonesian and Malay): A Malay vampire whose head and trailing entrails fly from her body at night to suck the blood of newborns and mothers. She steeps her innards in vinegar, so she smells sour. Thorny branches around windows ensnare her, and sunrise forces her home.
- Orang bunian (Indonesian and Malay): The invisible, beautiful hidden folk of Malay forests, dwelling in unseen villages parallel to ours. They sometimes abduct humans to live among them, who return after what feels like days but are years. Their gifts and courtesy mask a world with its own rules.
- Hantu Raya (Indonesian and Malay): The greatest of Malay ghosts, a powerful servant spirit inherited through generations that can mimic its owner perfectly, lend supernatural wealth and perform dark tasks. Its price is steep, binding families into dangerous pacts. A superb source of faustian bargains, doubles and betrayals.
- Barong (Balinese): The benevolent, lion-like guardian of Bali, a shaggy-maned spirit danced by two performers to ward off plague and drive away evil. Beloved by villagers, he is sacred, protective and playful. Opposite to Rangda, his presence blesses ceremonies, defends communities and symbolizes the light side of cosmic balance.
- Rangda (Balinese): The Balinese demon queen of witches, a hideous widow with fangs, fiery tongue, and long claws who leads armies of leyaks. Terrifying and powerful, she personifies disease, death and chaos. In ritual dance she is both villain and necessary opposite of the Barong.
- Leyak (Balinese): The Balinese black-magic practitioner who can detach her head with dangling organs and fly through the night in search of blood and the unborn. Disguised by day among villagers, she is hidden menace. Barong rituals and protective offerings keep her at bay, delivering fine horror.
- Neak Pean serpent (Cambodian): The entwined naga serpents encircling the sacred island temple of Neak Pean at Angkor, said to heal illness with its waters. They embody water, renewal and divine protection. In play, they might guard a healing spring or a temple, rewarding pilgrims and punishing desecrators.
- Ap (Cambodian): A Khmer night-flying spirit, a witch-like woman whose head and entrails detach to prey on the living, especially the sick and weak. Villagers fear her glow and rely on charms and thorns. A cousin of the Krasue and Penanggalan, she adds regional flavour to vampire legends.
- Phi Kong Koi (Laotian ghost): A Laotian one-legged hopping ghost that feeds on blood and haunts rural nights, drawing victims in with eerie hops and a pale glow. Said to attack lone travellers, it can be driven away by charms, monks and bright lights. Simple but unnerving and memorable.
### Ainu and Okinawan
- Kamuy: The spirit-gods of the Ainu, who inhabit animals, plants, tools and natural forces and visit the human world in disguise. Respect, ritual and thanks keep them favourable. Each kamuy has its own domain and temper, offering a rich pantheon of patrons, tricksters and wrathful powers.
- Kimun Kamuy: The bear god of the Ainu, a revered mountain spirit whose bear form visits humans as a gift of meat and fur. Honoured in the iomante ceremony, which sends his spirit home with prayers. He is powerful, noble and demanding of respect from hunters.
- Akkorokamui: A colossal, red-hued giant octopus of Hokkaido's Funka Bay, with tentacles that drag boats under and a dread of the sea. It can regrow limbs and devour fishermen, yet also has a place in Ainu worship. A towering sea boss, vast, ancient and unknowable.
- Kijimuna: A mischievous red-haired Okinawan tree sprite living in old banyan trees, who plays pranks, fishes at night and may bring prosperity to those he befriends. He fears the octopus and the smell of burning. Charming yet touchy, he rewards kindness and punishes insults.
- Shisa: A guardian lion-dog statue perched on Okinawan rooftops and gateways, with one mouth open to drive off evil and one closed to hold fortune in. Fierce yet welcoming, it can come alive in stories. As a protector it makes a loyal construct or ward.
- Uminchu: A sea-hunter spirit of Okinawan fishing lore, an ancestor-like presence guarding the reef fishers and channelling the sea's moods. Calm waters and good catches follow respectful offerings; storms and drownings follow neglect. A mariner's patron or spectral guide for island seafaring stories.
- Nuyukitsune: An ancient fox spirit with trickster powers, wise with centuries, capable of shape-shifting, illusions and uncanny insight. Playful, cunning and sometimes dangerous, it tests mortals with riddles and pranks. It might serve as an enigmatic mentor, rival or capricious guardian of old places.
- Yuta: An Okinawan folk medium, usually a woman, who communicates with ancestors and spirits, diagnoses spiritual illness and performs rituals for the dead. Called upon in crisis, her trance carries messages and warnings. She works well as a spiritual guide, healer or reluctant oracle.
- Hitotsume-kozo: A one-eyed child goblin of Japanese folklore, a harmless but startling spirit that leaps out at night walkers to give them a fright. Short, cheerful and mischievous, it rarely harms. It adds light spookiness to roadside encounters and can serve as a minor guide or messenger.
### Hebrew and Kabbalistic
- Golem: A man-shaped being of clay animated by sacred Hebrew letters or a divine name placed in its mouth. Immensely strong, obedient and mute, it protects its maker yet may run amok. Erasing a letter, turning emet (truth) into met (death), destroys it.
- Dybbuk: The restless soul of a dead person that clings to a living host, speaking through them in a changed voice and driving them to madness. Born of unfinished business or sin, it can be cast out by a rabbi's exorcism. A tragic possession tale with strong horror.
- Lilith: A primordial demoness of Jewish folklore, said to be Adam's first wife who refused submission and fled to the Red Sea. She stalks infants and tempts sleeping men, with wings and long hair. Amulets bearing angels' names protect against her, making her a powerful, ambiguous figure.
- Leviathan: A colossal primordial sea serpent of Hebrew scripture and legend, so vast that its coils ring the world and its breath boils the sea. At the end of days it is said to be slain and served as a feast. A titan boss and symbol of chaos.
- Behemoth: A massive primeval land beast of Hebrew lore, paired against Leviathan and Ziz, said to graze a thousand hills and drink a river dry. Unstoppable and ancient, it embodies earthly might. As a creature, it is a living mountain whose rampage threatens whole realms.
- Ziz: A gigantic bird of Hebrew legend whose wingspan blots out the sun and shields the world from storms. Ruler of the sky as Behemoth is of land and Leviathan of sea, it also has protective instincts. A majestic and terrifying avian titan for sky encounters.
- Shedim: Hebrew demon spirits that hover between angels and men, neither fully divine nor fully mortal, often created at twilight before the first Sabbath. They roam ruins and wilderness, harassing the unwary. Some are mischievous, others deadly, making them versatile as tricksters, tempters or minions.
- Malakh: The Hebrew word for angel, a messenger and servant of the divine will sent to guide, test, warn or smite. Appearances range from plain wanderers to blazing beings. As characters they embody authority and purpose, and are seldom gentle, since their errand matters more than comfort.
- Sefirot guardians: Ten radiant sentinels of the mystic tree of life in Kabbalah, each embodying an aspect of the divine such as wisdom, mercy, judgment and beauty. They guard the paths of ascent, testing seekers. Each can be a themed boss, trial or gate in a mystical journey.
- Rabbi Loew: The sixteenth-century Maharal of Prague, legendary for sculpting a clay golem to defend the Jewish quarter from persecution. A scholar, mystic and statesman, he commands deep learning and sacred names. As a hero he is a wise maker whose creation threatens to outgrow him.
- Ruach: The Hebrew word for spirit, wind or breath, the animating divine force that moves over the waters and fills prophets. It can be gentle inspiration or storming power. As a character or force it offers possession, prophecy, weather magic and a haunting presence that cannot be seen.
- Ba'al Shem: A wonder-working healer and mystic who uses divine names to cure illness, banish demons and perform miracles, as with the Baal Shem Tov. Humble yet powerful, he travels among the poor. A good archetype for a holy healer, exorcist or folk sage with sacred knowledge.
- Mazzikin: Harmful spirits and demons of Jewish folklore that lurk in unclean places, shadows and ruins, causing sickness, accidents and nightmares. Invisible and numerous, they cluster around the careless. Blessings, amulets and prayers keep them at bay, making them ideal swarm enemies or ever-present hazards.
- Ofanim: The wheel-angels of Jewish tradition, interlocking blazing wheels full of eyes that move beside the divine chariot. Awesome, strange and tireless, they are among the highest orders. Their alien appearance makes them striking guardians, otherworldly judges or bewildering heavenly sentries.
- Seraphim: Six-winged burning angels who sing before the divine throne, calling holy, holy, holy, and whose fire purifies the lips of prophets. Overwhelming in radiance and devotion, they are the highest messengers. They suit a role as divine guardians, purgers of sin or terrifying heralds.
### North African and Berber
- Ghoul: A shape-changing desert demon that haunts graveyards and lonely roads, luring travellers with false voices and feasting on corpses and the unwary. It appears as a hyena or hideous woman. Cunning and ravenous, it is defeated by a single decisive blow, as a second revives it.
- Ifrit: A powerful, fiery jinn of cunning and might, often a spirit of the dead or a master of smoke and flame. Proud, vengeful and grandiose, it can be bound by Solomon's seal or clever bargains. A strong adversary, wish-granting menace or tragic figure in Arabian tales.
- Marid: The mightiest and most arrogant class of jinn, usually dwelling in the sea and capable of vast feats of magic and destruction. Proud and rebellious, they resist binding and defy humans. Only the greatest sorcerers can command them, so they serve as formidable villains or reluctant, dangerous allies.
- Aisha Qandisha: A seductive jinn of Moroccan lore, a beautiful woman with goat or camel hooves who lures men to love and madness near rivers and springs. Possessing and tormenting her victims, she is placated through trance rituals by the Hamadsha brotherhood. Alluring, vengeful and dangerous, she embodies temptation.
- Teghiwin: A Berber ghostly woman spirit of the mountains, long-haired and pale, who wanders passes and ravines luring herders or terrifying travellers. Sometimes sorrowful and sometimes deadly, she haunts places of old tragedy. A moody mountain apparition for ambushes, omens or tragic backstory.
- Tamawayt: A shape-shifting trickster spirit of Berber tales who takes human or animal form to test, tease and deceive. Clever and unpredictable, it rewards cleverness and punishes greed. It makes an excellent folkloric guide, rival or puzzle-giver whose true nature is hard to pin down.
- Berber sorceress: A mountain witch of the Atlas who brews charms, curses and remedies from herbs, bones and incantations, serving as feared healer and cursemonger. Isolated yet influential, villagers seek her aid in secret. She is a strong ambiguous figure, ally or antagonist depending on price.
- Sand jinn: A desert spirit that whips up storms and mirages, leading caravans astray and burying the unwary beneath dunes. It appears as whirlwinds, vanishing oases and whispers on the wind. Respect and charms offer some safety, making it an environmental hazard with personality and malice.
- Bori spirits (North African): The spirits of the Bori possession cult found across Hausa and North African communities, each with distinct personality, domain and demand. Mediums host them in dance and trance to heal, seek counsel or appease them. They offer a lively pantheon of capricious, powerful and human-like spirits.
- Anzar: The Berber rain god, a benevolent sky spirit tied to storms and springtime fertility, honoured in ceremonies where villagers pray for rain with a ladle doll. Said to appear as a rainbow, he feeds crops. A generous but fickle patron, offended by drought or neglect.
- Touareg desert lord: A veiled nomad chieftain of the Sahara, commanding camel caravans and clan warriors across vast sands. Proud, honourable and mysterious, he wears indigo robes and carries sword and shield. He is an excellent noble, ally or rival in desert journeys, steeped in hospitality and codes.
- Nile spirit: A river guardian of flood and fertile silt, embodying the life-giving yearly inundation that feeds Egypt. Benevolent when honoured, destructive when slighted, it can appear as a bearded figure, crocodile or current. A fine patron for river realms, with blessings of plenty and wrath of drought.
### Central and East African
- Enkai (sky god): The Maasai supreme sky god, who has dual aspects: benevolent Engai Narok, black god of rain, and wrathful Engai Nanyokie, red god of drought and lightning. Giver of cattle and life, he is distant yet attentive. Prayers, sacrifices and ethical living shape his favour.
- Buda (evil eye): An Ethiopian figure of the evil eye, a blacksmith or tanner believed to transform into a hyena and curse others with a glance, causing sickness and misfortune. Feared and shunned, they are blamed for illness. Amulets and healers counter it, offering social tension and subtle menace.
- Zar spirits: Ethiopian and East African spirits that possess people, particularly women, causing illness and strange behavior until appeased through music, dance and coffee ceremonies. Each zar has name and demands. They make ideal sources of possession plots and memorable named spirits with personalities.
- Qole: An Ethiopian spirit-ancestor that speaks through mediums, often tied to the Oromo and demanding offerings and ritual. It guards the lineage, gives counsel and punishes neglect. As a presence it lends ancestral authority and oracle potential, with local rituals and shrines shaping encounters.
- Kalanoro: A small, hairy, humanlike forest creature of Madagascar with backward feet, who steals rice and hides in the woods. Elusive and shy, it may be bargained with using offerings. Its tricks and secrecy make it an ideal puckish forest dweller and local legend.
- Tsiboka: A Malagasy spirit or monster associated with a river-dwelling creature or rain of stories, feared by travellers and fishers. Shrouded in oral tradition, it is flexible in form. Treat it as a mysterious water hazard with local taboos, offerings and unexplained disappearances to investigate.
- Mokele-mbembe: A legendary Congo River basin creature, a long-necked, sauropod-like beast said to haunt the Likouala swamps and overturn boats. Never captured and hotly debated, it fuels cryptid expeditions. Huge, elusive and territorial, it is a perfect lost-world monster for swamp exploration.
- Mami Wata: A water spirit worshipped across West and Central Africa, a mermaid-like woman with snakes and mirror, bringing wealth, beauty and healing to devotees, but drowning the disloyal. Seductive, powerful and capricious, she bridges sea and city. A patron of fortune, trade and danger.
- Popobawa: A bat-winged, one-eyed shadowy spirit of Zanzibar that attacks sleepers at night, said to sodomize men and menace families, spreading panic. Once appeased only by telling others, it feeds on fear. A modern folkloric terror that suits paranoia-driven horror.
- Zimwi: A Swahili ogre or monstrous spirit that devours children and lures victims with a clever voice or disguise. Typically outwitted by quick-thinking youngsters in cautionary tales. Cannibalistic and gullible, it works as a fairy-tale villain, stalking tales of wit over brawn.
- Shetani: A Swahili spirit or devil, often mischievous or malevolent, causing sickness, accidents and possessions, and haunting lonely places. Capable of many forms, it demands rituals and exorcisms to appease or expel. A versatile antagonist, tempter or source of unexplained misfortune.
- Nyami Nyami (river god): The Tonga river god of the Zambezi, a serpent-bodied, fish-headed guardian whose anger split a people when the Kariba Dam was built. Protective of the river and its people, he brings floods and earthquakes. Proud and ancient, he anchors environmental myths.
- Tikoloshe (Bantu): A small, mischievous water sprite summoned by sorcerers to harm enemies, said to sneak into bedrooms and cause illness or death. Villagers raise their beds on bricks to avoid it. Invisible when it swallows a pebble, it is a vivid, creepy household menace.
- Mhondoro (lion spirit): A royal ancestral spirit of the Shona that takes the form of a lion and possesses mediums to guide kings, bring rain and protect the land. Revered and powerful, it demands moral order. A majestic guardian and oracle central to political and spiritual life.
- Akamba witch: A wise or malevolent sorceress of Kenyan Akamba lore, trading in charms, curses and healing, her power inherited or learned. Respected and feared, she may protect the village or poison it. A morally ambiguous figure for quests, bargains or accusations in a community.
- Ngai (Kikuyu): The Kikuyu supreme god, who dwells on Mount Kenya, the sacred mountain, and shapes the people, land and rains. Distant but attentive, he is addressed in prayers under the fig tree. As a patron he governs fertility, law and fate, with the mountain as his throne.
### Southern African
- Impundulu (Zulu): The lightning bird of Zulu belief, a huge black-and-white bird that brings storms and acts as a witch's familiar, its blood and fat used in dark magic. It can take human shape to seduce. Dangerous, glamorous and tied to witch-hunt tension.
- Tokoloshe (Zulu): A dwarfish water spirit summoned by sorcerers to terrorize enemies, creeping into homes to cause misery and death. Vanishes by swallowing a stone, so nobody sees it. Raising beds on bricks prevents harm. A creeping, sinister household menace of Zulu folklore.
- Inkanyamba (storm serpent): A gigantic, horse-headed serpent of Zulu legend dwelling in waterfalls and pools in KwaZulu-Natal, said to whip up tornadoes and storms when angered. Revered and feared, it demands respect and ritual. A strong weather elemental, a boss guarding a mist-shrouded gorge.
- Umkhovu: A reanimated corpse enslaved by a sorcerer, stripped of its tongue and mind and made to do evil by night. Mute, grotesque and relentless, it bows to its master's will. It supplies a classic undead servant, and its fate evokes pity as well as fear.
- Mamlambo: A river monster of the Mthatha River, said to have a horse's head, a crocodile body and snaky tail, giving wealth to its owner at deadly price. Sorcerers use it as a familiar demanding sacrifice. A gruesome patron and an ominous river legend.
- Hili-bird (Xhosa): A Xhosa lore bird associated with magic and omens, appearing as a great black bird whose shriek foretells death or sorcery. Often a witch's familiar, it flits across moonlit hills. A harbinger of dark fate, it suits an eerie omen or minor magical servant.
- Kaggen (mantis trickster): The San trickster-creator, a praying mantis who made the eland and the world, shifting between wise god and clumsy fool. He tricks, creates and repairs through absurdity. His cleverness and unpredictability make him a lovable, chaotic patron and a source of origin myths.
- Gauwa (San): The San god of death and evil, a dark spirit who sows sickness and malice and rivals the trickster Kaggen. He lurks beyond the firelight and tempts the unwary toward ruin. A brooding adversary, he is a menacing but mythic embodiment of death.
- Kholumolumo (Basotho): A monstrous giant of Basotho legend, a devourer who swallowed people and cattle whole until released by a brave hero cutting him open. Gluttonous and huge, he is the ultimate threat to communities. A classic swallower monster, whose belly holds a hidden world of survivors.
- Ndadzi (Venda): A Venda water spirit or serpent associated with sacred pools and rain, guarding the fertility of the land and demanding offerings. Linked to the legendary lake Fundudzi, it holds the community in reverence. Offended, it withholds rain or drowns trespassers, giving it strong spiritual authority.
- Zwidutwane (Venda): Small, one-legged, one-armed Venda forest dwarfs who snatch children or lead travellers astray in the woods, often tied to witchcraft and strange pranks. Shy and mischievous, they fear bright light. They add folkloric weirdness to forest travel and curious cautionary stories.
- Modjadji (Ndebele rain queen): The legendary Rain Queen of the Balobedu, a hereditary female ruler believed to command clouds and bring rain through secret rites. Living in seclusion, she is revered by neighbouring kings. A potent figure of magical sovereignty, her power ties a kingdom's harvest to her life.
- Heitsi-eibib (Khoikhoi): The Khoikhoi hero and trickster who died and was reborn many times, leaving stone cairns as graves, and who defeated monsters and a cannibal giant. Magical, resilient and clever, he blends ancestor, hero and sorcerer. He is perfect as a legendary trickster champion.
### West African empires and traditions
- Sundiata (hero king): The founder of the Mali Empire, a lame child who rose to heal, stand and defeat the sorcerer-king Sumanguru at Kirina. His epic is sung by griots. A heroic underdog with great destiny, he embodies resilience, leadership and a kingdom's origin story.
- Griot (Mali): A hereditary West African bard, historian and praise-singer who preserves genealogies, epics and counsel through song and kora music. Respected and sometimes feared for their words, they advise kings and shape reputations. A superb lore-keeper, diplomat or storyteller companion with social power.
- Askia (Songhai): The great Songhai emperor Askia Muhammad, who expanded the empire, reformed administration and made a famed pilgrimage to Mecca. A devout, shrewd statesman, he promoted scholarship and trade. He fits as a regal patron, strategist or historical model of a wise conqueror.
- Timbuktu scholar (Songhai): A learned jurist, astronomer or manuscript-keeper of fabled Timbuktu, whose libraries held thousands of volumes of law, science and poetry. Wise, devout and well-travelled, he advises rulers and guards precious texts. An excellent sage, quest-giver or keeper of lost knowledge.
- Amazons of Dahomey (Benin): The fearless all-female royal warriors of the Kingdom of Dahomey, trained from youth, disciplined and renowned for ferocity in battle. Armed with muskets, machetes and blades, they were the king's elite. They make powerful allies, rivals and iconic heroic soldiers.
- Oba (Benin): The divine king of the Kingdom of Benin, ruler of bronze-casting artisans, a sacred figure who holds spiritual and political authority. Surrounded by ritual and court splendour, he commands warriors and priests. He is a majestic ruler, patron and central figure of court intrigue.
- Asante warriors (Ashanti): Fierce soldiers of the Asante Empire, organised in disciplined armies and rallied around the Golden Stool, the symbol of the nation. They fight with muskets, swords and shields. Loyal, formidable and proud, they supply strong soldiers, defenders and tactical foes.
- Anansi (Ashanti): The spider trickster of Akan lore, who won all the world's stories from the sky god through cunning and now spins tales. Clever, greedy and mischievous, he outwits stronger foes. A beloved trickster hero or schemer who thrives on wit, wordplay and bargains.
- Shango (Orisha): The Yoruba orisha of thunder, lightning and kingship, wielding a double-headed axe and quick to anger. Charismatic, vain and powerful, he was a legendary king of Oyo before becoming a god. A flamboyant storm patron, warrior and sovereign for dramatic, fiery heroes.
- Oya (Orisha): The Yoruba orisha of winds, storms, death and transformation, a fierce warrior queen who guards cemeteries and rules the Niger River. She sweeps change and wields lightning with Shango. Ferocious and protective, she is a rich patron of rebirth, tempests and warrior women.
- Ogun (Orisha): The Yoruba orisha of iron, war and labour, a blacksmith and hunter who clears the path with his machete. Fierce, solitary and exacting, he is patron of craftsmen and soldiers. A fitting archetype of the forge, battle and the price of progress.
- Yemoja (Orisha): The Yoruba orisha mother of waters, protector of women and children, associated with the Ogun River and the sea. Nurturing yet fierce when slighted, she gives fertility and can drown the wicked. A majestic maternal guardian and a deity of oceans and families.
- Eshu (Orisha): The Yoruba orisha trickster and messenger, guardian of crossroads who carries offerings between humans and gods. Mischievous, unpredictable and enforcing balance, he rewards respect and punishes carelessness. A pivotal guide, chaos agent or gatekeeper, essential to opening and closing any path.
- Ogbanje (Igbo): A child-spirit that repeatedly dies and is reborn to the same mother, tormenting a family with grief until its hidden iyi-uwa token is found and destroyed. Often precocious and unsettling, it tests parents. A haunting tale of cyclical loss with a clear way to break the curse.
- Ala (Igbo): The Igbo earth goddess of morality, fertility and the underworld, guardian of law and the ancestors buried in her soil. She enforces taboos and punishes crimes against the land. A stern yet nurturing mother figure, she ties community ethics to the ground.
- Nommo (Dogon): Ancestral water spirits of the Dogon, amphibious twin beings said to have descended from the sky and taught knowledge of the cosmos. Often shown as fish-tailed or serpentine, they renew life and order. A mysterious, otherworldly patron of creation, wisdom and the sacred waters.
- Mawu-Lisa (Fon): The Fon dual creator deity, Mawu the moon-mother and Lisa the sun-father, who together shaped the world and rule through lesser gods. Balanced, cosmic and benevolent, their union binds opposites. They provide a majestic creator pair, patrons of harmony and the grand order of nature.
- Bori spirits (Hausa): The spirits of the Hausa Bori possession cult, who ride mediums in dance and drum trance, bringing healing, guidance or affliction. Each spirit has a personality, name and demands. They offer a colourful pantheon, and their mediums serve as healers, oracles and social outsiders.
- Fulani herders: Nomadic cattle people of the Sahel who roam with vast herds, valuing poetry, endurance and pastoral freedom. Proud, graceful and skilled with animals, they carry staffs and travel the savannah. They suit as wandering allies, guides, traders or guardians of drovers' roads and wells.
- Tuareg: Veiled, blue-robed caravan warriors of the Sahara, masters of desert navigation and trade, famed for indigo veils and swords. Honourable, fierce and mysterious, they guide caravans across vast dunes and defend their clans. Excellent as desert guides, raiders, nobles or rivals bound by custom and hospitality.
- Kano warrior: An armored cavalry fighter of the Hausa city state of Kano, mounted in quilted padding and chain, wielding spear and sword behind great walls. Disciplined and prestigious, he serves the emir. A heavy, imposing soldier archetype for caravan escorts, sieges and sultanate campaigns.
### Native American regions
- Raven: Trickster and culture hero of Pacific Northwest peoples, a shape-shifting black bird who stole the sun, stars and moon to bring light to the world. Greedy, clever and endlessly curious, he works as a charming quest-giver whose bargains always carry a cost, and whose pranks can backfire.
- Thunderbird (Pacific Northwest): Colossal supernatural bird whose wingbeats roll thunder and whose blinking eyes flash lightning. A powerful, proud protector spirit who battles water serpents and underworld beasts, it can be a boss, an ally summoned by worthy heroes, or a storm that punishes disrespect.
- Sasquatch (Pacific Northwest): Towering, shaggy forest-dweller of Coast Salish tradition, rarely seen and often smelled first. Gentle but fiercely private, it guards remote wilderness, leaves enormous tracks, and hurls stones at intruders. A fine stealth-avoidance encounter, a reluctant guide, or a hunted secret.
- Dzunukwa (wild woman): Giant, black-skinned cannibal ogress of Kwakwaka'wakw story, with pendulous lips and a basket for carrying stolen children. Drowsy and dim-witted, she is easily tricked, yet her house holds vast copper wealth. A deadly forest hag who can be outwitted for treasure.
- Kushtaka: Shape-shifting land otter spirit of Tlingit and Tsimshian lore that lures drowning or lost people with cries like a baby or a woman. It transforms victims into otter-people unless they use fire, copper or dog's urine. A cunning shoreline predator for fog-bound coastal tales.
- Sisiutl (double-headed serpent): Fearsome sea serpent of Kwakwaka'wakw belief with a snake head at each end and a fanged human face in the middle. Its gaze can kill or transform, yet its blood grants invulnerability. A chaotic guardian monster, and a prize for warriors seeking supernatural protection.
- Bakwas: Wild man of the woods and drowned spirit in Kwakwaka'wakw ceremonies, pale and gaunt, who feeds ghosts and lost souls with ghostly food. Anyone who eats his fare joins his band of the dead. A haunting temptation for travelers, and a ritual masked figure.
- Thunderbird (Plains): Immense storm-spirit bird of Plains nations whose eyes flash lightning and whose wings thunder across the prairie, enemy of the underwater beings. It rewards brave seekers with visions and power, but punishes arrogance with fire from the sky. A sacred, awe-inspiring force rather than a mere monster.
- Iktomi: Spider trickster of the Lakota, a shape-shifter in human or spider form who delights in schemes that often catch himself. He taught language and wit, yet cheats and deceives for amusement. A clever, comic antagonist or helper whose lessons arrive through embarrassment and consequence.
- White Buffalo Calf Woman: Sacred Lakota messenger who appeared in the guise of a beautiful woman, delivered the sacred pipe and taught seven rites, then turned into a white buffalo. Radiant, benevolent and uncompromising, she tests the people's sincerity. A holy mentor who punishes disrespect, blessing the worthy with peace and abundance.
- Wakinyan: Lakota thunder beings, winged spirits whose bodies hold storms, with lightning-flashing eyes and thunderous voices. They war on Unktehi, the water monsters, and regulate the balance of sky and earth. Fearsome, sacred and unpredictable, they fit as storm guardians that strike down arrogance and respond to ritual respect.
- Kokopelli: Hunched, flute-playing Hopi and Pueblo figure carrying a sack of seeds, associated with fertility, music, and the coming of spring. Playful and mischievous, he brings rain, crops and laughter wherever he wanders. A friendly traveling trickster-minstrel whose melodies charm creatures and heal the land.
- Skinwalker: Navajo witch capable of shape-shifting into animals by wearing their pelts, bearing malice and dark magic rather than natural form. Feared and rarely named, it stalks isolated roads at night, mimics voices and stirs dread. Handle with care: a terrifying, culturally sensitive antagonist for horror stories.
- Coyote (Southwest): Ubiquitous trickster-creator of the Southwest who scatters stars, steals fire and brings both blessing and chaos through hubris and hunger. He cheats death, plays tricks on gods, and fumbles his own plans. An unreliable ally and comic villain whose schemes reshape the world.
- Katsina (kachina): Spirit beings of Pueblo and Hopi tradition who bring rain, fertility and blessings, impersonated by masked dancers and represented by carved dolls. Hundreds exist, each with domain, personality and attire. Benevolent but demanding of respect, they can serve as nature guardians or ceremonial guides.
- Spider Woman: Creator and teacher in Hopi and Navajo belief who spun the world and taught weaving. Wise, nurturing and powerful, she aids heroes with gifts such as spider silk, counsel or guidance through trials. A grandmotherly mentor who shows the way, but expects her lessons to be honored.
- Wendigo (Eastern Woodlands): Emaciated, ice-hearted cannibal spirit of Algonquian winters, embodying hunger, greed and the taboo of consuming human flesh. Towering and skeletal, it hunts through blizzards, grows larger with each meal, and can possess starving humans. A ferocious winter horror that resists conventional weapons.
- Stonecoat: Cannibal giant of Iroquois and Seneca lore whose skin is hard as flint and impervious to weapons. It hunts people, but a hero eventually tricks it, learning its weakness. A relentless armored brute, defeated by cunning, fire or sacred ritual rather than force.
- Little People: Diminutive, mischievous spirits of many eastern nations who live in forests and caves, dwelling in secret, stone-working and shy. They help the respectful with gifts and punish those who spy or disturb their homes. Playful guardians of the wild who bargain, pranks and leave small tokens.
- Flying Head: Iroquois monster that is a giant head with long streaming hair and flaming eyes, flying through the night to devour victims, said to be spawned by a dead witch. A ravenous, sleepless nightmare to be repelled with fire or ritual, and perfect for fast aerial ambushes.
- Underwater Panther: Horned, long-tailed feline monster of lakes and rivers across the Eastern Woodlands, master of water and lord of the lower world. It can create storms and drag victims below, but offers copper and power to those who appease it. Dangerous, awe-inspiring water guardian.
- Mishipeshu: Great Lakes water lynx with horns, copper scales and a spiny back, ruler of the deep and keeper of copper. Its tail churns whirlpools and its passage brings storms and drownings. A dangerous but bargainable guardian of treasure, demanding offerings from every canoe.
- Manitou: Algonquian word for the spirit force that infuses all things, from rocks and rivers to great powers like Gitche Manitou. Manitous may be benevolent or malicious, and can be bargained with, invoked or avoided. A flexible tool for spirit-world design, from small nature spirits to cosmic powers.
- Windigo (Great Lakes): Ojibwe cannibal spirit of icy winters, tall and gaunt with a heart of ice, whose hunger can never be sated. It stalks lone travelers and may possess greedy people, transforming them into monsters. A relentless hunter whose weakness is fire, melting its frozen heart.
- Uktena: Cherokee horned serpent of enormous size, with a glittering crystal on its forehead and scales that glow like stars. Its gaze is deadly and its breath poison, yet the Ulunsuti crystal grants great power. A legendary boss guarding a priceless relic that corrupts or exalts.
- Yehasuri: Cherokee wild man of the Smoky Mountains, a hairy forest dweller who is sometimes helpful and sometimes dangerous. Usually shy, he gives warnings and guidance to the respectful and punishes the careless with fright. An ambiguous woodland neighbor suited to mentor, trickster or reclusive hermit roles.
- Selu: Cherokee corn mother, first woman, who produced maize and beans from her own body for her family. Her sons discovered her secret and killed her, and from her blood the crops spread across the world. A tragic, generous earth goddess embodying sacrifice, harvest and the cost of curiosity.
- Sedna: Inuit goddess of the sea and its creatures, once a mortal girl whose fingers were cut off and became seals, whales and walrus. She dwells at the ocean floor, angry at human wrongdoing. Shamans must descend to comb her hair and soothe her to restore the hunt.
- Tuutsuk: Inuit giant of the Arctic wastes, sometimes called Tornit, a massive, primitive people strong enough to hurl boulders and wrestle bears. Dim and shy, they vanish from the world before human arrival. A hulking ice-age relic for gentle-giant or wilderness encounters.
- Nanook: Inuit polar bear spirit and master of bears, who decides whether hunters will succeed and rewards respect with plentiful game. A noble, solitary and spiritually powerful presence of the Arctic, it punishes waste and disrespect by withholding the hunt, or by becoming the hunter.
- Hodadeion: Iroquois mythic hero and stone-giant slayer whose adventures involve protecting the people from evil beings. Sometimes recounted as a forest-dwelling guardian figure with immense strength and cunning. A heroic frontier legend and a dependable ally for characters pursuing justice in the woods.
- Stone giants: Iroquois cannibal giants whose bodies are armored in rock, immune to arrows and relentless in the hunt for human flesh. They stomp through the forests of the Haudenosaunee stories, undone by trickery or by sacred fire. Heavy, near-invulnerable brutes defeated by a clever hero.
### Amazonian and Brazilian
- Curupira: Backward-footed forest guardian of Brazilian tradition, a red-haired dwarf whose reversed feet leave trails that lead hunters astray. It protects animals and trees, punishing poachers and loggers with confusion and madness. A mischievous wilderness warden who can be bribed with tobacco and honey.
- Saci: One-legged prankster of Brazilian folklore, a Black youth with a red cap and pipe who whirls in dust devils. He sours milk, hides objects and tangles horse manes. Capturing his cap grants wishes, making him a comic trickster and treasured, if unruly, ally.
- Boto: River dolphin shape-shifter of the Amazon who becomes a charming man in a white suit and hat, hiding his blowhole beneath his brim. He seduces women at festivals and vanishes into the water, leaving pregnancies behind. A smooth, dangerous glamour-weaver in river-town intrigue.
- Mapinguari: Giant sloth-like beast of the Amazon, shaggy, one-eyed, with a mouth in its belly and a stench that paralyzes prey. Said to be immune to bullets and hunting jungle intruders. A towering cryptid for survival horror with a vulnerable belly or navel.
- Iara: River mermaid of Brazilian tradition, a beautiful woman with a fish tail whose song lures fishermen into the water. Once a human woman cast into the river by jealous brothers, she now takes men to her underwater realm. A seductive, tragic siren with a vengeful past.
- Boitata: Fire serpent of Tupi-Guarani myth, a huge glowing snake with fiery eyes that emerges after a great flood and guards the fields from fire-setters. It burns anyone who harms nature. A flame-wreathed protector and sinister will-o-wisp, aiding or punishing those who burn the forest.
- Cuca: Crocodile-headed witch of Brazilian lullabies, a hag who comes for children who do not sleep. Stooped, scaly and cackling, she brews potions and carries naughty children away in a sack. A bedtime bogeywoman and a potent hag antagonist for darker stories.
- Mula sem cabeça: Headless mule of Brazilian folklore, a woman cursed for loving a priest, who gallops through the night breathing fire from her neck. Her hooves clatter on lonely roads on Thursday nights. A flaming, shrieking omen that avoids those who pray, with iron shoes and a chain.
- Anhangá: Forest demon of Tupi tradition, a shape-shifting spirit that appears as a white deer with fiery eyes and misleads hunters and the faithless. It guards game and punishes cruelty, leading wrongdoers to ruin. A vengeful nature spirit whose illusions drive outsiders mad.
- Yacumama: Giant river snake of the Peruvian Amazon, said to be dozens of meters long, drawing prey through the water with its breath. Revered as the mother of waters, it sleeps in lagoons and surfaces during storms. A colossal aquatic guardian, dangerous to boats and fearless of firearms.
- Chullachaqui: Forest guardian of the Peruvian Amazon with one human foot and one hoof-like foot, who takes the form of friends or family to lead travelers astray. It punishes harm to the jungle and tests those who respect it. A cunning illusionist, exposed by his mismatched feet.
- Tunchi: Whistle spirit of the Peruvian Amazon, a wandering soul of the unburied dead that whistles in the night, with a sound that pierces the dark. Hearing it foretells death or misfortune, and it lures wanderers astray. A chilling presence for jungle horror, and a harbinger the listener cannot ignore.
- Jurupari: Forest lawgiver spirit of Amazonian myth, a divine son who established social laws and male initiation rites, and whose secret music is forbidden to women. Powerful, stern and symbolic of order, he is sometimes cast as a demon. A complex culture-hero and sacred taboo-keeper.
