- Emerald Tablet: An ancient engraved slab holding the secrets of transmutation, containing the cryptic maxim as above, so below. Said to be written by Hermes himself, the green tablet reveals the unity of all things, and any who decipher it may command matter, making it a coveted artifact of obsessive scholars.
- Abraxas: A lion-cock-serpent, a cosmic figure with a rooster's head, human torso and serpent legs, wielding whip and shield, embodying both good and evil. Invoked on amulets as a lord of time and the heavens, it is a paradoxical power that terrifies and protects, ripe for esoteric cults and cosmic bargains.
### Pantheons: gods by culture
- Zeus: King of the Greek gods, wielder of the thunderbolt who rules from Mount Olympus, bearded, majestic and notoriously lustful. He upholds justice, hospitality and oaths, but his many affairs and wrathful temper spawn heroes, monsters and endless family feuds, making him both patron and dangerous tyrant.
- Hera: Queen of Olympus and goddess of marriage, regal, jealous and implacable, she persecutes her husband's lovers and their children. Guardian of oaths and fidelity, she can be a ruthless adversary to heroes like Heracles, yet she also blesses loyal families and royal brides with powerful favor.
- Poseidon: Greek god of the sea, earthquakes and horses, trident in hand, surging from his underwater palace with a moody, tempestuous nature. He raises storms, shakes cities and forges monsters in anger, while sailors and cities court his favor, and his grudge against Odysseus shows his vengeance.
- Demeter: Greek goddess of grain and harvest, a nurturing mother whose grief over Persephone's abduction brought winter and famine. Patient but implacable, she blesses farmers and mysteries at Eleusis, withholding fertility from the unjust, and her fierce maternal love can bend even the gods.
- Athena: Greek goddess of wisdom, strategy and craft, born fully armored from Zeus's head, with an owl and a shield bearing the Gorgon's head. Cool-headed and brilliant, she patronizes heroes like Odysseus and Perseus, rewarding cunning, though her pride and fury at insult can ruin rivals.
- Apollo: Greek god of the sun, music, prophecy, healing and archery, a radiant youth with lyre and bow who rules Delphi. Orderly and artistic, he both heals and sends plague, offers cryptic oracles and punishes arrogance like Marsyas, balancing brilliance with cruel vengeance.
- Artemis: Greek goddess of the hunt, wilderness and the moon, a fierce virgin huntress with silver bow and a retinue of nymphs. She protects young girls and wild animals but strikes down trespassers like Actaeon, making her a swift, merciless patron of hunters and guardian of untamed places.
- Ares: Greek god of war, bloodlust and battle fury, armored and brutal, loved by few and hated even by his father Zeus. He delights in slaughter and chaos, accompanied by Fear and Terror, and though strong he is often beaten by Athena's strategy, making him a savage, impulsive warmonger.
- Aphrodite: Greek goddess of love, beauty and desire, born from sea foam, whose charms and magic girdle sway gods and mortals. Vain and vengeful when slighted, she sparks wars like Troy's, aids lovers, and uses passion as a weapon, a seductive patron or capricious meddler in any story.
- Hephaestus: Greek god of fire, metalwork and craftsmen, lame and soot-streaked yet the greatest smith, forging the gods' weapons and clever automata. Gruff but gentle, he builds marvelous traps and treasures, like his chain-net for Aphrodite, and offers artisans powerful gear, though he nurses old rejection's bitterness.
- Hermes: Greek messenger god, trickster and guide of souls, quick and clever with winged sandals and caduceus, patron of travelers, thieves and merchants. A cheerful rogue who stole Apollo's cattle as a baby, he escorts the dead to Hades and slips between worlds, aiding heroes with wit.
- Dionysus: Greek god of wine, revelry, theater and ecstatic madness, accompanied by maenads and satyrs and crowned with ivy. Twice-born and unpredictable, he grants joy and liberation but also drives mortals into frenzy and violence, as Pentheus learned, and punishes those who deny his rites.
- Hades: Greek lord of the underworld and the dead, grim, wealthy and unyielding, he rarely leaves his shadowy realm and wears a helm of invisibility. Not evil but strictly just, he guards his subjects jealously, bargains coldly with heroes and abducted Persephone to be his queen.
- Persephone: Greek queen of the underworld and goddess of spring, torn between her mother Demeter and her husband Hades, spending half the year below. Both gentle maiden and stern ruler of the dead, she can show mercy to heroes, and her cycle of departure and return marks the seasons.
- Jupiter: Roman king of the gods and sky, wielder of the thunderbolt, who guarantees oaths and the might of Rome from his Capitoline temple. Stately, authoritative and stern, he rewards piety and punishes treachery, serving as the divine patron of the state and a majestic judge of cosmic order.
- Juno: Roman queen of the gods and protector of marriage, women and the state, a stately matron crowned and accompanied by peacocks. Fiercely loyal to Rome and its families, she favors faithful wives, nurtures the city and persecutes its enemies, like Aeneas, with long-burning, ruthless wrath.
- Neptune: Roman god of the sea, freshwater and horses, a trident-wielding sovereign of waves who answers sailors' prayers and ritual sacrifice. Moody and powerful, he calms or churns the ocean, grants safe voyages to the pious, and can drown fleets that offend him, acting as a respected maritime patron.
- Mars: Roman god of war and father of Romulus and Remus, an armored, disciplined warrior revered by legions and farmers alike. Unlike the Greek Ares, he is dignified and honored, embodying martial valor and ordered violence, and is called on to defend borders, empower soldiers and bless spring campaigns.
- Venus: Roman goddess of love, beauty and prosperity, mother of Aeneas and ancestor of Caesar's line, graceful and adorned with doves. She inspires passion, fertility and victory, bringing charm and political fortune to favorites, while her wrath toward those who scorn love can bring ruin and heartbreak.
- Minerva: Roman goddess of wisdom, strategy, trade and craftsmanship, armored and accompanied by an owl, patron of artisans, teachers and soldiers. Calm and clever, she rewards skill and planning, guiding heroes through trials by counsel and craft, while punishing arrogance in the manner of her Greek counterpart Athena.
- Vulcan: Roman god of fire, volcanoes and the forge, a brawny, soot-covered smith who crafts the gods' weapons beneath mountains. Both feared and honored, he can unleash infernos upon cities or craft gear for champions, and temples placed outside Rome's walls guard against his fiery destruction.
- Mercury: Roman messenger god and patron of merchants, thieves and travelers, swift with winged cap and sandals and carrying a caduceus. Charming, cunning and ever in motion, he carries divine messages, guides souls and protects trade, offering advantage to those who bargain boldly or sneak past guards.
- Bacchus: Roman god of wine, festivals and uninhibited celebration, the counterpart of Dionysus, crowned with grapevines and followed by a rowdy retinue. He brings joy, liberty and drunken inspiration to cults of initiates, yet unchecked revelry can lead to violence, and the Senate once crushed his rites.
- Pluto: Roman lord of the underworld and wealth hidden in the earth, stern and shadowy, ruler of the dead alongside Proserpina. Rarely invoked and deeply feared, he presides over judgment and mineral riches, rewarding no one for trying to cheat death and demanding strict adherence to his domain's laws.
- Saturn: Roman god of agriculture, time and the golden age, an old sickle-bearing father who devoured his children in myth, yet presided over bountiful harvests. His festival Saturnalia upended social order with feasting and gift giving, making him a patron of renewal, wealth, and dark cyclical devouring.
- Odin: Norse Allfather, one-eyed god of wisdom, war, poetry and death, who sacrificed an eye for knowledge and hung on Yggdrasil for runes. Cloaked, spear in hand and followed by ravens and wolves, he schemes constantly toward Ragnarok, gathering heroes in Valhalla while manipulating mortals as pieces.
- Thor: Norse god of thunder, strength and protection, a red-bearded giant-slayer who wields the hammer Mjolnir and rides a goat-drawn chariot. Boisterous, brave and unsubtle, he defends gods and men from giants, with a mighty appetite and temper, though his slow wit makes him easy for tricksters to fool.
- Loki: Norse trickster, shapeshifter and blood-brother to Odin, whose clever schemes both save and endanger the gods, from stealing Sif's hair to engineering Baldr's death. Charming, mischievous and treacherous, he is destined to lead chaos at Ragnarok, a perfect ambiguous ally whose loyalty is never certain.
- Freyja: Norse goddess of love, beauty, war and seidr magic, who rides a boar or cat-drawn chariot and claims half the battle-slain for her hall. Fierce, sensual and shrewd, she wears the necklace Brisingamen, fiercely pursues her desires, and teaches sorcery to those bold enough to ask.
- Frigg: Norse queen of the gods, wife of Odin and goddess of foresight, marriage and motherhood, who knows all fates yet speaks none. Wise and sorrowful, she tried to save her son Baldr by extracting oaths from all things, a poignant figure of love, prophecy and mournful helplessness.
- Tyr: Norse god of war, law and justice, who sacrificed his right hand to bind the wolf Fenrir. One-handed, honorable and steadfast, he stands for oaths and the courage to accept personal loss for the common good, embodying disciplined valor rather than reckless bloodlust, and appealing to principled fighters.
- Baldr: Norse god of light, beauty and peace, beloved by all and invulnerable to everything but mistletoe, by which Loki had him killed. Gentle, radiant and doomed, his death presages Ragnarok, and his return in the renewed world gives hope, making him a symbol of lost innocence and tragic loss.
- Heimdall: Norse watchman of the gods, guardian of the rainbow bridge Bifrost, who sees hundreds of miles and hears wool growing on sheep. Keen, vigilant and nearly sleepless, he holds the Gjallarhorn to herald Ragnarok, and is destined to fall slaying Loki in a duel of ancient rivals.
- Hel: Norse ruler of the realm of the dead, daughter of Loki, half living woman and half rotting corpse, who presides over a cold hall for those who die without glory. Stern, impartial and implacable, she bargains over souls and keeps Baldr until the world weeps for him.
- Ra: Egyptian sun god and king of the gods, who sails the heavens each day in a solar barque and battles the serpent Apep nightly in the underworld. Falcon-headed and crowned with a sun disc, he embodies creation, order and kingship, aging yet formidable, and demands loyalty from pharaoh and priesthood.
- Osiris: Egyptian god of the dead, resurrection and fertile land, murdered by his brother Set, reassembled by Isis, and reborn as lord of the afterlife. Green-skinned and mummy-wrapped, he judges souls with serene authority, symbolizing renewal and justice, and his story underpins funerary rites and royal legitimacy.
- Isis: Egyptian goddess of magic, motherhood and healing, who resurrected Osiris and protected her son Horus through cunning and spells. Winged and devoted, she learned Ra's secret name through a trick, wields powerful words of power, and serves as a protector, healer and formidable sorceress-queen of the Nile.
- Horus: Egyptian falcon-headed god of the sky and kingship, son of Osiris and Isis, who fought Set for the throne and lost an eye that became a symbol of protection. Vengeful and noble, he embodies the pharaoh, bringing victory and divine order while pursuing justice for his murdered father.
- Set: Egyptian god of chaos, storms, deserts and foreigners, who murdered Osiris and contested Horus for the throne, yet also defended Ra's barque against Apep. Red-haired and animal-headed, he is a powerful, ambiguous strongman, feared as a usurper but needed as a protector against greater cosmic disorder.
- Anubis: Egyptian jackal-headed god of embalming, cemeteries and the weighing of the heart, who guides souls through the underworld. Dark, solemn and meticulous, he guards tombs, oversees mummification and protects the dead from desecration, making him a respected psychopomp whose scales decide a soul's fate.
- Thoth: Egyptian ibis-headed god of writing, wisdom, magic and the moon, scribe of the gods who records judgments of the dead and invented hieroglyphs. Learned, impartial and cunning, he mediates divine disputes, heals Horus's eye, and guards the secrets of magic in books that mortals risk everything to find.
- Bastet: Egyptian cat goddess of home, fertility and protection, once a lioness warrior and later a gentle feline, guarding families against disease and evil spirits. Playful yet fierce, she delights in music and festivals, scratches intruders and demands respect for sacred cats, serving as a loyal household guardian.
- Sekhmet: Egyptian lioness goddess of war, plague and healing, sent by Ra to punish humanity and nearly destroying it until tricked into drinking red-dyed beer. Blood-hungry and unstoppable, she commands both devastating pestilence and cures, and her priests appeased her with rituals to turn her fury.
- Hathor: Egyptian goddess of love, music, joy and motherhood, shown as a cow or woman with horns and sun disc, who also welcomes the dead in the west. Warm, generous and festive, she grants fertility and celebration, but in her rage as Sekhmet becomes terrifying, giving her a double nature.
- Ptah: Egyptian creator god of Memphis, patron of craftsmen and architects, who spoke the world into being through thought and word. Mummiform, bald-headed and wise, he is a calm, productive deity who shapes the cosmos with intellect and art, blessing builders, sculptors and priests with careful craftsmanship.
- Anu: Mesopotamian sky father and king of the gods, an ancient remote deity whose authority sanctions kingship and heavenly decrees. Seldom active, he grants the Bull of Heaven to Ishtar in anger, and presides over councils of gods as an august, distant figure whose will shapes the order of the cosmos.
- Enlil: Mesopotamian lord of wind, air and command, who holds the Tablet of Destinies and decides the fate of cities and people. Stern and capricious, he sent the great flood when humans grew too noisy, a harsh overseer whose decrees can doom kingdoms, and whose favor makes a ruler legitimate.
- Enki: Mesopotamian god of fresh water, wisdom and craft, lord of the Abzu, a clever trickster who saved humanity from the flood and designed civilization's arts. Generous and sly, he outwits fellow gods with ingenious schemes, grants gifts of skill and magic, and acts as humankind's cunning patron and ally.
- Marduk: Babylonian chief god and storm-warrior, who slew the sea dragon Tiamat and built the world from her body, thereby taking supreme kingship among the gods. Radiant, many-eyed and armed with winds and a net, he is a glorious champion, patron of Babylon and judge of destinies.
- Ishtar: Mesopotamian goddess of love, sex and war, fierce, beautiful and vengeful, who descended into the underworld and unleashed the Bull of Heaven on Gilgamesh. Armed with lions and a star crown, she inspires passion and bloodshed, bestowing glory on lovers and kings while wrecking those who spurn her.
- Tiamat: Mesopotamian primordial goddess of the salt sea, a chaos dragon-mother who birthed the gods and then waged war on them, leading a horde of monsters against Marduk. Vast, serpentine and furious, she embodies untamed chaos and the raw power of creation, a world-ending boss whose body forms the sky and earth.
- Nergal: Mesopotamian god of war, plague and the underworld, lord of burning heat and sudden death, who rules Kur alongside Ereshkigal. Lion-faced and armed with scimitar and mace, he brings pestilence, fever and slaughter, and is placated by fearful rites, making him a feared patron of soldiers and executioners.
- Dagda: Irish father-god of the Tuatha De Danann, a huge, ungainly but all-powerful figure with a cauldron that never empties, a club that kills and revives, and a harp that commands seasons. Jovial and ravenous, he is the generous patron of druids, feasters and clans, wise beneath his crude appearance.
- Brigid: Celtic goddess of poetry, healing, smithcraft and sacred flame, patron of bards, physicians and blacksmiths, later enshrined as a saint. Triple-aspected, she tends eternal fires and wells of inspiration, cares for the sick and craft, and kindles creativity, serving as a gentle yet unwavering patron of the hearth.
- Lugh: Celtic many-skilled god of light, craft and kingship, a champion of the Tuatha De Danann, who wielded a deadly spear and slingshot to slay the Fomorian Balor. Gifted in every art, he uses brilliance and cunning to turn the tide of war, an ideal charismatic hero-god and leader.
- Morrigan: Celtic goddess of war, fate and death, a shapeshifting crow or raven who hovers over battlefields, prophesying doom and inspiring bloodlust. Triple and ambiguous, she tempts heroes like Cu Chulainn, bestows victory or ruin, and washes the armor of those fated to die, a terrifying harbinger and patron.
- Cernunnos: Celtic antlered god of wild places, animals, fertility and abundance, seated cross-legged with a torc and snakes in his hands. Silent and primeval, he presides over forests and beasts, mediating between hunters and the hunted, an enigmatic spirit whose worship was woven into stag-haunted woodlands.
- Brahma: Hindu creator god in the divine triad, four-faced and seated on a lotus emerging from Vishnu's navel, reciting the Vedas. Once deeply worshiped, he is now a remote, scholarly deity who grants boons to ascetics, sometimes unwisely, and stands as the origin of cosmic order and the source of dangerous blessings.
- Vishnu: Hindu preserver of the cosmos, blue-skinned and four-armed, who rests on the serpent Shesha and descends as avatars like Rama and Krishna whenever dharma falters. Serene, benevolent and all-seeing, he wields a discus and conch against demons, restoring balance and offering salvation through devotion.
- Shiva: Hindu destroyer and transformer, an ash-smeared ascetic with matted hair, a third eye and a trident, who dances the cosmic dance and holds the river Ganga in his locks. Both terrifying and compassionate, he grants boons readily, burns desire to ash, and renews the universe through destruction.
- Lakshmi: Hindu goddess of wealth, fortune and prosperity, consort of Vishnu, seated on a lotus with golden coins pouring from her hands. Radiant, gracious and fickle, she blesses households that are diligent and generous, abandons the greedy and arrogant, and symbolizes beauty, abundance and auspicious beginnings.
- Saraswati: Hindu goddess of knowledge, music, art and speech, serene in white with a veena, riding a swan or peacock. She inspires scholars, poets and musicians, imparting clarity and creative fire, and grants eloquence to those who revere her, while fleeing the proud who wield learning with arrogance.
- Durga: Hindu warrior goddess astride a lion or tiger, many-armed with the weapons of the gods, who slew the buffalo demon Mahishasura when no god could. Fierce, protective and radiant, she defends the righteous, overturning tyrants in a blaze of power, and symbolizes feminine strength and cosmic victory.
- Amaterasu: Japanese sun goddess and ancestor of the imperial line, enthroned in the High Plain of Heaven and enshrined at Ise. Her withdrawal into a cave once stole the light from the world, and her radiance, dignity and sovereignty make her both the supreme deity and a beacon of order.
- Susanoo: Japanese storm and sea god, a rowdy, banished younger brother who wrecked heaven's rice fields yet slew the eight-headed serpent to save a princess. Wild, brash and ultimately noble, he wields thunderous winds and a legendary sword, embodying raw nature as a redeemed trickster-hero.
- Inari: Japanese deity of rice, fertility, foxes and commerce, worshiped at thousands of vermilion-gated shrines where stone foxes keep watch. Androgynous and generous, Inari nurtures fields and business, sends kitsune as messengers, and provides prosperity to the sincere while punishing the dishonest with misfortune.
- Hachiman: Japanese god of war, archery and protection, patron of samurai and the Minamoto clan, often depicted as a warrior or deified Emperor Ojin. Stern and martial yet protective of the people, he blesses armies, grants victories, and is invoked at shrines by those seeking courage in battle and justice.
- Jade Emperor: Chinese supreme ruler of heaven and head of the celestial bureaucracy, who oversees gods, immortals and the destiny of mortals from his jade throne. Dignified, impartial and exacting, he issues decrees, convenes councils and bestows rank, often outwitted by Monkey King but respected as the final authority.
- Guanyin: Chinese bodhisattva of compassion, a graceful, white-robed figure holding a vase of healing water and willow branch, who hears the cries of all suffering. Gentle, merciful and tireless, she appears as many forms to rescue the desperate, bestowing children, safe passage and protection to the devoted.
- Guan Yu: Chinese deified general of the Three Kingdoms, a red-faced, long-bearded warrior wielding the green dragon crescent blade, venerated as a god of war, loyalty and wealth. Righteous and incorruptible, he stands as a paragon of brotherhood and honor, and protects shops, secret societies and soldiers alike.
- Nezha: Chinese child-god and warrior, a rebellious boy born from a ball of flesh, who fights on lotus-flower wheels with a fire-tipped spear and cosmic rings. Hot-tempered, brave and tragic, he cut himself free of his family, was reborn as a lotus, and now defends heaven against demons with youthful fury.
- Huitzilopochtli: Aztec god of sun and war, patron of Tenochtitlan, born armed and fully grown to slay his sister Coyolxauhqui and her brothers. Fierce, hummingbird-adorned and ever hungry, he demands blood sacrifice to keep the sun moving, driving the empire's conquests and ritual warfare as a relentless divine warlord.
- Tlaloc: Aztec god of rain, lightning and fertile earth, a goggle-eyed, fanged figure who commands storm clouds and mountain springs. Generous with harvests yet capable of drought, flood and sacrificial demand, particularly of children, he rules a paradise for those killed by lightning or water, making a dual-natured nature god.
- Quetzalcoatl: Aztec feathered serpent god of wind, learning, priesthood and the morning star, who created humankind from bones and corn, and is said to have exiled himself and promised return. Wise, benevolent and ambiguous, he opposes human sacrifice in some tales, his departure and return inspiring prophecy and drama.
- Coatlicue: Aztec earth goddess and mother of the gods, wearing a skirt of writhing serpents and a necklace of hands and hearts, who became pregnant with Huitzilopochtli by a ball of feathers. Terrifying and creative, she embodies both life and devouring earth, a primal mother whose awesome form inspires dread.
- Itzamna: Maya creator and sky god, an aged, toothless sage credited with inventing writing, medicine and the calendar, and patron of priests and scribes. Calm, wise and benevolent, he is associated with the sun and the heavens, offering healing and knowledge to petitioners and mediating among the gods.
- Kukulkan: Maya feathered serpent deity of wind, rain and learning, honored at Chichen Itza, where the equinox shadow of a serpent descends the pyramid. Related to the Aztec Quetzalcoatl, he is a wise creator and civilizing founder who blesses rulers and astronomers, symbolizing the union of earth and sky.
- Chaac: Maya rain god with a long reptilian nose and axe of lightning, who splits clouds to release the rains on which maize depends. Capricious yet beloved, he appears in four directional forms, brings life-giving storms or devastating flood, and is entreated with ritual offerings by anxious farmers.
- Inti: Inca sun god and divine ancestor of the emperors, depicted as a golden disc with a face and rays, whose gold-lined temple Coricancha gleamed in Cusco. Benevolent and radiant, he ripens crops and legitimizes the Sapa Inca, demanding ceremonies and tribute, and his eclipse or absence signals turmoil.
- Viracocha: Inca creator god who emerged from Lake Titicaca to shape the world and people, then wandered as a bearded, robed beggar-teacher before vanishing over the sea. Mysterious and wise, he rewards humility, punishes arrogance with floods, and his foretold return shaped the empire's reaction to strangers.
- Pachamama: Andean earth mother and goddess of fertility, planting and mountains, to whom farmers pour chicha and offer coca leaves before sowing. Nurturing yet powerful, she provides abundant harvests and shelter when honored, but quakes and famine when neglected, representing the sacred living landscape of the Andes.
- Perun: Slavic god of thunder, lightning and oak trees, chief of the pantheon, an axe-wielding, red-bearded warrior who fights Veles. Mighty and just, he enforces oaths and splits the sky with his storms, striking down serpents and wrongdoers, and presiding over warriors, kings and treaty-sealing.
- Veles: Slavic god of cattle, earth, waters, magic and the underworld, a shaggy serpentine or bear-like trickster who steals Perun's herds and flees the thunder. Cunning, magical and tied to the cycle of death and renewal, he is an eternal rival whose wiles and wealth fascinate poets and sorcerers.
- Mokosh: Slavic goddess of earth, fertility, spinning and women's work, maternal and powerful, honored with offerings at wells and springs. Close to the rhythms of the land and household, she presides over weaving and fate, rewarding diligent women and protecting livestock, while being fierce when disrespected.
- Tangaroa: Polynesian god of the ocean, creator and patron of fishermen, who rules the seas and their creatures, sometimes described as the first being and father of all fish. Deep, powerful and sometimes wrathful, he can calm or rage, shaping voyages and fisheries while demanding respect from all who navigate.
- Maui: Polynesian demigod and trickster hero who fished up islands, snared the sun to slow its path, and stole fire from the underworld. Cheeky, inventive and shape-shifting, he wields a magic fishhook, defying gods and death itself, though his boldest ambition to conquer mortality ended in tragedy.
- Pele: Hawaiian goddess of volcanoes, fire and lava, who shapes islands in her fiery temper and dwells in Kilauea's crater. Beautiful, passionate and volatile, she appears as a young woman or old crone, rewards the respectful with safe passage, and blasts the disrespectful with molten fury.
- Olodumare: Yoruba supreme creator, the distant source of all being and destiny, who sends the orisha as intermediaries and rarely intervenes directly. Remote yet ultimate, he grants ase, the life-force, and the power to create and decree, a mysterious cosmic authority that shapes all fortune and existence.
- Shango: Yoruba orisha of thunder, lightning and kingship, a fiery former king of Oyo who wields a double-headed axe and hurls thunderstones. Charismatic, proud and fierce, he punishes liars and thieves with lightning, loves drumming and dance, and was deified after his tragic death by hanging.
- Oya: Yoruba orisha of wind, storms, lightning and the cemetery gates, a fierce warrior queen and consort of Shango who guides the dead and heralds change. Bold and unstoppable, she wields a sword and whirlwind, sweeping away the old with tempests and standing guard over transitions between life and death.
- Mawu: Fon creator goddess of West Africa, a moon-bound mother who shaped the world and its people, paired with her twin Lisa the sun. Wise and gentle, she grants fertility and rest, rules the cool night, and sends her many offspring to govern thunder, sea and earth on her behalf.
- Perkunas: Baltic thunder god, bearded and armed with an axe or hammer, who rides a fiery chariot to smite devils and uphold oaths and fertility. Fierce but righteous, he strikes sacred oaks and the unholy with lightning, a protector whose storms bless fields and punish evildoers.
- Laima: Baltic goddess of fate and fortune who spins the destiny of every newborn, attended by sister fates who weave the threads of life. Gentle yet unalterable, she presides over birth, marriage and death, and can be petitioned for luck, but her decrees are largely set from the start.
- Ukko: Finnish sky and thunder god, an aged, bearded father of the heavens who wields a hammer or lightning and answers prayers for rain, harvest and protection. Powerful yet patient, he is called upon by heroes like Vainamoinen, directing storms and weather and upholding order among the elements.
- Louhi: Finnish witch-queen of the northern land Pohjola, a cunning shapeshifter who commands frost, storms and sorcery and holds the magic mill Sampo. Cold, calculating and ruthless, she sets impossible tasks for suitors, steals the sun and moon, and is a classic formidable foe of Kalevala heroes.
- Mithra: Persian god of oaths, contracts, light and the sun's covenant, a vigilant warrior who rides a chariot and sees every lie. Just and fierce, he punishes oathbreakers with merciless pursuit, guards the truth and was later venerated in Roman mystery cults, a patron of soldiers and honest bargains.
- Anahita: Persian goddess of waters, fertility and healing, a radiant, tall maiden with a jeweled crown who rules rivers and the heavenly source of all streams. Pure and benevolent, she grants fertile lands, easy births and victory to her devotees, and cleanses the world of impurity and evil.
## Societies and groups
### Secret societies and mystery schools
- Freemasons: A brotherhood of builders using ritual, symbols and secret handshakes, with compasses, square and lodge degrees drawn from stonemason lore. Members swear oaths of mutual aid and moral improvement, forming influential networks of merchants, nobles and thinkers, shrouded in rumors that suit conspiracy plots.
- Illuminati: A conspiratorial order of enlightened elites pulling hidden strings, founded in Bavaria to promote reason against superstition, then mythologized as a shadowy cabal controlling governments. Whether real or invented, its masked agents, secret ciphers and infiltrated institutions make a delicious mystery for paranoid heroes to chase.
- Rosicrucians: A secretive mystic brotherhood of alchemists and healers, said to preserve the wisdom of a legendary founder buried in a sealed vault. Invisible, learned and altruistic, they work to reform society through knowledge and medicine, and their manifestos spawned centuries of seekers hunting an unseen order.
- Knights Templar: Warrior monks who guarded pilgrims and hoarded wealth, bound by vows of poverty and fighting in white mantles with red crosses. Rich bankers and fearsome crusaders, they were destroyed by a jealous king, leaving legends of lost treasure, secret rites and survivors who hold ancient secrets.
- Hashshashin (Assassins): A medieval Nizari order of fanatical killers who struck rulers with daggers from mountain fortresses, led by the Old Man of the Mountain. Disciplined, patient and fearless, they used stealth and disguise to eliminate enemies publicly, creating a myth of drugged devotees and unstoppable infiltrators.
- Priory of Sion (fiction): A fabricated secret order claiming to protect a hidden royal bloodline and sacred treasure, born from a twentieth-century hoax and popularized by thrillers. Its forged documents, Grand Masters and cryptic clues make a ready source of conspiracy plot, a mysterious brotherhood that may not exist at all.
- Eleusinian mystery cult: Initiates of a sacred Greek rite of Demeter and Persephone, held annually near Athens, promising a blessed afterlife through secret ceremonies and a sacred drink. Sworn to silence, they emerged transformed, and their hidden revelations remain a tantalizing puzzle of mystic vision and ritual terror.
- Order of the Golden Dawn: Robed occultists practicing ceremonial magic and ritual in a Victorian lodge, with elaborate degrees of Kabbalah, tarot, astrology and Egyptian symbolism. Its quarreling members, including poets and magicians, built a hierarchy of mystic initiations and lasting influence on modern esoteric tradition and fiction.
- Thuggee: Stranglers who ambush travelers in service of a dark goddess, befriending victims on the road and killing them with silken scarves before burying the bodies. Organized, ritualistic and hereditary, they vanish into ordinary society, evoking dread and making a chilling cult for suspenseful investigation.
- Skull and Bones: An elite collegiate secret society with macabre initiation rites, meeting in a windowless tomb where members swear loyalty and share confessions. Its influential alumni and rumors of stolen skulls and hidden power make it a shorthand for privileged conspiracy and old-money networks.
- Hellfire Club: Debauched aristocrats holding scandalous rituals in hidden caves and abbeys, mocking religion with feasts, mock-masses and wild revelry. Wealthy, bored and daring, members cross lines of morality and law, leaving a legacy of rumor about blasphemy, power games and the corruption of the elite.
- Rebecca riots: Toll-gate raiders disguised as women protesting unfair taxes in nineteenth-century Wales, led by a figure called Rebecca who rallied farmers by night. Cloaked in dresses and blackened faces, they smashed gates and defied authorities, a humorous yet determined band of rural rebels with just grievances.
- Triads: Tattooed criminal brotherhoods rooted in secret rebel societies that once sought to overthrow the Qing, now running rackets, smuggling and gambling. They keep elaborate initiation oaths, hierarchical ranks and ritual symbols, offering a dangerous underworld ally or enemy with deep local ties and ruthless discipline.
- Yakuza: Tattooed organized crime clans bound by loyalty and ritual, with strict hierarchies, sake-sealed oaths and finger-cutting penance for failure. Sharply dressed and feared, they control gambling, protection and nightlife, adhering to an old code of honor that creates both menace and a fascinating duty-bound outlaw culture.
- Carbonari: Masked revolutionary conspirators plotting liberation in secret lodges, organizing charcoal-burner symbolism and oaths to overthrow foreign rulers across nineteenth-century Italy. Idealistic and clandestine, they communicate by code, stage uprisings and are hunted by police, offering classic roles for conspirators, agitators and doomed romantic patriots.
### Historical empires and kingdoms (additional)
- Khmer Empire: A temple-building jungle empire of great stone cities, centered on Angkor with its vast reservoirs and carved sandstone temples dedicated to Hindu gods and Buddha. Its god-kings commanded armies, canals and elephants, and its mysterious collapse leaves ruins thick with vines, stone faces and haunted splendor.
- Majapahit: An island maritime empire ruling much of the archipelago from eastern Java, famed for fleets, spice trade and the oath of Gajah Mada to unite the islands. Hindu-Buddhist in culture, it flourished with courtly poets, temples and diplomacy, offering a rich setting of naval power and royal intrigue.
- Srivijaya: A seafaring trade empire controlling straits and spice routes from Sumatra, whose navy taxed all passing ships and whose Buddhist scholars drew pilgrims. Wealthy, mercantile and cosmopolitan, it ruled a web of ports through fleets and alliances, making a fine backdrop for pirates, traders and naval conflicts.
- Great Zimbabwe: A stone-walled trading kingdom of gold and cattle wealth in southern Africa, its enormous dry-stone enclosures and towers dominating the highlands. Its rulers traded with Swahili merchants and distant lands, and the enigmatic ruins, soapstone birds and abandoned grandeur offer a haunting, mysterious setting for adventure.
- Kingdom of Kush: A river kingdom of pyramid builders and iron smelters south of Egypt, ruled by queens and kings who once conquered Egypt as pharaohs. Skilled archers and metalworkers, they built steep pyramids at Meroe, creating a proud African power with distinctive culture, gods and fierce warrior-queens.
- Mali Empire: A gold-rich West African empire of scholars and caravans, led by Mansa Musa, whose pilgrimage to Mecca flooded the world with gold. Timbuktu's libraries and mosques, griot storytellers and salt caravans fill a prosperous, learned realm of mounted warriors, merchants and sorcerer-kings.
- Ethiopian Empire: A highland Christian kingdom of rock churches and solomonic kings, claiming descent from Solomon and Sheba and guarding the Ark of the Covenant at Axum. Isolated by mountains, its negus emperors, monasteries and warriors resisted conquest, creating a distinct, deeply devout and ancient civilization.
- Mughal Empire: A gunpowder empire of splendid monuments and Persian courts, ruling most of India from Delhi and Agra with artillery, elephants and artful bureaucracy. Its emperors built the Taj Mahal, patronized miniature painting and poetry, and balanced diverse faiths, providing a lavish setting for intrigue and war.
- Maurya Empire: A vast ancient Indian empire united by a ruthless chancellor, Chanakya, who guided Chandragupta to the throne and wrote of statecraft and spies. Later ruled by Ashoka, who turned from conquest to Buddhist peace, it spanned the subcontinent through armies, elephants and an elaborate bureaucracy.
- Gupta Empire: A golden age empire of mathematicians, poets and artists, credited with the concept of zero, classical Sanskrit drama and exquisite temple sculpture. Prosperous and cultured, its monarchs patronized scholars like Kalidasa and Aryabhata, offering a refined court setting threatened by invading Huns at its frontiers.
- Ottoman Empire: A sprawling gunpowder empire led by sultans and janissaries, spanning three continents from Istanbul's palaces with cannon, galleys and a vast bureaucracy. Its slave-soldiers, scholars and harem intrigues, along with a tolerant millet system, make a vibrant world of diplomacy, war and cosmopolitan trade.
- Safavid Empire: A Persian empire of shahs, poets and fervent warriors, establishing Shia Islam as the state faith and building Isfahan's blue-tiled glory. Its Qizilbash cavalry, miniature painters and silk merchants fought Ottoman rivals, offering a dazzling setting of religious zeal, artistry and fierce frontier conflicts.
- Byzantine Empire: The eastern Roman empire of emperors, golden domes and intrigue, centered on Constantinople with its mighty walls, Hippodrome and Hagia Sophia. Famed for Greek fire, elite guards, eunuch courtiers and plotting dynasties, it survived centuries by diplomacy and a labyrinthine court of poisons and betrayals.
- Holy Roman Empire: A patchwork realm of emperors, princes and church politics, loosely uniting German lands, free cities and bishoprics under an elected emperor. Rivalries between pope, electors and knights fuel endless feuds, making a fractious, ceremonial setting for diplomacy, religious conflict and shifting alliances.
- Spanish Empire: A global realm of conquistadors, galleons and silver, stretching across the Americas, the Philippines and Europe with ships heavy with treasure. Zealous missionaries, inquisitors and ruthless adventurers fuel exploration and conquest, creating a gilded, brutal setting of piracy, rebellion and colonial intrigue.
- Inca Empire: A mountain empire of road builders and terraced farms, ruled by the Sapa Inca from Cusco and linked by a vast network of stone roads and rope bridges. Runners carried messages with knotted quipu, and a structured labor system built fortresses like Machu Picchu in the clouds.
- Aztec Triple Alliance: A warrior league ruling the valley from a lake city, the alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan dominated tributary states with fearsome armies. Jaguar and eagle knights fought flower wars to capture sacrifices, and the glittering island capital with causeways and markets sat on constant ritual tension.
- Maya city-states: Rival jungle cities of astronomers, priests and ball players, each ruled by a divine king and linked by trade, war and alliance. Their pyramids, hieroglyphic inscriptions and calendars reflect deep cosmic knowledge, and their tangled dynastic conflicts and mysterious collapses provide rich material for drama.
- Hanseatic League: A merchant league of trading cities and armed cogs around the Baltic and North Sea, protecting commerce with shared law, fleets and monopolies. Wealthy guild merchants dealt in furs, timber and grain, enforcing their interests with blockades and pirates-hunting, a pragmatic power of ledgers and ships.
- Venetian Republic: A lagoon republic of merchant princes, galleys and masked intrigue, ruled by a doge and a secretive council whose spies watched everyone. Built on water, with an arsenal churning out ships, it grew rich from eastern trade, giving a glittering setting of carnivals, assassins and political scheming.
### Indigenous nations and confederacies
- Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy: A league of five, later six, northeastern woodland nations bound by the Great Law of Peace and governed through clan mothers and a council of sachems. They live in longhouses and farm the Three Sisters. Use them for diplomacy plots, consensus politics and disciplined forest warfare.
- Lakota: Horse-riding plains people who follow the great bison herds across the grasslands, living in tipis and organized into bands and warrior societies. Buffalo hunts, sun dances and vision quests shape their year. They suit mounted skirmishers, fierce defenders of sacred land, and spiritual guides.
- Cheyenne: Proud plains nation whose life is organized around military societies such as the Dog Soldiers, each with its own rites, rules and bravery oaths. They hunt bison, trade widely and guard their sacred arrows. Ideal for honor-bound warriors, disciplined war bands and tragic last stands.
- Comanche: Masters of the southern plains who turned the horse into the deadliest weapon of their age, raiding enemies from astonishing distances. Their riders fire arrows from beneath a galloping mount's neck. They make superb fast-striking antagonists, feared horse-lords or elusive allies who control vast, dangerous territory.
- Apache: Fierce desert and mountain peoples of the southwest, famed for ambush, endurance and an intimate knowledge of every hidden spring and canyon. Bands of raiders and hunters move light and vanish into rock. Perfect for guerrilla fighters, elusive scouts and defenders who exploit terrain against stronger armies.
- Navajo: Desert herders and weavers of the southwest, whose sheep, silver and intricate woven patterns carry deep cultural meaning, and whose language became an unbreakable code in modern war. They suit craft-driven characters, wise storytellers, and communicators whose secret tongue can decide a battle.
- Cherokee: Southeastern nation of farmers, town chiefs and councils who devised their own written syllabary and published newspapers. They balance tradition with adaptation under mounting pressure from settlers. Good for stories of scholarship, political resilience, forced removal, and keepers of rich healing and storytelling lore.
- Choctaw: Southeastern farming nation of villages, orators and diplomats, famed for the fast, brutal stickball game that doubles as ritual and a substitute for war. Their mound-rooted heritage and treaty struggles offer material for rivalries settled by contest, resourceful negotiators and communities enduring displacement.
- Seminole: Fighters and families who built a new people in the Florida wetlands from refugees and Creek kin, resisting forced removal through long wars. They know every hidden hammock and cypress channel. They make strong models for swamp guerrillas, canoe raiders, and stubborn survivors who never surrendered.
- Pueblo peoples: Farming villagers of the arid southwest who built multi-story adobe towns and cliff dwellings, grew corn in dry land, and keep kachina ceremonies and kivas. Peaceful but capable of coordinated revolt. They offer fortress-village settings, ritual specialists, masked spirit dancers and patient, defensible communities.
- Mississippian culture: Mound-building river farmers whose great earthwork cities, such as Cahokia, held divine chiefs, temples and far-reaching trade. Their society rested on corn surpluses and sacred hierarchy. Use them for a vanished priest-kingdom, ominous mounds, sun-chiefs and ruins hiding forgotten ritual secrets.
- Inuit: Arctic hunters superbly adapted to ice and darkness, using kayaks, sled dogs, snow houses and sealskin tools to survive where few others can. Their stories speak of sea spirits and shamans. They serve as expert survivalists, patient seal hunters and guides through lethal frozen wilderness.
- Aleut: Sea hunters of the fog-bound, windswept island chain, who paddled skillful kayaks, harpooned whales and seals, and wove fine grass baskets and waterproof parkas. Their volcanic homeland is harsh. Good for island seafarers, expert boat handlers, and communities squeezed between sea and foreign colonists.
- Maori iwi: Tattooed seafaring tribes of canoe voyagers who crossed the Pacific, organized by iwi and hapu, with powerful chiefs and ritual haka. Their carved meeting houses and fortified pa are striking. They provide fearless warriors, ancestral navigators, and a culture where honor, genealogy and spirit are tightly bound.
- Aboriginal clans: Ancient desert and coastal peoples whose clans keep law and land through Dreaming stories, songlines and ceremony, some of the oldest continuous cultures on earth. Each clan holds sacred sites and totems. They suit lore-keepers, trackers who read the land, and myth-driven landscapes alive with ancestral beings.
- Mapuche: Fierce southern Andean warriors who resisted both Inca and Spanish conquest for centuries through mobile cavalry and fortified councils under elected war leaders. Their shamans, the machi, heal and speak to spirits. Use them for stubborn defenders, brilliant guerrilla commanders and forest-hill resistance campaigns.
- Guarani: Forest and river people of farming villages, language and legend, who cultivate manioc and maize and speak a tongue still alive today. Their stories tell of a Land Without Evil. They fit migrating pilgrims, prophetic leaders, jungle guides and keepers of potent healing and plant knowledge.
- Haida: Island seafarers of the Pacific northwest, master carvers of towering totem poles and builders of huge ocean-going cedar canoes. Their society is ranked by clan and crest, and wealth is displayed in feasts. They make ideal raiding sailors, artisan-chiefs and bearers of raven and killer-whale myths.
- Tlingit: Coastal clans of carvers, traders and fishers who host lavish potlatches to confirm rank and honor the dead, ruling a rainforest shore of inlets. Clan crests of raven and eagle matter greatly. They suit status-driven political plots, shrewd merchants and spirit-haunted cedar-and-fjord settings.
- Sami reindeer herders: Arctic herders who follow reindeer across tundra beneath the northern lights, living in tents and singing the ancient joik. Their drummers once guided noaidi in trance journeys. They offer nomadic wanderers, aurora-lit mysticism and quiet folk who know weather, snow and the long dark.
- Ainu: Northern island hunters and fishers who honor bears and other animals as visiting gods, holding the iomante ceremony to send their spirits home. Their embroidered robes and tattooed women are distinctive. They suit forest hunters, reverent spirit-speakers and a people caught between expanding neighbors.
### Guilds and trades across eras
- Merchant guild: Wealthy traders who control markets, prices and contracts, backed by charters, private guards and ledgers thick with debts owed. They bribe magistrates and bankroll wars. Use them as patrons of expeditions, monopolists squeezing a town, or rivals whose caravans make tempting, well-defended targets.
- Thieves guild: Organized underworld syndicate of pickpockets, burglars and fences who divide a city into districts, pay tribute upward and obey strict rules of loyalty. Secret signs and hideouts mark their trade. They give heists, lockpicking mentors, dangerous favors and a rival to the city watch.
- Assassins guild: Secretive brotherhood of contract killers who accept commissions through intermediaries, train for poison, stealth and disguise, and treat murder as a refined craft. Their code forbids unsanctioned kills. They offer chilling antagonists, reluctant employers, and a ruthless web of obligations to escape or exploit.
- Mages guild: Organized spellcasters who license and regulate magic, run academies and libraries, and police forbidden practices. Ranks, robes and politics govern advancement. They provide quest givers, enchanters for hire, rivalry between factions of scholars, and officious enforcers who hunt unlicensed sorcerers.
- Smith's guild: Master metalworkers forging weapons, tools and armor, guarding trade secrets through apprenticeship and a proud mark stamped on every blade. Their forges ring day and night. They supply legendary arms, repair and upgrade services, and stern craftsmen who judge a hero by their worthiness.
- Bardic college: Institution that trains singers, poets and storytellers in music, lore, diplomacy and subtle magic of song. Graduates travel as entertainers, spies and chroniclers. It offers lore-rich mentors, rival performers, historic archives of ballads and heroes who use charm and melody as weapons.
- Scribes' order: Ink-stained record keepers who copy scrolls, draft contracts and keep secrets for kings and temples, trained in rare scripts and codes. Their scriptoria hold forgotten knowledge. Use them for information brokers, forgers, archivists guarding dangerous texts and quiet witnesses to history.
- Mercenary company: Professional soldiers for hire who sell their swords to the highest bidder, organized under a captain with a banner, contract and code of pay. Loyalty lasts exactly as long as the coin. They make useful allies, treacherous rivals, and a ready army for any ambitious lord.
- Pirate brotherhood: Outlaw sailors sharing plunder under a black flag, electing captains, splitting shares by articles and haunting hidden coves. Their ships are fast and their reputation fearsome. They offer sea raids, smuggling networks, treasure maps, and a rough democracy that outlaws and adventurers can join.
- Hunter's lodge: Gathering of trackers and trappers who share tales, kills and wilderness lore around a trophy-lined hall, hunting beasts for pelts and bounty. Members swap tips on monsters and weather. It provides guides, monster-slaying contracts, rugged mentors and a base at the edge of the wild.
- Alchemists' circle: Secretive experimenters brewing potions and chasing transmutation, the philosopher's stone and eternal life from smoky laboratories. They guard recipes jealously and risk explosions and poisoning. Use them for potion suppliers, eccentric mentors, dangerous experiments gone wrong and obsessive seekers of forbidden formulas.
- Sailors' union: Seafaring workers who bargain, strike and protect crews against cruel captains and unsafe ships, pooling funds for widows and injured hands. Their halls keep harbor gossip. They make good sources of passage and rumors, labor politics on the docks, and champions of ordinary deckhands.
## Cultures and peoples
### Europe
- Greek: Ancient and classical Hellenic culture of rival city-states, philosophers, athletes and epic poets, steeped in a crowded pantheon of meddling gods. Hoplites, oracles and sea traders define it. Use it for heroic quests, mythic monsters, political intrigue between poleis and tragic fates decreed by capricious divinities.
- Roman: Disciplined empire builder whose legions, roads, law and aqueducts shaped the Mediterranean, run through senators, generals and gladiatorial spectacle. Civic pride and ambition drive its politics. It offers military campaigns, scheming nobles, arena fighters and a vast bureaucratic machine that can crush or reward heroes.
- Norse: Seafaring raiders, farmers and traders of the northern lands, living by honor, fate and saga, sailing longships and worshipping gods such as Odin and Thor. Skalds, berserkers and shield-maidens flourish. They suit raiding parties, doom-laden prophecies, mead-hall feuds and chilling frost giants.
- Germanic: Forest tribes of central and northern Europe, loyal to war-chiefs who reward followers with rings and feasts, resisting Roman expansion in dark woods. Their myths speak of wild hunts and sacred groves. Useful for fierce barbarian warbands, oath-bound retainers and ancient woodland spirits.
- Celtic: Warrior and druidic peoples of Iron Age Europe, famed for knotwork art, hillforts, bards and cattle raids, honoring sacred groves and the turning seasons. Their tales feature otherworld mounds and shapeshifters. They provide druid mentors, chariot warriors, feasts and haunted, fae-touched landscapes.
- Slavic: Peoples of the eastern European plains and forests whose folklore teems with household spirits, forest dwellers, witches such as Baba Yaga and river maidens. Village life follows seasons and ritual. They offer rich fairy-tale monsters, wise old crones, bold princes and deeply atmospheric woodland adventures.
- Finnish: Northern forest and lake people known for sauna, sisu stubbornness and the epic Kalevala, with wizards like Vainamoinen who sing the world into being. Hunters, smiths and shamans share a mystical north. Use them for rune-singers, tireless survivors and magic that works through song.
- Baltic: Pagan-descended peoples of the Baltic shore, whose amber trade, hillforts and sky-and-thunder gods held out against crusaders for centuries. Folk songs preserve ancient names. They suit amber merchants, stubborn defenders of sacred groves and eerie rites of forest and storm.
- British and Irish: Island cultures woven from Celtic, Roman, Saxon and Norman strands, with castles, knights, hedge witches, fairy mounds and legendary kings such as Arthur. Weather and ruins lend atmosphere. They provide chivalric romance, haunted moors, clever tricksters and tangled feuds among lords and clans.
- French: Culture of chivalry, cathedrals, wine, courtly intrigue and revolution, from Charlemagne's paladins to musketeers and peasants of the countryside. Elegant etiquette hides sharp politics. Use it for swashbuckling duels, scheming courtiers, fairy-tale castles and sweeping social upheaval.
- Iberian: Peninsula cultures shaped by Moorish, Christian and Jewish interplay, from conquistadors and knights to flamenco-singing villagers and sea explorers. Reconquista warfare, mountain bandits and bustling ports define it. It supports adventures of faith, rivalry, daring voyages and cultural crossroads.
- Italian: Heirs to Rome who produced city-states, merchant princes, artists, condottieri and the Church's heart. Rival families duel with poison and patronage. It offers Renaissance intrigue, brilliant inventors, vendettas, and a sunlit landscape of ruins, vineyards and masked carnival.
- Icelandic: Isolated volcanic-island settlers who preserved the sagas, practiced lawspeaking at the Althing and share a landscape of elves, trolls and hidden folk. Feuds fester slowly over generations. Use them for grim blood-feuds, poets, outlaws in lava fields and hospitality tested by harsh winters.
- Scandinavian: Peoples of Sweden, Norway and Denmark, from Viking raiders to later fishermen and farmers, rich in trolls, nisse household spirits, midsummer festivals and long dark winters. Cooperation marks village life. They suit mountain trolls, fjord settings, folk magic and cozy yet uncanny tales.
- Sami: Indigenous reindeer people of the far north, with shamanic drums, joik chanting and sacred stones, moving with the seasons across tundra and forest. Their spirit world is closely tied to land and animals. They offer noaidi mystics, herders and guides through arctic wilderness.
- Romanian: Carpathian culture of mountain villages, boyars, shepherds and a dense folklore of strigoi, vampires, werewolves and fate-spinning spirits, with the shadow of Vlad the Impaler. Orthodox ritual mingles with older superstition. Fits gothic horror, haunted castles and warding charms.
- Hungarian: Descendants of mounted steppe horsemen who settled the Danube plain, mixing fierce warrior pride with folk music, paprika-laden feasts and tales of the miraculous stag and wondrous hunters. Castles dominate the plain. Use them for horse-archers, noble hussars and legends of white horses.
- Balkan: Mountainous crossroads of Slavic, Greek, Ottoman and Byzantine heritage, with clan loyalties, blood feuds, haidouk outlaws and vampiric folklore. Borders shift and old grudges linger. Good for brigands in the hills, rival faiths, mountain fortresses and tense, treacherous politics.
- Czech: Bohemian culture of castles, alchemists, golems and puppet theaters, with Hussite warriors and the legend of Prague's clockwork and rabbi-made clay giant. Beer halls and forests hide water sprites. Use it for alchemical mysteries, religious rebels and spooky old-town atmosphere.
- Slovak: Mountain people of the Tatras, shepherds and woodsmen with a folk hero in Janosik the outlaw, wooden churches, and legends of sleeping knights beneath hills. Embroidered costumes mark each valley. Fit highland outlaws, shepherd magic and quiet valleys that guard old secrets.
- Polish: Land of winged hussars, proud nobles, amber and forests, with folklore of Slavic spirits, the Wawel dragon and wise witches. Resilient through partitions and invasions. Use them for cavalry charges, noble assemblies, dragon slayers and a culture that survives by stubborn memory.
- Estonian: Small Baltic-Finnic nation of forests, bogs and islands, with ancient runic songs, giant hero Kalevipoeg and reverence for sacred groves and stone. Singing gatherings maintained identity under foreign rule. They suit rune singers, hardy island fishers and gentle, deeply rooted nature mysticism.
- Latvian: Baltic farmers and amber traders whose folk songs, called dainas, hold their gods, sun maiden and winter solstice bonfires. Rural homesteads and river valleys shape tradition. Use them for song-based lore, midsummer rites and quiet, resilient communities guarded by nature spirits.
- Lithuanian (specifics): Last pagan state in Europe, a grand duchy of pagan princes and forest sanctuaries that fought crusaders and expanded to the Black Sea. Sacred oaks, serpent worship and thunder-god Perkunas feature. It offers pagan grand dukes, besieged hillforts and ritual snakes.
- Albanian: Mountain clans governed by the Kanun's oral code of honor, hospitality and blood feud, descended from ancient Illyrians, famed for Skanderbeg's resistance. Besa, the sacred word of honor, binds everything. Use them for feuding clansmen, oath-bound protectors and fierce highland resistance.
- Greek (modern folk): Village Greece of Orthodox saints, nereids, vampires called vrykolakas, evil-eye charms, island fishermen and shepherds, wedding dances. Ancient myths survive as local legend. It suits seaside superstition, protective talismans and cunning peasants in everyday hospitality-driven tales.
- Maltese: Island people at the Mediterranean crossroads, marked by megalithic temples, the Knights of St John, fortified harbors and a Semitic-rooted language. Sea raids and sieges shaped their identity. Use them for knightly orders, corsairs, fortress cities and ancient temple mysteries.
- Swiss: Alpine confederation of cantons, mountain farmers and hardy mercenaries who guarded popes, famous for neutrality, bankers, watchmakers and William Tell's crossbow legend. Cowbells ring over high pastures. They suit disciplined pikemen, mountain guides, precise craftsmen and secret vaults.
- Alpine: Highland communities of the Alps who live with avalanches, passes and glaciers, tending cattle and carving masks for winter spirits like Krampus and Perchten. Isolation bred strong folk custom. Use them for mountain pass guardians, masked ritual processions and wild spirits.
- Austrian: Habsburg heartland of emperors, waltzes, coffee houses and baroque palaces, with Alpine villagers and Tyrolean rebels. Court ceremony and music define the capital. Use it for imperial intrigue, duels and elegant balls hiding conspiracies, plus mountain folk with hunting and yodeling traditions.
- Dutch and Flemish: Lowland peoples who reclaimed land from the sea with dikes and windmills, prospered as merchants and painters, and fought Spanish rule. Guilds, canals and stubborn independence are hallmarks. They offer sea traders, burghers, artists and flood-threatened defenders of liberty.
- Roma (Romani) traditions: Wandering people originating in India, traveling in caravans with music, horse trading, fortune telling and fierce family loyalty, and often persecuted. Their tales feature curses and clever tricksters. Use them for itinerant seers, musicians, craftsmen and resilient clans with deep oral memory.
- Faroese and Greenlandic: North Atlantic islanders living by fishing, whaling and sheep on cliff-ringed, fog-wrapped rock, with ballad chains, seal-folk legends and hidden huldufolk. Settlements cling to fjords. They suit remote storm-bound communities, selkie tales and hardy sea hunters.
- Cornish and Manx specifics: Celtic island and peninsula cultures of tin mines, sea cliffs and fishing coves, with piskies, knockers, the Buggane and Manx fairy bridge superstitions. Smugglers and wreckers haunt the coast. Use them for miner spirits, haunted headlands and charm-wielding villagers.
- Irish Traveller and wandering folk: Itinerant communities of tinkers, horse dealers and tinsmiths who travel the roads in caravans, with their own cant language and strong kin ties. Fairs and weddings gather them. They provide wandering craftsmen, wise-women, storytellers and outsiders who know every back road.
### Middle East and Central Asia
- Arabian: Desert and trading peoples of the peninsula, from caravan cities to oasis dwellers, steeped in poetry, hospitality, camel herding and tales of djinn, flying carpets and lost cities. Honor and tribal lineage matter. Use them for sandy epics, bazaars and wonder-filled legendary journeys.
- Persian: Heirs of great empires, with poets, gardens, fire temples and kings such as Cyrus, plus a mythology of heroes, divs and the simurgh. Courtly refinement coexists with battle prowess. It offers lavish courts, mounted archers, miniature-painted epics and cunning viziers.
- Mesopotamian: Cradle of cities between two rivers, with ziggurats, cuneiform tablets, priest-kings and gods like Marduk, Ishtar and Enki, plus Gilgamesh's quest for immortality. Floods and canals sustain farming. Use for ancient temples, scribes, demons and epic heroism in the first cities.
- Hebrew: Ancient people of Israel and Judah, shaped by covenant, prophets, judges and kings, with law, temple ritual and rich scripture. Wandering, exile and return form their story. They fit prophetic figures, scribes, shepherd kings, and moral dramas around faith, trial and survival.
- Turkic: Horse-borne steppe peoples who spread from Central Asia across to Anatolia, organized in clans under khans, with shamanic sky-god Tengri and grey-wolf lineage tales. Yurts and herds travel together. They supply mounted archers, empire founders and wide-horizon nomadic adventures.
- Caucasus: Rugged mountain region of many tribes, languages and fortress towers, famed for hospitality, feuds, horsemen and legends of Prometheus chained to its peaks. Isolated valleys keep distinct customs. Use them for mountain clans, blood vendettas, sword-dancing warriors and secretive highland strongholds.
- Siberian: Vast northern taiga and tundra peoples such as the Evenki and Yakut, practicing shamanism with drums and animal spirits, herding reindeer and hunting in extreme cold. Spirit journeys heal or curse. They suit shamans, trackers and survivors of endless frozen forests.
- Central Asian: Peoples of the steppes, deserts and Silk Road oasis cities, from nomad horsemen to caravan merchants, scholars and poets of Samarkand and Bukhara. Yurts and khanates contrast with mosques and markets. Use them for trade intrigue, horse tribes and fabled cities of learning.
- Bedouin: Nomadic desert Arabs who herd camels and goats, live in black tents and follow strict codes of hospitality, honor and tribal loyalty. Falconry, poetry and star navigation guide their lives. They offer desert guides, raiders, protective hosts and keepers of oral genealogy.
- Kurdish: Mountain people spread across several borders, with clan chiefs, shepherds, fierce fighters and a rich tradition of epic song and folk dance. Their homeland is rugged and contested. Use them for highland warriors, steadfast allies without a state and tales of resistance and kinship.
- Yazidi and Druze traditions: Secretive faiths with syncretic beliefs, closed communities and persecuted histories; Yazidis venerate the Peacock Angel, while Druze hold a hidden doctrine and reincarnation. Initiates guard sacred knowledge. They suit mysterious sects, shrine guardians and tight-knit mountain villages.
- Afghan and Pashtun: Tribal mountain peoples governed by Pashtunwali, a code of hospitality, honor, and revenge, who have repelled empires from Alexander onward. Jirga councils settle disputes. Use them for fierce highlanders, ambush masters in passes, and loyal protectors with unforgiving feuds.
- Uyghur: Turkic oasis people of the Silk Road's Taklamakan edge, known for muqam music, melon-rich bazaars, Sufi shrines and desert caravan lore. Buried cities lie beneath the dunes. Use them for caravan traders, musicians and sand-buried ruins guarded by old stories.
### South Asia
- Indian regional: The many regional folk cultures of India, from Rajasthani bards and Tamil temple towns to Bengali river villages. Each carries its own gods, epics, dress and spirits. Useful as a patchwork of heroes, wandering ascetics, village guardians and trickster tales for varied characters.
- Tibetan: Highland Buddhist culture of the Himalayan plateau, shaped by monasteries, prayer flags and thin air. Lamas, oracles, yak herders and tantric adepts populate its stories. A source of wrathful protector deities, hidden valleys, reincarnation plots and ritual magic.
- Bengali and Bangladeshi: Delta people of rivers, monsoons and rich literary tradition, mixing Hindu, Muslim and folk Baul beliefs. Boatmen, mystic minstrels and tiger-haunted mangrove villagers feature prominently. Offers river spirits, Sundarbans tiger lore and wandering singer-philosophers for story hooks.
- Punjabi and Pakistani: Land of five rivers and the Indus, blending Sikh, Muslim and Hindu heritage. Known for warrior pride, Sufi shrines, harvest festivals and tragic romance ballads. Good for proud soldiers, saintly poet-mystics, bold traders and fierce honour-bound clan feuds.
- Nepali: Mountain kingdom people of Kathmandu valley and high Himalaya, where Hindu and Buddhist traditions overlap. Famous for Gurkha soldiers, Sherpa guides and living goddess traditions. Provides stoic mountaineers, temple guardians, shamanic healers and yeti legends for adventurous settings.
- Sri Lankan: Island culture of Sinhalese, Tamil and Moor communities with Buddhist, Hindu and demon-exorcism traditions. Masked dancers, tea-hill workers and ancient kings shape its lore. Offers devil dancers, giant-tailed yakshas, relic guardians and jungle-reclaimed ruins.
### East and Southeast Asia
- Chinese: Vast, ancient civilization of dynasties, scholars, martial artists and a deep spirit world. Folklore features immortals, dragons, fox spirits and hungry ghosts. A bottomless source of kung-fu heroes, imperial intrigue, alchemists and bureaucratic gods.
- Japanese: Island culture of samurai, shrines and seasonal ritual, rich with yokai and kami. Traditions run from ninja and geisha to tea masters and wandering ronin. Ideal for honour-bound warriors, shapeshifting foxes, haunted castles and spirit bargains.
- Korean: Peninsular culture of hanbok-clad scholars, shamans called mudang and fierce mountain tigers. Folklore includes gumiho nine-tailed foxes, dokkaebi goblins and grim reapers. Offers resilient commoners, shamanic rites, palace conspiracies and trickster goblins who reward or punish.
- Ainu: Indigenous people of Hokkaido and nearby islands who revere kamuy spirits in bears, owls and fire. Known for epic oral poetry, bear festivals and intricate embroidery. Offers hunter-shamans, spirit-sending rituals and a struggle against assimilation as story hooks.
- Okinawan: Island people of the Ryukyus with distinct language, karate origins and priestess-led religion. Noro and yuta women mediate with ancestors and sea gods. Provides martial arts masters, shisa guardian lions, reef spirits and a proud independent kingdom heritage.
- Thai: Culture of Buddhist temples, spirit houses and elaborate royal tradition. Folklore holds ghostly krasue, tiger-spirits, naga and guardian yaksha. Useful for spirit-warding monks, Muay Thai fighters, amulet makers and haunted jungle villages.
- Burmese: Culture of golden pagodas and river plains, blending Theravada Buddhism with the thirty-seven nat spirit cult. Spirit mediums dance in trance at festivals. Provides nat lords, tattooed protective magic, alchemists and royal courts haunted by murdered ghosts.
- Vietnamese: Culture of rice paddies, ancestor altars and a long history of resisting empires. Legends feature dragon ancestors, mountain spirits and the heroic Trung sisters. Offers fierce defenders, village guardian spirits, river dragons and wandering ghosts needing proper burial.
- Filipino: Archipelago people of mixed Austronesian, Spanish and Chinese heritage with rich spirit lore. Aswang, tikbalang and diwata populate its tales, alongside babaylan healers. Good for shapeshifting night predators, tree-dwelling spirits, folk healers and island datu rulers.
- Indonesian: Sprawling island nation of hundreds of ethnic groups, from Javanese courts to Dayak longhouses. Wayang shadow puppetry carries epic tales and spirit magic. Offers dukun healers, volcano gods, pocong ghosts, pirate sultanates and elaborate ritual theatre.
- Malay: Maritime culture of sultanates, trade ports and pencak silat fighters, shaped by Islam over older animist belief. Bomoh healers handle spirits and curses. Provides pontianak ghosts, hantu forest spirits, seafaring raiders and keris blades said to hold souls.
- Balinese: Hindu island culture where daily offerings and temple dance keep balance between good and evil forces. Barong and Rangda battle in sacred performance. Offers masked dancers, trance rituals, rice-terrace priests and demons that must be appeased rather than destroyed.
- Cambodian: Khmer culture heir to the Angkor empire, with temple ruins, apsara dancers and Buddhist devotion. Arak guardian spirits and neak ta village protectors persist. Provides forgotten jungle temples, divine kings, serpent naga lore and survivors of a scarred modern history.
- Laotian: Lowland and highland Lao peoples along the Mekong, devoted to Buddhism with strong spirit traditions. Phi ghosts lurk in forests and fields. Provides naga river lore, spirit-calling baci ceremonies, ancient Plain of Jars mysteries and monks who tame hauntings.
- Miao (Chinese minority): Highland people of southwest China known for silver headdresses, embroidered clothing and ancestral migration songs. Their lore includes butterfly mother origins and gu poison craft. Offers poison-makers, mountain village clans, dragon-boat festivals and fierce resistance against imperial armies.
- Yi (Chinese minority): Mountain people of Sichuan and Yunnan with an ancient script, torch festivals and a priestly bimo tradition. Once ruled by aristocratic clans with strict caste. Offers ritual scholars, warrior nobles, fire festivals and epic genealogies chanted to bind communities.
- Zhuang (Chinese minority): China's largest minority, centered on Guangxi karst hills, famed for antiphonal love songs and bronze drums. Their culture honors the frog god and ancestral heroes. Provides singing contests, rice-terrace farmers, drum-guided rituals and shamanic healers who bargain with ancestors.
- Tibetan-Qiang (Chinese minority): Mountain peoples of the Sichuan borderlands, with Qiang watchtowers, white-stone worship and shaman priests called duangong. They endured earthquakes and conquest. Offers stone-tower fortresses, ritual sheepskin dances, cliff villages and spiritual traditions older than Buddhism in the region.
- Taiwanese Indigenous: Austronesian peoples of Taiwan, including Atayal, Amis and Paiwan, with face tattoos, headhunting history and ancestral spirit belief. Festival songs and weaving carry clan memory. Offers mountain hunters, rainbow-bridge afterlife, ritual elders and the root culture of the wider Pacific.
- Mongolian steppe specifics: Nomadic herders of horse, yurt and open sky who worship Tengri and practice shamanism. Eagle hunters, throat singers and khans define their image. Offers horse archers, spirit-calling shamans, sacred mountains, blue-wolf ancestry and sweeping raids across endless grassland.
- Hmong and highland peoples: Upland farming communities of Southeast Asia and southern China, noted for story cloths, shaman healers and clan loyalty. Spirit journeys retrieve lost souls. Offers refugee survivors, soul-calling shamans, hidden jungle villages and fierce guerrilla traditions shaped by war and migration.
### Africa
- Egyptian: Nile valley civilization of pharaohs, pyramids and a complex afterlife of judged souls. Priests, scribes and embalmers served a pantheon of animal-headed gods. Offers cursed tombs, mummy lords, divine kings, desert guardians and magic words that bind spirits.
- North African/Berber: Amazigh and Arab peoples of the Maghreb, from Atlas mountains to Saharan oases. Tuareg veiled nomads, Sufi saints and corsair ports mark the region. Offers caravan raiders, djinn-haunted dunes, fortified granaries and marabout holy men.
- Central/East African: Diverse cattle herders, farmers and lake peoples of the Rift region, including Maasai, Kikuyu and Buganda. Elders, warrior age-sets and diviners hold social order. Offers lion-hunting warriors, rainmakers, sacred groves and kingdoms around the Great Lakes.
- Southern African: Bantu, Khoisan and Zulu-descended peoples of savanna, veld and coast. Sangomas diviner-healers, great Zulu impis and Great Zimbabwe builders feature. Offers ancestral spirit mediums, warrior kings, rain queens, trickster hares and trance-dancing San healers.
- West African: Griots, empires and masquerades from Mali and Benin to Yoruba and Akan lands. Ancestors, orisha and spirit masks shape daily life. Offers storytelling bards, gold-trading kings, trickster spider Anansi, secret societies and powerful bronze-casting guilds.
- Malagasy: People of Madagascar, with Austronesian and African roots, who honor the dead through famadihana bone-turning rituals. Ancestor taboos called fady govern life. Offers lemur spirits, royal tombs, baobab shrines, ombiasy diviners and isolated island ecologies of strange beasts.
- Nubian and Sudanese: Peoples of the upper Nile, heirs to Kush pyramid kings and later Christian kingdoms. Sufi orders, Mahdist movements and riverine villages continue the story. Offers black pharaohs, desert archers, whirling dervishes and ruins drowned or buried by sand.
- Somali: Pastoral nomads of the Horn of Africa, famed for oral poetry, clan law and seafaring trade. Poets shape politics and wage verbal duels. Offers camel-herding clans, sultanates, incense traders, pirate coasts and Sufi saints with shrines on remote ridges.
- Swahili coast: Cosmopolitan Indian Ocean trading cities such as Kilwa, Lamu and Zanzibar, blending Bantu, Arab and Persian culture. Dhow captains and Islamic scholars dominated commerce. Offers monsoon merchants, jinn-haunted coral ruins, sultan courts and spirit-possession cults like the pepo.
- Baka (Central African forest people): Rainforest hunter-gatherers of Cameroon and Congo basin, known for polyphonic song and deep forest knowledge. They honor the forest spirit Jengi. Offers elusive trackers, medicine gatherers, initiation rites and conflicts with logging and outside settlers.
- Mbuti (Central African forest people): Pygmy hunter-gatherers of the Ituri forest who regard the forest as a benevolent parent. Net hunts and molimo song festivals bind the band. Offers skilled tracking, ritual music that awakens the forest, and tension with farmers and outside armies.
- Ethiopian highland specifics: Mountain kingdom heritage of Aksum, Orthodox Christianity and Amhara, Oromo and Tigray peoples. Monolithic rock churches, ark legends and coffee ceremonies mark it. Offers priest-scribes, zar spirit possession, buda evil-eye smiths and the legendary guarded Ark of the Covenant.
- Gullah Geechee (Afro-diaspora): Descendants of enslaved West Africans on the Sea Islands of the American southeast, preserving language, rice craft and spiritual practice. Haints and root work shape belief. Offers conjure workers, haint-blue doors, sweetgrass weavers and preserved African ways.
- Maroons (Afro-diaspora): Communities of escaped slaves who built free settlements in mountains and swamps across Jamaica, Suriname and Brazil. Fierce guerrilla fighters, they preserved African religions. Offers hidden settlements, rebel leaders, obeah and skilled jungle warriors who treated with colonial powers.
### Americas
- Aztec: Nahua empire of Tenochtitlan, ruled by warrior nobility and blood-hungry gods like Huitzilopochtli. Priests, jaguar and eagle knights and merchants shaped its life. Offers obsidian-blade sacrifice rites, floating gardens, calendar prophecy and tributary wars to feed the sun.
- Maya: Classic city-state civilization of astronomer priests, ballgame rivals and glyph-writing scribes. Gods of maize, rain and underworld Xibalba shape their myths. Offers jungle pyramids, divine kings, hero twins, jaguar warriors and cyclical doom by calendar.
- Inca: Andean empire of Cusco, run by a sun-king, road runners and terrace farmers. Mummified ancestors and mountain apus were revered. Offers quipu record-keepers, high-altitude sacrifices, stone masonry fortresses and a vast road network binding diverse peoples.
- Native regional: The wide variety of Indigenous nations across North America, from Plains horse cultures to Pacific Northwest totem carvers and Southwest pueblo builders. Each has its own language, lore and governance. Offers vision seekers, trickster Coyote and Raven, medicine societies and sacred landscapes.
- Amazonian: Rainforest peoples of the Amazon basin, who live along rivers with deep plant knowledge and spirit belief. Shamans use ayahuasca to journey and heal. Offers curare hunters, jaguar-shifters, river dolphin spirits, uncontacted tribes and forest guardians like the curupira.
