- Brazilian: Blended culture of Indigenous, Portuguese and African roots, from the Amazon to the favelas. Capoeira, carnival and Afro-Brazilian faith shape it. Offers boto dolphin seducers, saci one-legged tricksters, backland cowboys, cangaceiro bandits and the curupira.
- Mexican: Modern culture rooted in Indigenous and Spanish heritage, famed for Day of the Dead, mariachi and vibrant folk Catholicism. Offers la llorona, curanderos, lucha libre heroes, alebrijes, witch-owls and revolutionary rebels full of dramatic colour.
- Appalachian: Mountain folk of Scots-Irish, German and Cherokee descent in the eastern American uplands. Granny witches, hollers and ballad singers shape its lore. Offers haints, Jack tales, mining ghosts, moonshiners, bell witches and herb-wise healers living in isolated coves.
- Cajun: French-descended Acadian people of the Louisiana bayou, known for music, spicy food and traiteur faith healers. Swamp life breeds legends of the rougarou and feu follet. Offers werewolves, will-o-wisps, bayou trappers and healers who treat with prayer.
- hoodoo: African American folk magic of the American South, using roots, herbs, candles and charms. Conjure doctors lay tricks and remove curses. Offers mojo bags, crossroads deals, haint-warding blue paint, root workers and personal magic for love, luck and justice.
- American tall tales: Frontier legends of impossibly large heroes such as Paul Bunyan, Pecos Bill and John Henry. Exaggeration and humor mark them. Offers giant lumberjacks, steel-driving men, cowboys riding twisters and comic monsters like jackalopes and hodags.
- Canadian: Northern culture blending Indigenous nations, French voyageurs and British settlers. Forests, ice and long winters shape its myths. Offers wendigo hunger spirits, loup-garou, lumberjack tales, Mountie lawmen and the haunting chasse-galerie flying canoe.
- Taino and Garifuna: Taino were Caribbean island Arawak peoples who worshipped zemis, while Garifuna arose from shipwrecked Africans mixing with Carib people. Both keep ancestral rituals alive. Offers zemi idols, cacique chiefs, ancestor ceremonies and resilient coastal communities.
- Mapuche and Patagonian: Fierce southern Andean people who resisted Inca and Spanish conquest, led by machi shaman healers. Patagonian nomads roamed windswept steppe. Offers machi drum rituals, sacred rewe altars, serpent spirits and hardy hunters of the far south.
- Quechua and Aymara (Andean specifics): Highland peoples of the Andes who maintain Pachamama earth-mother worship and coca offerings. Yatiri ritualists read leaves and the future. Offers high-altitude herders, apu mountain spirits, textile symbolism and ancient traditions persisting under Catholic overlay.
- Metis and First Nations (specifics): Canadian Indigenous peoples and the mixed-heritage Metis, famed fur-trade partners and buffalo hunters. Fiddling, sashes and Red River carts mark Metis identity. Offers resistance leaders, trapper-guides, trickster tales and the weight of treaty and land struggles.
- Louisiana Creole: Mixed French, Spanish, African and Caribbean people of New Orleans and the bayous, with rich cuisine and music. Voodoo queens and free people of colour shaped its history. Offers gris-gris charms, masked balls, quadroon society intrigue and Marie Laveau legend.
- Pennsylvania Dutch: German-descended communities of Pennsylvania, including Amish and Mennonite, who practice braucherei folk healing and hex signs. Plain dress and barn-raisings mark them. Offers powwow healers, protective hex symbols, witch-lore and stern but communal farm folk.
- Cowboy and Texan: Frontier ranch culture of cattle drives, saloons and gunfights, bound by a code of grit and independence. Texas adds Alamo legend and Rangers. Offers lone gunslingers, trail bosses, outlaw gangs, ghost riders and desert showdowns at high noon.
- Greenlandic Inuit: Arctic hunters of Greenland who survive ice, seals and darkness through skill and community. Angakkoq shamans negotiate with the sea goddess Sedna. Offers kayak hunters, drum-dance songs, soul-travel journeys, storm spirits and extreme survival lore.
### Oceania
- Aboriginal Australian: Ancient peoples of Australia with the world's oldest continuous culture, grounded in Dreaming stories and songlines across country. Elders keep law and sacred sites. Offers rainbow serpent, trickster spirits, bush trackers and songlines that map both land and meaning.
- Polynesian: Voyaging peoples of the Pacific triangle who navigated by stars and swell. Shared gods like Tangaroa and Maui, plus tapu rules, unite them. Offers master navigators, demigod tricksters, tattooed warriors, canoe voyages and volcanic island legends.
- Maori: Polynesian people of Aotearoa New Zealand, famed for moko tattoo, haka war dance and rich whakapapa genealogy. Tohunga priests hold sacred knowledge. Offers fierce warriors, taniwha river guardians, carved meeting houses and tapu rules with grave consequences.
- Hawaiian: Island culture of chiefs and kahuna priests, with gods Pele, Kane and Ku. Kapu laws governed life. Offers volcano goddess legends, surfing royalty, night marchers, hula traditions, heiau temples and mana-based spiritual power.
- Melanesian: Diverse peoples of Pacific islands from Fiji to New Guinea, often organized around big-men and sorcery. Hundreds of languages exist. Offers ritual exchange networks, masked spirits, cargo cult prophets, canoe-faring traders and feared sorcerers.
- Micronesian: Atoll and island peoples of the western Pacific, including Chuukese and Marshallese, famed for stick-chart navigation. Spirits and ancestors guard small coral homes. Offers stick-chart navigators, stone money banks, ghost canoes and ocean-bound communities defying isolation.
- Papua New Guinea peoples: Hundreds of distinct tribes in rugged highlands and coastal villages, with bird of paradise finery. Sorcery, bride-price and long-standing warfare mark society. Offers mud-men, spirit houses, sing-sing gatherings, sorcerers and uncontacted jungle clans.
- Fijian: Melanesian-Polynesian islanders with chiefly hierarchy, kava ceremony and fire-walking. Warriors once fought famous cannibal wars. Offers fire-walkers of Beqa, kava rituals, ancestral spirit gods like Degei the serpent and island chiefs commanding war canoes.
- Samoan: Polynesian culture of matai chiefs, fa'a Samoa communal ways and elaborate tattoos called pe'a. Orators hold great power. Offers tattooed chiefs, fono councils, spirit aitu, sea-faring warriors and the legend of Nafanua the war goddess.
- Tongan: Polynesian kingdom with a long maritime empire and stratified nobility. Sacred kings were once separated from daily life. Offers giant trilithon monuments, ocean-going double canoes, royal burial mounds and proud seafarers who raided across the Pacific.
- Tahitian: Society Islands people of lush mountains and lagoons, with arioi performing troupes and ritual temples called marae. Gods Oro and Ta'aroa ruled. Offers dancer-priests, voyaging canoe builders, paradise isle mystique and fierce chiefly rivalries with human sacrifice.
- Rapa Nui (Easter Island): Remote Polynesian island culture that carved massive moai statues and wrote rongorongo script. Birdman cult competed for power. Offers mysterious statue-builders, ecological collapse warnings, birdman races and ancestor-spirits watching from stone faces.
## Religions and belief systems
- Greek: Ancient Olympian religion of gods like Zeus, Athena and Hades, along with heroes, oracles and mystery rites. Myths explain nature and fate. Offers capricious deities, monsters, prophetic Pythia, tragic heroes and curses bound by hubris and divine whim.
- Roman: State religion of household gods, augurs and emperor worship, borrowing heavily from Greek myth. Ritual correctness mattered more than faith. Offers vestal virgins, haruspices, legion standards with divine power and household lares guarding hearths.
- Norse: Viking-age religion of Odin, Thor and Loki, with a doomed cosmos ending at Ragnarok. Seers, berserkers and valkyries shape its lore. Offers rune magic, mead-hall oaths, Yggdrasil travel, giants and heroes seeking glory in Valhalla.
- Egyptian: Religion of Ra, Osiris, Isis and Anubis, with a pantheon tied to the Nile and the weighing of hearts. Priests guarded temple mysteries. Offers embalming rites, heka magic, solar barque journeys, cursed tombs and judgement in the underworld.
- Mesopotamian: Sumerian, Akkadian and Babylonian faith of Enlil, Inanna and Marduk, with gods dwelling in ziggurats. Omen priests and exorcists held sway. Offers demons like Lamashtu, epic quests like Gilgamesh, descent to the underworld and divination by liver.
- Celtic: Iron Age and medieval Irish, Welsh and Gaulish belief in sacred groves, the Otherworld and gods like Lugh and the Morrigan. Druids preserved lore. Offers faerie courts, cursed geasa, sacred wells, heads as power vessels and hero champions.
- Slavic: Pre-Christian beliefs of Perun, Veles and Mokosh, with forest and house spirits. Folk tales mix with later Christian layers. Offers Baba Yaga, leshy, domovoi, rusalka, vodyanoy and heroes bargaining with ancient witches.
- Finnish: Karelian and Finnic belief centered on bear reverence, sauna spirits and the singing wizard Väinämöinen of the Kalevala. Sampo, forest and water spirits abound. Offers rune-singers, shamans called tietäjä, forest haltija and mythic quests across the north.
- Aztec: Nahua religion of Huitzilopochtli, Quetzalcoatl and Tezcatlipoca, with a precarious cosmos that required sacrifice to keep the sun moving. Offers priests in flayed skins, calendar rituals, shapeshifting nahuales, jaguar-eagle warrior orders and cosmic cycles.
- Maya: Religion of cyclical time, divine rulers and cosmic world trees. Gods like Kukulkan and Chaac governed rain and wind. Offers bloodletting kings, underworld ballgame, hero twin myths, jade-masked priests and astronomy-driven prophecy.
- Inca: Sun-centered state religion of Inti and Viracocha, supported by huacas, sacred places. Priests and virgins of the sun maintained cult. Offers mummy veneration, mountaintop capacocha sacrifice, coca divination and huacas that speak.
- Aboriginal: Dreaming-based belief in ancestral beings who shaped land and law. Sacred sites and songlines carry moral and practical knowledge. Offers rainbow serpent, clever men, ritual ceremonies, totem kin and cosmic order bound to specific places.
- Polynesian: Pacific belief in gods like Tangaroa, Tane and Pele, along with mana and tapu governing power and restriction. Chiefs and priests mediated. Offers navigator priests, demigod Maui stealing fire, sacred marae and curses from broken taboo.
- Judaism: Monotheistic covenant faith of the Hebrew people with law, prophets and ritual calendar. Rabbis, cantors and scholars interpret sacred texts. Offers golems, dybbuks, angels, prophets, wandering exile themes and mystical ideas of tikkun and covenant.
- Christianity (beings and archetypes): Angels, demons, saints, martyrs, apostles and the Devil, drawn from scripture and medieval tradition. Hierarchies of heaven and hell structure its cosmos. Offers seraphim, fallen angels, miraculous saints, exorcists, inquisitors and apocalyptic horsemen.
- Islam: Monotheistic faith centered on the Quran and Muhammad, with five pillars and a global community. Scholars, judges and mystics shape practice. Offers djinn and angels, pilgrim caravans, calligrapher-scribes, ascetic dervishes and tales from the Thousand and One Nights.
- Hinduism: Diverse tradition of many gods such as Shiva, Vishnu and Devi, with karma, rebirth and yogic paths. Epics like Mahabharata guide it. Offers avatars, sadhus, demon asuras, divine weapons, temple priests and cosmic cycles of creation and destruction.
- Buddhism: Path of awakening taught by the Buddha, emphasizing impermanence and compassion. Monks, nuns and teachers spread it across Asia. Offers bodhisattvas, wrathful guardians, hungry ghosts, rebirth realms, temple martial monks and meditation-born powers.
- Zoroastrianism: Ancient Persian dualist faith of Ahura Mazda against Angra Mainyu, with sacred fire and ritual purity. Magi priests tend flames. Offers fire temples, towers of silence, divine yazatas, final judgement bridge and cosmic struggle between truth and lie.
- Daoism: Chinese philosophy and religion of the Dao, with immortals, alchemy and ritual priests. Followers seek harmony and longevity. Offers elixir-brewing alchemists, talisman-wielding exorcists, mountain hermits, feng shui and the Eight Immortals.
- Shinto: Japanese native faith of kami spirits in nature, shrines and ancestors, centered on purity and festival. Priests and miko maidens serve. Offers torii gates, sacred swords, fox messengers of Inari, purification rites and spirits dwelling in rocks and trees.
- Jainism: Indian ascetic faith emphasizing ahimsa nonviolence, karma purification and liberation of the soul. Monks sweep paths to avoid harming insects. Offers tirthankara saints, fasting ascetics, sky-clad monks, strict vows and a cosmic cycle of time.
- Sikhism: Monotheistic Punjabi faith founded by Guru Nanak, stressing equality, service and devotion. Khalsa warriors keep the five Ks. Offers saint-soldiers, langar communal kitchens, the Guru Granth Sahib scripture and a tradition of defending the oppressed.
- Vodou: Afro-Haitian religion with lwa spirits like Papa Legba and Baron Samedi, served by houngans and mambos. Drums and possession connect worlds. Offers crossroads gates, zombie lore, veves, spirit possession and syncretism with Catholic saints.
- Catholic roles and saints (Christianity): Roman Catholic priests, bishops, nuns, monks and patron saints, with sacraments and relic veneration. Inquisitors and exorcists form darker archetypes. Offers miracle workers, martyrs, relic quests, holy orders and patron saints for every trade.
- Orthodox roles and saints (Christianity): Eastern Orthodox clergy, monastic elders, icon painters and holy fools, rooted in Byzantine tradition. Mount Athos monks and desert fathers inspire. Offers wonder-working icons, hesychast mystics, staretz spiritual guides and liturgy thick with incense and chant.
- Protestant roles (Christianity): Reformation-descended preachers, reformers, missionaries and lay prophets rejecting papal authority. Puritans, Methodists and revivalists vary widely. Offers fiery itinerant preachers, witch-hunting magistrates, plain-living congregations and tent revival healers.
- Coptic roles and saints (Christianity): Egyptian Christian monks, desert fathers and martyrs of the oldest Christian churches in Africa. Monasteries preserve ancient liturgy. Offers hermit ascetics, wonder-working saints like St. Anthony, icon-lined churches and endurance under persecution.
- Sunni imam (Islam): Prayer leader and community scholar of the majority Muslim tradition, trained in law and Quranic recitation. Judges and muftis issue rulings. Offers wise jurists, mosque custodians, community mediators and conservative authority figures guiding daily life.
- Shia imam (Islam): Revered successors of Ali in Shia belief, plus clerics like ayatollahs who interpret law. Karbala martyrdom shapes ritual mourning. Offers hidden imam messianic hopes, passion plays, scholar-jurists, devoted pilgrim processions and themes of righteous suffering.
- Sufi mystic (Islam): Islamic mystics who seek union with the divine through dhikr remembrance, poetry and trance. Orders include whirling dervishes. Offers wandering dervishes, saintly shrine keepers, poet-lovers like Rumi, miraculous healers and ecstatic ritual.
- Theravada monk (Buddhism): Forest and village monks of the Pali tradition across Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, following strict vinaya rules. Meditation seeks arhat enlightenment. Offers amulet-blessing monks, forest ascetics, alms-round walkers and masters of jhana trance.
- Mahayana bodhisattva (Buddhism): Compassionate figures of East Asian Buddhism who delay nirvana to save beings, like Guanyin and Manjushri. Pure Land and Chan schools thrive. Offers merciful saviors, temple sages, vow-keeping monks and celestial helpers.
- Vajrayana lama (Buddhism): Tantric teachers of Tibet and the Himalaya who use mantra, mudra and visualization. Tulkus are recognized reincarnations. Offers wrathful deity yidam practice, sky burial, mandala painters, oracle monks and secret initiation lineages.
- Zen master (Buddhism): Teachers of Chan and Zen in China and Japan, who use koans, zazen and sudden insight. Monastery life is austere. Offers sword-saints, tea masters, paradoxical riddles, calligraphy, rock gardens and shouting abbots who strike the unready.
- Shaiva devotee (Hinduism): Worshippers of Shiva, including ash-smeared sadhus, Aghori ascetics and lingam temple priests. Yoga and fierce austerity define them. Offers cremation-ground mystics, trident-bearing wanderers, cosmic dancers and ascetics with dangerous powers.
- Vaishnava devotee (Hinduism): Worshippers of Vishnu and his avatars Rama and Krishna, emphasizing bhakti devotion. Temples, kirtan chanting and pilgrimage are central. Offers kirtan singers, temple priests, devoted pilgrims and heroes inspired by divine incarnations.
- Shakta devotee (Hinduism): Worshippers of the Goddess in forms like Durga and Kali, often through tantric rites and fierce festival. Shakti is cosmic power. Offers blood-fed temple rites, tantric adepts, warrior goddess invocations and fierce maternal protection.
- Hasidic rebbe (Judaism): Charismatic leaders of pious Eastern European Jewish communities, emphasizing joy, song and devotion. Courts gather around the rebbe. Offers miracle-working tzaddikim, ecstatic dancers, tale-spinning masters and tightly knit communities in black coats.
- Kabbalistic mystic (Judaism): Jewish mystics who study the Zohar and sefirot, seeking hidden divine structure. Practical Kabbalah uses names of power. Offers golem makers, amulet scribes, angelic names, soul-ascent meditations and forbidden secrets of creation.
- Baha'i: Faith founded in nineteenth-century Persia teaching unity of religion and humanity, with figures Baha'u'llah and Abdu'l-Baha. Communities elect spiritual assemblies. Offers persecuted idealists, nine-sided temples, interfaith pioneers and peaceful reformers resisting oppression.
- Mandaeism: Gnostic baptizing faith of Iraq and Iran, revering John the Baptist and rejecting Jesus. Priests perform repeated river baptisms. Offers river-water rituals, light-world cosmology, ancient scrolls, persecuted minority and mystical cosmic ladders of ascent.
- Yazidi: Kurdish people with an ancient faith centered on Melek Taus, the Peacock Angel, and sacred Lalish valley. Caste-based priesthood guards secret hymns. Offers persecuted survivors, peacock angel lore, fire and sun reverence and misunderstanding as devil worshippers.
- Druze: Secretive faith born from Ismaili Islam in the Levant, with belief in reincarnation and the divine Caliph al-Hakim. Initiated uqqal guard the doctrine. Offers closed mountain communities, hidden wisdom, fierce clan loyalty and a veil of mystery to outsiders.
- Rastafari: Jamaican faith revering Haile Selassie I as divine, with Ethiopian zion longing and Babylon opposition. Dreadlocks, ganja and reggae drumming express it. Offers nyabinghi drum gatherings, prophetic elders, resistance against oppression and a return-to-Africa dream.
- Santeria: Afro-Cuban faith merging Yoruba orisha worship with Catholic saints, led by santeros and babalawos. Divination uses cowrie shells. Offers orisha possession, sacrificial rites, beaded necklaces, initiation in white and spiritual guardians like Elegua.
- Candomble: Afro-Brazilian religion honoring orixas, led by mae and pai de santo in terreiro houses. Drumming and dance invite possession. Offers initiation seclusion, orisha spirits like Iemanja and Xango, offerings of food and strong community ties.
- Umbanda: Brazilian spiritist religion mixing Kardecist spiritism, Afro-Brazilian faith and Catholic imagery. Mediums channel caboclos and preto velhos. Offers wise old slave spirits, indigenous warrior spirits, healing passes and trance mediums at crossroads shrines.
- Obeah: Afro-Caribbean folk magic and sorcery, practiced from Jamaica to Guyana, used for healing, protection and harm. Obeah men and women were feared and outlawed. Offers curses, spirit bottles, duppy ghost control and herbal remedies hidden from authorities.
- Wicca and neopagan paths: Modern nature religions drawing on witchcraft, goddess and horned god worship, seasonal sabbats and ritual circles. Covens train initiates. Offers coven priestesses, spell workers, herbalists, circle casting and eclectic reconstruction of ancient practices.
- Heathenry (Norse revival): Modern revival of Germanic and Norse belief, honoring Aesir and Vanir with blot and sumbel. Kindreds gather around oaths. Offers goði priests, rune casters, hall rituals, ancestor veneration and reconstructed Viking-age customs.
- Druidry: Modern and ancient Celtic nature spirituality, with ritual in groves and stone circles. Bards, ovates and druids represent three paths. Offers solstice ceremonies, tree lore, sacred oaths and keepers of memory and wisdom in forest sanctuaries.
- Hellenism: Modern reconstruction of ancient Greek religion, honoring Olympian gods with libations and festivals. Practitioners emphasize piety and household cult. Offers offering rites, hearth devotion to Hestia, philosophical devotion and temple festivals reviving classical tradition.
- Kemetism: Modern reconstruction of ancient Egyptian religion, honoring neteru through offerings and festivals. Followers practice ma'at ethics. Offers shrine-keeping priests, divine name invocation, Opet festival revivals and ritual cleanliness inspired by temple practice.
- Slavic Rodnovery: Modern Slavic native faith movement reviving worship of Perun, Veles and Mokosh in groves and at festivals. Volkhvy lead rites. Offers fire festivals, ancestral gods, folk magic, kupala night rites and strong ties to land and heritage.
- Animism and shamanism (general): Worldwide traditions where spirits inhabit animals, rocks and rivers, and shamans travel between worlds in trance. Drums, plants and chants aid them. Offers soul-retrieval healers, spirit guides, taboos, possession and negotiation with unseen powers.
- Tengrism and Bon: Tengrism is the sky-god faith of Turkic and Mongol steppe peoples; Bon is Tibet's pre-Buddhist indigenous tradition of shamans and ritual. Both honor sky and mountain spirits. Offers eternal blue sky, sacred mountains, ritual priests and ancient practices persisting beneath later religions.
- Cao Dai: Vietnamese syncretic religion founded in 1926, blending Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism and Christianity under the Divine Eye. Saints include Victor Hugo and Sun Yat-sen. Offers spirit-mediumship seances, colorful pagodas, hierarchical clergy and prophetic messages.
- Tenrikyo: Japanese new religion founded by Nakayama Miki, centered on joyous life and healing dance. Followers aim for a Joyous Life world. Offers pilgrimage to Jiba, healing rites, prophetic founder, communal service and a cosmic parent deity.
- Chondogyo (new religions of East Asia): Korean religion arising from the Donghak movement, teaching that humans are heaven. Rebels once rose for its cause. Offers peasant reformers, revolutionary prophets, incantation practice and egalitarian doctrine opposed to corrupt rulers.
- Manichaeism: Ancient Persian dualist religion founded by Mani, teaching a war of light against darkness. Elect and hearers formed its community. Offers gnostic cosmology, missionaries along the Silk Road, ascetic purity and persecuted heretic scriptures.
- Mithraism: Roman mystery cult of Mithras the bull-slayer, popular among soldiers, with initiation grades and underground mithraea. Banquets were sacred. Offers secret handshakes, cave temples, seven grades from Raven to Father and sacrificial bull-slaying iconography.
- Orphism: Greek mystery tradition attributed to Orpheus, with afterlife teachings, vegetarian purity and sacred poems. Initiates carried gold tablets to guide souls. Offers descent-to-underworld lore, Dionysian ties, ascetic purity and secret gospels of rebirth.
- mystery cults: Ancient secret religions such as Eleusis, Dionysus and Isis, promising initiates a better afterlife through rites. Oaths bound members to silence. Offers initiation rites, hidden knowledge, ecstatic revels and secret societies with masked ceremonies.
- Theosophy: Nineteenth-century esoteric movement founded by Helena Blavatsky, blending Eastern and Western occultism with hidden Masters. Society members seek universal brotherhood. Offers astral travelers, ascended masters, root races lore, seance scandal and occult scholars.
- Spiritualism: Victorian movement of contacting the dead through mediums, seances and automatic writing. Table-rapping drew crowds. Offers fraudulent and genuine mediums, ectoplasm, spirit guides, trance lecturers and rising supernatural investigations.
- Thelema: Occult philosophy by Aleister Crowley, summarized as Do what thou wilt, with the Book of the Law. Magick rituals pursue True Will. Offers ceremonial magicians, sex magick, Abbey of Thelema, Horus aeon prophecy and controversial adepts.
- Hermeticism: Western esoteric tradition tied to Hermes Trismegistus, alchemy, astrology and as above so below. Renaissance magi revived it. Offers alchemists, Emerald Tablet sayings, planetary magic, sealed secret societies and the quest for transformation.
- Cargo cults and prophet movements: Melanesian and other movements awaiting ancestral goods or liberation through ritual, often imitating foreign technology. Prophets lead followers. Offers bamboo airstrips, charismatic leaders, millennial expectation and colonial-era resistance wrapped in religion.
- Ancestor veneration: Widespread practice of honoring the dead through altars, offerings and festivals, found in China, Africa and beyond. Ancestors protect or punish. Offers ghost festivals, family shrines, spirit appeasement and hungry ghosts when rites are neglected.
- Santa Muerte (folk saint): Mexican skeletal folk saint, the Holy Death, venerated by outcasts and the desperate with candles and offerings. Robed Lady Bone grants protection and justice. Offers shrine keepers, narco devotees, dark miracle workers and Church condemnation.
- Saint Expedite (folk saint): Folk saint of urgent causes in New Orleans and Latin America, invoked for quick results with cake and pound-cake offerings. Said to be a Roman centurion. Offers last-minute miracles, small shrines, hurried petitioners and legends of a mislabeled crate.
- Other folk saints (etc.): Unofficial saints venerated outside church approval, such as Jesus Malverde, Gauchito Gil, San La Muerte and Don Pedrito Jaramillo. Devotees leave offerings for protection and favors. Offers outlaw patrons, roadside shrines, healers and uncanonized miracle workers.
## Europe (remaining)
### Czech, Slovak, Polish
- Vodník: A Czech water goblin, green-skinned and frog-like, who lives beneath millponds and keeps drowned souls trapped in upturned porcelain teacups. He is cranky but bargainable, trading safe passage for offerings. Players can free the captive souls or negotiate with him.
- Rusalka (Czech): The pale spirit of a young woman who drowned, often through heartbreak or betrayal, and who now haunts lakes and rivers with long wet hair and sorrowful eyes. She lures men to the depths with song, yet longs for release, making her tragic rather than purely hostile.
- Krakonoš: A bearded giant spirit lord of the Giant Mountains, who strides the peaks in a hunter's cloak and shapes the weather at will. He rewards the humble and honest with gifts, but punishes arrogant travellers with storms, fog and lost paths.
- Zmok: A house dragon of Slavic lore, a fiery serpent or flying creature that slips down chimneys to bring stolen grain and wealth to its master. It is loyal while fed well, but jealous and destructive if neglected or betrayed.
- Golem of Prague: A towering clay giant brought to life by a rabbi's sacred word to protect the Jewish quarter from persecution. Silent, tireless and immensely strong, it obeys its maker literally. The danger is its rampage if the animating word is removed or misused.
- Wawel Dragon: A fire-breathing beast that dwelt in a cave beneath Krakow's Wawel Hill, devouring livestock and townsfolk until a clever cobbler fed it a sulphur-stuffed sheep. It suits a boss defeated by cunning rather than brute force, with a thirst-driven weakness.
- Strzyga: A Polish vampiric hag born with two souls and two sets of teeth, who feeds on blood and life from sleeping victims at night. She appears as a sickly old woman or pale revenant. Burying the body face down or destroying its second soul can end her.
- Utopiec: The vengeful spirit of a drowned man, a pale, bloated water demon in Polish folklore who drags swimmers under to claim company in death. He gathers souls in jars beneath the surface. Those who respect the water and offer prayers may escape him.
- Leszy (Polish): A shape-shifting forest guardian who appears as a tall bearded man with green eyes, barkish skin and shoes worn on the wrong feet. He leads travellers astray among the trees but spares those who show respect, making him a moody warden.
- Bies: A horned, goat-legged demon of Slavic belief who tempts, torments and possesses mortals, whispering sins and sowing discord in villages. He can take human form to bargain for souls. Holy symbols and steadfast faith drive him off, offering moral tests for heroes.
- Boginka: A marsh sprite of Polish folklore, a pale, beautiful woman of the wetlands who steals unbaptised infants and leaves sickly changelings behind. She is shy and hard to catch in the open. Protective charms and iron keep her from cradles, giving a haunting village hook.
- Płanetnik: A weather wizard who rides storm clouds, directing hail, wind and rain over farmland, either blessing or ruining the harvest. Born with a caul and gifted with sky-sight, he can be hired by villages or provoked by slights. His power fades if the clouds are broken.
- Jánošík: A legendary Slovak highwayman and folk hero who robbed the rich and shared with the poor, outwitting soldiers with agility and magic belt-powers. Betrayed and hanged on a hook through the rib, he became a symbol of defiance. He is ideal as a charismatic outlaw ally.
- Baba Dziwozona: A wild woman of Polish forests, a huge, shaggy-haired crone with long, heavy breasts she slings over her shoulders. She lives in lonely thickets, steals children and is both feared and sought for forest wisdom. Clever travellers can trick her or bargain for her secrets.
- Wolf-knight of Krakow: An armored horseman who guards the city, cloaked in wolf pelts and borrowing a pack's cunning and howling signals to ambush invaders. Stoic and disciplined, he patrols the walls by night. His loyalty to the city is his strength and the lever others use against him.
### Estonian, Latvian, Lithuanian
- Kratt: A servant made of straw, hay or household scraps, brought to life by a pact with the devil who gives it a drop of the owner's blood. It steals wealth and fulfills tasks tirelessly, but must be kept busy with impossible chores or it will turn on its master.
- Äiatar: An Estonian sun-maiden whose beauty and magic could swell with the sun's glow, said to dwell in the skies and sometimes descend as a dazzling woman. She shapes seasons and light and inspires wonder. Her story offers a radiant ally whose mood sways the harvest.
- Tuuletark: An Estonian wind lord and sage of the skies, an old, wise being who commands gales and breezes and can be coaxed by sailors with song and offerings. He rides storms in a swirling cloak. His favour fills sails, while his anger scatters ships and crops.
- Päkapikud: Christmas elves of Estonian lore, small bearded helpers who hide in houses and are rewarded with treats left in shoes. They watch behaviour through winter and bring small gifts or mischief accordingly. They serve as whimsical informants, minor boons and playful pranksters.
- Velns: The Latvian devil, a cunning trickster who steals souls, bargains with peasants and is often outwitted by clever farmers. He appears as a shaggy black figure with horns and a tail, equal parts menace and comedy. He excels at fair-seeming deals with cruel fine print.
- Laima: A Baltic goddess of fate who spins the thread of each person's life and decides their fortune at birth, often appearing as a gentle woman near cradles and water. She is both generous and stern. Heroes may plead, bargain or defy her decrees at their peril.
- Dievs: The Baltic sky god, a distant, fatherly deity who watches over order, harvests and righteousness from the heavens. He rarely intervenes directly, instead sending omens, rain and blessings through lesser spirits. Players might encounter his judgment through weather and sacred oaths.
- Aitvaras: A house spirit that appears as a fiery rooster or flying dragon-bird, bringing stolen grain, milk and gold to its owner at night. It is precious but dangerous, since it burns the house if mistreated. Gaining it requires dark rites, and getting rid of it is harder.
- Laumė: A fairy-witch of Lithuanian folklore, a beautiful and capricious woman who weaves cloth by moonlight, steals children, and aids or curses households by whim. She loves bathing in streams and can be trapped by taking her garments. Her gifts of craft and luck always cost something.
- Kaukas: A tiny gnome-like household spirit that dwells in ovens and attics, helping with chores in return for food, warmth and respect. He can bring prosperity and protection but turns mischievous if neglected or mocked. Kind hosts earn a loyal companion with small boons.
- Perkūnas: The Baltic thunder god, a mighty, bearded warrior who rides a chariot across storm clouds and hurls lightning at devils and oath-breakers. He fights the underworld rival Velnias and fertilises the earth with rain. A towering patron for storm-themed champions and oath-bound warriors.
- Vilkolakis: A werewolf of Lithuanian lore, a human cursed or born under unlucky stars who transforms into a huge wolf at night. Often a victim of fate rather than a monster by choice, he guards or preys depending on the moon. His condition can be broken by ritual or kindness.
- Raganas: Witches of the Baltic lands, village women versed in curses, healing and shape-changing who gather on hilltops for midnight rites. Some serve the community and others spoil milk, harvest and health. They suit morally grey antagonists or uneasy helpers with sharp bargains.
### Albanian, Greek (folk), Maltese
- Kulshedra: A great Albanian dragon-hag, a monstrous multi-headed serpent woman who withholds water and floods the land, demanding sacrifices from villages. She spits fire and venom and rules lakes and wells. Only a drangue hero wielding lightning-born skill can slay her.
- Drangue: A winged hero-spirit born with a sign of a wing or sword mark, fated to fight the kulshedra and defend his people from storms and drought. Strong, noble and tied to the weather, he duels in thunderclouds. He suits a protector archetype with a fated, lonely burden.
- Zana e Malit: A mountain fairy of Albanian legend, a graceful and fierce guardian of peaks and wildlife who rewards the brave and punishes those who defile nature. She heals wounded heroes with herbs and sings across valleys. She works well as a guide, patron or wild judge.
- Shtriga: A night witch who creeps into houses as a moth or fly to drain the life of sleeping infants and the sick. By day she appears as an ordinary old woman. Cut her down with blessed implements or trick her to eat salt, and a village mystery builds around her secrecy.
- Lugat: A shadowy Albanian revenant or vampire that rises from the grave to prey on the living and spread sickness through villages. Pale, hungry and cunning, it flees from fire and holy symbols. It suits a creeping horror foe whose hunt starts with unexplained deaths in a hamlet.
- Greek vrykolakas: A restless vampire corpse of Greek folk belief, bloated and ruddy, who rises at night to strangle victims, knock on doors and call people by name. Those who answer will die. Dismemberment, burning or a priest's rites lay it to rest, giving a village-dread encounter.
- Kallikantzaroi: Mischievous Christmas goblins who emerge from underground during the twelve nights to chew the World Tree, wreck homes and terrify folk. They are dim, ugly, hairy and afraid of fire, salt and holy water. They make for comic yet threatening seasonal foes.
- Nereids (modern folk): Beautiful nymph-like spirits of Greek countryside, living at springs, caves and crossroads, who dance at noon and midnight. They bewitch, curse or lame those who stumble onto their revels, but also grant favours to the respectful. Encounters balance charm with sharp danger.
- Stoicheio: A tied place-spirit in Greek folk belief, bound to a ruin, bridge or well by ritual, often through a sacrificed life, to guard it forever. Invisible yet potent, it brings luck or ruin depending on how it is treated. It makes a puzzle-ready guardian with a tragic origin.
- Maltese Il-Belliegħa (bogey): A lurking bogey of Maltese nursery tales, a gaunt, dark thing said to swallow disobedient children whole who stray near wells or night streets. It hides in shadows and echoing alleys. Its cautionary dread makes a fine horror encounter built on stories told to the young.
- Gaħan: A trickster of Maltese folklore, a clever, scruffy fool whose absurd wit and cunning let him outsmart priests, landlords and devils alike. Always in trouble but never beaten, he wins by wordplay and bluff. Heroes can use him as a comic ally or a slippery foe.
- Sirena: A sea maiden of Maltese coasts whose enchanting songs lure sailors to wreck on rocks or fall beneath the waves. Half-woman and half-fish, she is lovely and deadly, and can be placated with offerings or silence. She suits maritime quests and sailor omens.
- Fairy hill folk of Gozo: Small hidden spirits who dwell in the hills and caves of the island of Gozo, appearing at dusk to dance, tend flocks and tempt shepherds. They are secretive and playful, rewarding kindness with gifts and mocking the greedy. They offer gentle, whimsical encounters on island paths.
### Swiss, Alpine, Austrian
- Krampus: A horned, hairy, cloven-hoofed demon who accompanies Saint Nicholas in Alpine tradition, carrying chains, bells and birch switches to punish naughty children and drag the worst away in a basket. He is a menacing winter figure suited to seasonal horror or punishing duels.
- Perchten: Alpine winter spirits who appear as masked processions of beautiful or hideous figures, banging bells and drums to drive out evil and bless the coming year. The fair Schönperchten bring luck while the ugly Schiachperchten terrify. They suit festival scenes and ritual encounters.
- Tatzelwurm: An Alpine worm creature with a cat-like head, short front legs and a thick scaly body, said to lurk in mountain gorges and hiss venom at hikers. Elusive and territorial, it appears in avalanche country. It makes a classic cryptid for a wilderness exploration encounter.
- Alpine dragon: A winged mountain wyrm that dwells in snowy caves and glacial caverns, hoarding crystals, bones and treasure, breathing frost or fire across the peaks. Ancient and territorial, it descends in storms to claim livestock. It serves as a regional boss with ice-and-cave terrain.
- Wild man of the mountains: A hairy, bearded hermit of the high forests and crags, strong as an ox and gifted with knowledge of herbs, weather and hidden springs. He shuns villages but aids lost travellers who treat him fairly. He offers a wise yet volatile recluse for guidance or confrontation.
- Wilde Jagd: A spectral hunt that rides stormy skies with howling hounds, ghostly horsemen and a pale master, sweeping up the unwary and heralding war or plague. Its horns and baying echo across valleys on winter nights. It brings dread and a chase in which hiding is the only defence.
- Nachtkrapp: A giant night raven of Alpine tales, a shadowy bird with a hoarse cry that snatches unwary children who wander in the dark. It glides silently over moonlit villages, its feathers swallowing light. It serves as a stalking creature of nursery terror and nocturnal ambush.
- Heidi-style goatherd: A cheerful mountain herder who wanders alpine meadows with her flock, barefoot and sunburned, friendly with every traveller and fluent in the language of animals and weather. She knows safe paths, hidden huts and local rumours. She makes a warm, innocent guide or neutral quest-giver.
- Berggeist: A grumpy mountain spirit who guards mines, passes and avalanche slopes, appearing as a gnarled old miner or a towering shadow of rock. He tests travellers with rockfalls and echoes, rewarding respect with ore and safe passage. Disturbing his domain unleashes cave-ins and curses.
- Glacier maiden: An icy spirit woman who lures climbers onto frozen slopes with soft singing and shimmering light, her form blending with snow and crevasse. Beautiful and cold, she claims the lost as companions in ice. She works as a seductive hazard for mountaineering and survival stories.
- Dwarf-king Laurin: A rose-garden dwarf ruler of the Dolomites who owns a cloak of invisibility, a magic belt and a hidden mountain realm. Proud and vengeful, he cursed his garden to be invisible by day or night after a wedding insult. He suits a regal, tragic antagonist.
### Dutch and Flemish
- Klaas Vaak: The Dutch sandman, a gentle old figure who sprinkles magic dust into children's eyes at night so they sleep and dream, appearing with a sack of sand and a soft pipe. He is kind and unobtrusive. He can offer rest, dream-visits or a sleep-spell ally.
- Zwarte Piet: A cheerful assistant to Sinterklaas in Dutch tradition, a costumed helper who tumbles through chimneys, hands out sweets and carries the gift sack. His modern portrayal is controversial and adaptable. He can appear as a playful helper, with changes to avoid offensive stereotypes.
- Nachtmerrie: A nightmare spirit that crouches on sleepers' chests, weighing down breath and filling dreams with dread, sometimes seen as a spectral horse or hag. It feeds on fear and fades at dawn. It suits dream-based encounters where players must wake or fight within the dream.
- Kabouter: A Dutch dwarf or gnome who lives under toadstools and in burrows, helping farmers and gardeners with small chores if treated kindly. Red-capped, bearded and secretive, he can turn mischievous if mocked. He makes a cozy helper or a trickster hindering the disrespectful.
- Witte Wieven: The white women of Dutch folklore, ghostly female spirits who appear in mist over heaths and burial mounds, healing the sick or leading travellers astray. They are ambivalent oracles with ancient roots. Respect brings healing herbs and wisdom, while insult brings fever and bad luck.
- Necker: A water spirit of the Low Countries and Germanic lands, a handsome, green-toothed man or shape-shifting horse who lures people to rivers and pulls them under. He loves music, especially fiddling. Bargains with him grant skill but risk drowning, making a seductive water hazard.
- Hellhound of the dikes: A spectral black dog with burning eyes that haunts flooded lowlands and dike paths at night, its howl presaging storm surges and drownings. It stalks lonely travellers along the embankments. It serves as an omen creature that can guard or doom depending on its mood.
- Plague doctor of Delft: A beaked-mask physician who walks plague-struck streets in a waxed coat, treating the sick with herbs, incense and cautious remedies. Grim yet dedicated, he knows how contagion spreads and who is hiding symptoms. He fits a morally weighty healer or sinister quarantine enforcer.
- Uilenspiegel: A legendary Flemish trickster who roams the countryside with pranks and satire, mocking nobles, clergy and tyrants while playing the fool. Quick-witted and impossible to catch, he turns every trap against the trapper. He is an ideal rogue ally or humorous agent of rebellion.
- Tulip merchant: A speculative trader of the Dutch Golden Age who deals in rare flower bulbs worth fortunes, always sizing up buyers with a slick eye and a ledger. Greedy yet charming, he knows markets and rumours. He can offer rare goods, scams or a high-stakes gambling quest.
### Roma traditions
- Roma fortune teller: A wandering seer who reads palms, cards and tea leaves in colourful scarves and jangling jewellery, offering hints of fate for a coin. Some are charlatans and others truly gifted. Her insights give quest clues, her curses carry weight, and she hides her real knowledge.
- Bori: Wise women of Roma communities who keep remedies, rites and lore, guiding birth, marriage and death with practical authority. Respected and sometimes feared, they bless or withhold luck. They serve as mentors, healers or gatekeepers of tribal law and knowledge.
- Mulo: The living dead of Roma belief, a restless spirit or revenant who returns to visit family, haunt enemies or feed on the living when death rites were neglected. It can appear as a shadowy relative. Proper burial customs and offerings can calm it, giving a ritual-puzzle hook.
- Beng: The devil in Roma folklore, a cunning, often comic tempter who trades in curses, shortcuts and soul-bargains but can be outwitted by clever travellers. He appears as a gaunt stranger, a dark animal or a flame. He is a persuasive antagonist whose deals always hide a snare.
- Dukkerin: A palm reader of Roma tradition who divines fortunes from lines, signs and quiet observation, adapting stories to each client. Equal parts performer and mystic, she gathers gossip and secrets. She can sell cryptic prophecy or use her read of people to manipulate them.
- Wandering horse trader: A nomadic dealer with a sharp eye and silver tongue who travels fairs and roads, selling spirited horses and sly bargains. He can spot weakness in both beasts and buyers. He offers mounts, rumours and the chance of haggling, or a swindle of his own.
- Baro Shero: The head of a Roma clan, an elder chosen for wisdom, fairness and standing who settles disputes, guards traditions and negotiates with outsiders. His word binds the camp, and his favour opens doors. He gives a authoritative quest-giver whose trust must be earned.
- Curse-breaker: A mystic who lifts hexes with charms, herbs and chanted verses, reading the source of the ill-luck and drawing it out with fire, salt or running water. Calm and wary, she knows what feeds a curse. She is a valuable specialist for haunted villages and cursed heroes.
- Vardo guardian: A caravan spirit that watches over the painted wagon and its family on the road, warding off thieves, fire and ill omens with quiet vigilance. Shown as a flicker in the lantern or a shape in the wheels, it expects respect and tradition. It makes a loyal, bound protector.
### Faroese and Greenlandic
- Nykur: A shape-shifting water horse of Faroese lakes, appearing as a handsome grey steed standing by the shore with backward-facing hooves. Anyone who mounts it is bound fast and dragged under to be devoured. Speaking its true name or whispering a charm can break its power.
- Marmennil: A merman of Faroese and Icelandic sea lore, half human and half fish, with weathered features and a shrewd mind. Fishermen who catch one may bargain for fortune or prophecy in exchange for its release. Cheating the bargain brings storms, drownings, and a long grudge.
- Skrímsl: A sea monster of the cold northern waters, often a vast serpentine or many-finned beast glimpsed rising beside fishing boats. Villagers read its appearance as an omen of famine or doom. It makes a perfect boss encounter for a stormy voyage, hunting vessels that stray too far.
- Huldufólk (Faroe): The hidden folk of the Faroe Islands, an unseen people living in rocks, hills and cliffs who look much like humans in finer clothes. They guard their homes jealously and punish those who build on their land. Respect, gifts and quiet courtesy win their help and protection.
- Qivittoq: A mountain outcast of Greenlandic tradition, a person who fled society from grief or shame and wandered into the wilderness until they became a ghostly, half-spirit hermit. Hunters fear its eerie presence in the high ice. It may hurt trespassers or, once pitied, guide a lost traveler home.
- Tupilak: A vengeful monster carved by an Inuit shaman from bone, skin and sinew, then ritually brought to life and sent to hunt a named enemy. It strikes silently from the sea. If its target has stronger magic, it turns on its own creator, a deadly twist for story hooks.
- Sedna: The Inuit goddess of the sea and its creatures, who dwells on the ocean floor with hair tangled by human sins. Her fury withholds seals and whales from hungry hunters. A shaman must dive to her lair and comb her hair, appeasing her to restore the hunt.
- Arctic fox spirit: A white trickster spirit that slips across snow and ice, nearly invisible against the drifts, leaving only pawprints that fade. It leads hunters astray, steals bait, or guides the clever to hidden game. Its playful mischief can turn lethal in blizzards, rewarding patience and cunning.
- Northern lights ancestors: The dancing souls of the dead, glowing green and violet across the polar sky. Some traditions say they play ball with a walrus skull, and whistling at them draws them down. They offer guidance, blessings and warnings, but disrespect invites them to snatch the careless away.
### Cornish and Manx
- Spriggans: Small, grotesque guardians of buried treasure and ancient stones in Cornwall, ugly of face but able to swell to giant size when angered. They guard cairns and barrows, steal children, and blight crops of the disrespectful. Bribery and honest courtesy are the safest way past them.
- Piskies: Mischievous little folk of Cornish moors and hedgerows who delight in leading travelers astray with false lights and winding paths. They tangle horses' manes and pinch careless maids, yet reward kindness with small gifts. Turning a coat inside out or carrying bread breaks their enchantment and sets walkers right.
- Knockers: Tiny spirits of Cornish tin mines who tap and knock within the rock, warning miners of cave-ins or guiding them to rich lodes. Tradition demands leaving a bit of pasty crust as tribute. Whistling or cursing underground offends them, and ignoring their taps brings tragedy.
- Bucca: A Cornish sea spirit, sometimes a bearded old man of the tides, who must be appeased with portions of the catch and drink left on the shore. Generous fishermen enjoy full nets and calm seas. Those who skimp suffer wrecks and storms, making him an ambiguous guardian of coastal communities.
- Mermaid of Zennor: A sea maiden of Cornish legend who was drawn ashore by the voice of a chorister, Mathey Trewella, in Zennor church. She lured him beneath the waves and he was never seen again. Her carved likeness on a bench end endures, a siren story of beauty, music and loss.
- Buggane: A Manx troll-like monster, huge, hairy and ill-tempered, with a ferocious roar and a habit of lurking in ruined churches and caves. It once tore the roof off a half-built chapel in rage. Defeating it usually relies on quick wits, holy ground, or tricking it into leaving.
- Fenodyree: A helpful giant of Manx folklore, a shaggy, strong, hairy farmhand spirit who mows meadows and herds sheep in a single night. He was cast out for failing to understand human customs and wept for his lost home. He is a loyal but easily offended companion.
- Moddey Dhoo: A Manx ghost hound, a huge black shaggy dog with burning eyes that haunts Peel Castle's passages. Soldiers who saw it were stricken with terror, and one who followed it later died mute. It makes an eerie guardian or omen of death in castle ruins and corridors.
- Cabyll-ushtey: A Manx water horse, a handsome stallion that rises from lakes and sea to tempt riders onto its back. Once mounted, the rider is carried into the water and torn apart, leaving only the liver on the shore. Iron and a quick dismount may offer escape.
- Glashtyn: A shaggy water horse spirit that lurks along Manx island shores, sometimes taking the form of a rough-haired man with a taste for stolen cattle. It seizes lone travelers at dusk and drags them toward the sea. It fears iron and crosses, offering clear counterplay to wary players.
- Fairy Bridge guardian: A little folk watcher at the Manx Fairy Bridge, who demands a polite greeting from travelers crossing the stone span. Those who say "Hello, fairies" pass in luck, while the rude suffer mishaps and bad weather. It embodies island superstition and the cost of disrespecting unseen neighbors.
### Irish Traveller and wandering folk
- Tinker: A metalworker nomad who roams Irish roads mending pots, pans and tin vessels from a horse-drawn wagon. Skilled with fire and hammer, he knows the countryside and its gossip. Villages trust his work but remain wary of outsiders, so he makes a fine merchant, informant or crafter of enchanted tin.
- Pavee seer: A wandering fortune teller of the Traveller community who reads omens along the road in tea leaves, palms, birds and weather. Respected and sometimes feared, she delivers warnings that shape journeys. Her prophecies are cryptic and costly, a good source of quest hooks and double-edged advice.
- Horse dealer: A sharp bargainer trading animals at fairs across the countryside, with an eye for good flanks and a tongue for flattery. His skill at patching up poor horses to look sound is notorious. He offers mounts, rumors and deals, though buyers must haggle carefully or be cheated.
- Storyteller: A traveling bard who spins tales around the fire, carrying legends, genealogies and gossip from camp to camp. His voice can calm a hostile crowd or stir listeners to action. He remembers old lore that may unlock secrets, and his stories often hide truth beneath embroidery.
- Cant-speaker: A keeper of the secret language of Irish Travellers, Shelta or Cant, used to speak openly among outsiders without being understood. Fluent in the tongue and its slang, he can pass hidden messages and warnings. Knowing the words earns trust, while mimicry by strangers invites suspicion.
- Fortune teller: A traveling reader of futures who works at fairs and doorways with cards, palms or crystal, trading hope and warning for coin. Some are shrewd entertainers, others truly gifted. Her predictions can steer plots, set traps for the gullible, or reveal danger to a wary party.
- Holy well keeper: A guardian tending a sacred spring and its offerings of ribbons, coins and prayers. Pilgrims seek cures and blessings at the water, and the keeper guides rituals and preserves the well's stories. Offending the spring may sour its power, while respect grants healing and visions.
- Hedge-school teacher: A secret rural tutor who teaches lessons outdoors beneath hedgerows, during times when formal schooling for the Irish was banned. He teaches Latin, Greek, mathematics and local lore, risking arrest. Scholarly yet defiant, he can supply knowledge, spark rebellions, or hide students from authorities.
## Middle East and Central Asia (remaining)
### Bedouin
- Desert guide: An expert navigator leading caravans by stars and wells, reading wind, dune shapes and animal tracks as others read books. He knows every oasis and danger of the sands. Hiring him can mean the difference between survival and a dry grave, though his loyalty is earned by honor.
- Falconer: A hunter who trains falcons to take hare and bustard, bonded with a hooded bird perched on a leather glove. Patient and watchful, he treasures his birds as family and as status. He offers scouting from above, hunting food, and a proud, noble reputation among the tribes.
- Raider chief: A cunning leader of mounted desert plunderers, who strikes caravans and rival camps at dawn and vanishes into the dunes. He follows a code of honor that spares hospitality guests. Both villain and anti-hero, he commands loyal riders and knows secret routes and hidden camps.
- Tribal poet: An honored verse maker preserving clan history and glory in oral poetry, praising allies and shaming enemies with equal skill. His words can make or break reputations and settle feuds. A powerful ally for diplomacy, he also remembers genealogies and old grievances.
- Ghoul of the dunes: A shapeshifting desert monster preying on lost travelers, appearing as a beautiful woman, a stranger or a donkey before revealing its fangs. It feeds on corpses and the dying. Iron, a sharp blade struck once, or steady vigilance can break its illusion.
- Camel rider: A swift desert scout racing across the dunes on a tall dromedary, carrying messages, patrolling wells and shadowing strangers. Tough and sun-weathered, he endures thirst and heat. He provides speed and information, and can lead pursuit or escape across open sand.
- Water-finder: A tracker who senses hidden wells in barren land, reading plant roots, insect flight and subtle changes in sand. Often seen as gifted or blessed, he guides clans to life-saving water. He is invaluable on desert journeys, and rivals would kidnap him to control the oases.
- Storyteller: A tent-side raconteur who weaves tales of heroes, djinn and ancient wars across long desert nights. He keeps traditions alive and entertains guests as a duty of hospitality. His stories carry hidden advice and warnings, and he is a ready source of rumor and lore.
- Sand djinn: A smokeless fire spirit swirling out of desert whirlwinds, capricious and powerful, able to take human or animal shapes. It grants strange favors, but its bargains are twisted and wordplay is dangerous. Solomon's seal, iron or clever phrasing can bind it.
### Kurdish
- Peshmerga (fighter): A Kurdish mountain warrior, literally one who faces death, defending his homeland with rifle, rugged terrain and fierce loyalty. He moves through passes and caves with practiced stealth. Proud and disciplined, he offers formidable skirmishing, guerrilla tactics and resilience in hard country.
- Kurdish shepherd: A highland herder watching flocks over rugged peaks, wrapped in a heavy cloak and carrying a staff and reed flute. He knows hidden trails, weather and wolves. Hospitable but wary, he can offer shelter, news of the mountains, and guidance through dangerous high routes.
- Shahmaran: A queen of serpents with a woman's upper body and a snake's lower body, ruling an underground realm of wisdom and healing. Her knowledge makes her sought by kings, and betrayal by a human leads to her death. She offers cures and secrets at a terrible price.
- Sheikh: A tribal elder and respected leader who settles disputes, mediates feuds and presides over councils with authority earned by age and wisdom. He commands loyalty and hosts guests in his guest tent. A diplomat and judge, he can grant sanctuary or become an obstacle to overcome.
- Dengbêj: A Kurdish bard who preserves history, love stories and battles through unaccompanied sung epics, performing in village houses at night. His memory holds centuries of lore. He is a keeper of identity and rumor, able to inspire a crowd or deliver coded messages in song.
- Mountain sage: A reclusive wise elder of high cliffs and caves, who studies stars, herbs and scripture in isolation. Few reach him, but those who do receive riddling counsel. He may grant a quest, a blessing or a hard lesson, guarding knowledge from those unready for it.
- Cave spirit: A hidden presence haunting mountain caverns, echoing with whispers and cold drafts. It protects sacred places and punishes intruders with confusion, collapse or vanishing paths. Offerings and respect appease it, while greed turns the cave into a labyrinth of dread.
- Nowruz fire keeper: A guardian leading new year bonfire rites, tending the spring-equinox flame that symbolizes freedom, renewal and the defeat of tyranny. Villagers leap the fire to burn away misfortune. He holds ritual knowledge, and his festival provides a vivid setting for celebration, resistance and hidden plots.
### Yazidi and Druze traditions
- Peacock Angel (Melek Taus): The chief angel of the Yazidi faith, a radiant peacock-form being who shaped creation under God's command. Misunderstood by outsiders, he is revered as a benevolent guardian. His jeweled plumage and symbolism of repentance and renewal make him a majestic, enigmatic divine figure.
- Sheikh (spiritual): A Yazidi or Druze religious leader of a hereditary lineage, who guides rituals, offers counsel and maintains spiritual purity. He wears distinct garb and keeps ancient secrets. His blessing is prized, and his moral authority can unite or divide a community.
- Pir: A holy elder who guides disciples and keeps sacred lore, often connected to a lineage of saints. He teaches through parables and ritual, and his word guides marriages, burials and festivals. A mentor figure, he can bestow protection, esoteric knowledge, or stern judgment.
- Ajaweed council: A wise group of elders leading the community, chosen for knowledge of faith and law. They deliberate in private, balancing tradition against outside pressure. Their ruling can grant sanctuary, resolve feuds or exile offenders, making them a powerful institution in any story.
- Mountain village elder: A patient, grey-haired leader of a hill community who knows every family, grudge and harvest. He welcomes travelers with tea and measured questions. Rooted in tradition, he can offer shelter, local history and tasks, and defends his villagers with quiet resolve.
- Hidden-wisdom keeper: An initiate who guards secret teachings across generations, passing them only to worthy successors through oath and ritual. Outsiders see only a humble villager. His knowledge of reincarnation, cosmic cycles and sacred law can unlock mysteries, but extracting it demands trust.
### Afghan and Pashtun
- Pashtun warrior: A proud tribal fighter bound by honor and hospitality, following the code of Pashtunwali that demands revenge for insult and protection for guests. He carries a rifle or blade with practiced pride. Fiercely loyal, he is a formidable ally and a relentless enemy.
- Jirga elder: A council elder who settles disputes by consensus, sitting in a circle with other greybeards to weigh evidence, tradition and compensation. His judgment binds clans. He mediates feuds, brokers peace and can launch or end a conflict with a single ruling.
- Poet-fighter: A warrior bard composing verses between battles, praising comrades and mocking foes in the Pashto tradition of the landay and ballad. His songs rally men and preserve memory. Both swordsman and storyteller, he moves hearts and armies with equal skill.
- Pari: A fairy of Persian and Afghan lore, a beautiful winged spirit of mountains and gardens who can bless or bewitch. Often alluring and capricious, she may marry mortals or lure them astray. Her gifts are generous but come with taboos whose breaking brings sorrow.
- Div: A monstrous demon-giant of Persian and Afghan tales, horned, huge and cruel, dwelling in remote fortresses or ruins. It devours travelers and hoards treasure, defeated only by heroic cunning or strength. A classic villain whose power rivals armies, yet whose pride makes it exploitable.
- Kuchi nomad: A wandering herder moving camps with camels and tents across Afghan plains and passes, following the seasons. Resilient and self-reliant, he trades wool and livestock and knows secret paths. He offers supplies, guidance and rumors, but distrusts authority and borders.
- Buzkashi horseman: A rider fighting for a goat carcass at full gallop in Afghanistan's national game, wielding whips and horsemanship in chaotic contests. Muscular and fearless, he is celebrated for daring. He suits chases, tournaments and mounted combat, bringing speed, strength and reputation.
- Opium trader: A shadowy smuggler moving poppy goods through mountain routes, bribing officials and hiring armed escorts. Wealthy but hunted, he knows hidden passes and corrupt contacts. He can be employer, informant or antagonist, bringing moral gray areas and danger to a story.
- Mountain pass guard: A watchful sentry controlling a narrow high route, collecting tolls, checking caravans and scanning the cliffs for raiders. Cold and weathered, he can be bribed, charmed or fought. He controls the chokepoint of a journey, making him an obstacle, gatekeeper or ally.
### Uyghur
- Silk Road merchant: A trader who moves silk, spices, jade and news across oasis towns on camel caravans, speaking several languages and bargaining with skill. Cosmopolitan and shrewd, he finances expeditions and carries rare goods. He is a prime source of quests, items and gossip from distant lands.
- Muqam singer: A classical vocalist performing epic suites with lute accompaniment, preserving the twelve muqam cycles of Uyghur music. Her voice can last hours, weaving love, mysticism and history. She is an artistic and cultural treasure, able to move courts and rouse spirits with song.
- Sufi pilgrim: A wandering devotee visiting shrines in humble robes, chanting and fasting as he travels the oases. He seeks union with the divine and shares blessings and wisdom with strangers. Gentle yet resolute, he may heal, counsel or reveal the sacred sites hidden in the desert.
- Desert sage: A wise hermit living among dunes and ruins, who reads sand, stars and old inscriptions to find truth. Solitary and cryptic, he offers advice to those who endure the journey. His knowledge of buried cities and desert spirits can guide or warn adventurers.
- Oasis guardian: A watcher protecting precious water and green groves, sworn to keep the spring from contamination and theft. Part sentinel, part steward, he defends villagers against raiders and drought. Respect earns shelter, while threats to the oasis bring swift, fierce retaliation.
- Taklamakan ghost: A spirit that lures travelers into the shifting sands, calling in familiar voices or showing phantom caravans and cities. The desert's name is said to mean go in and you will not come out. It preys on thirst and despair, defeated only by discipline and sound guidance.
- Camel caravan master: A seasoned leader guiding traders across vast deserts, managing beasts, water, guards and bargains. He reads weather and loyalties alike and keeps order under harsh conditions. Hiring him offers safety and routes, while a betrayal or a bad omen can doom an entire expedition.
## South Asia (remaining)
### Bengali and Bangladeshi
- Bonbibi: The forest protector of the Sundarbans, a benevolent goddess revered by Hindus and Muslims alike, who guards honey collectors and woodcutters from tigers and demons. She defeated the tiger god in legend. Prayers to her bring safe passage, while greed and arrogance invite disaster.
- Dakshin Rai: A tiger god and demon king of the southern Sundarbans, who rules the mangrove forests and demands tribute from those entering his domain. He commands tigers and eats the greedy. Defeated by Bonbibi, he remains a feared, ambiguous power of the wild.
- Sundarbans tiger spirit: A forest guardian taking tiger form in the mangroves, stalking the tidal channels with silent steps and gleaming eyes. It punishes poachers and the disrespectful while sparing the humble. Villagers wear masks on the back of their heads to confuse it.
- Pishach: A flesh-eating ghoul that haunts graveyards and lonely places, gaunt and fierce, feeding on corpses and the unwary. It sours food, spreads disease and whispers madness. Fire, mantras and holy ash drive it away, making it a menacing nocturnal foe.
- Brahmadaitya: The ghost of a Brahmin who died unfulfilled, haunting a banyan or peepul tree in a white thread and robe. It is protective of travelers and village members yet fearsome if disrespected. Offerings and respect appease it, while its knowledge of scripture may aid scholars.
- Shankhchunni: A ghost bride, the vengeful spirit of a married woman, who wears white shell bangles and red sari while lurking in trees near water. She seizes passersby and wrings them dry. Treated with cunning and prayers, she may be pacified, but anger makes her deadly.
- Aleya: A marsh ghost light, a drifting glow over the Bengal wetlands that lures fishermen and travelers into bog and water. Said to be the spirits of those who drowned, it vanishes when approached. Following it spells danger, while discipline and fixed landmarks preserve life.
- Baul singer: A wandering mystic minstrel with a one-string ektara, singing songs of love, freedom and the divine within the body. He rejects caste and orthodoxy, wearing patched robes and long hair. His music carries spiritual wisdom, and his road-worn freedom makes him a gentle sage or free-spirited guide.
- Bengal tiger: A powerful striped predator of the river delta forest, swimming tidal creeks and stalking the mangroves for prey. Villagers fear and revere it. As a beast, it is a dangerous apex hunter, while as a symbol it embodies the wild power and the spirits of the Sundarbans.
- River pirate: A boat raider ambushing traders along delta waterways, striking from hidden creeks with fast country boats and knives. He knows tides and channels intimately and vanishes into the mangroves. He serves as a lawless foe or reluctant ally with knowledge of secret routes.
### Punjabi and Pakistani
- Heer and Ranjha: tragic lovers from Punjab's most famous folk romance, a cowherd and a wealthy landowner's daughter kept apart by family pride and a forced marriage. Their story ends in poison and grief, making them ideal doomed-romance NPCs or quest givers seeking to reunite separated souls.
- Sufi qawwal: devotional singer who leads a group in rhythmic chants and call-and-response poetry, wearing flowing kurtas and clapping in time. Their music builds into ecstatic trance that entrances crowds, making them a natural buffer, healer, or crowd-controlling support character.
- Pir: revered Sufi spiritual master who guides disciples along the mystic path, often dressed in simple robes and carrying prayer beads. Villagers seek the pir for counsel, charms, and miracles, so he works as a wise mentor whose blessings can heal, protect, or curse.
- Jatt warrior: sturdy farmer-fighter of the Punjab plains, broad-shouldered, mustachioed and proud, quick to defend village and land with a staff or sword. Fiercely loyal and stubborn about honour, he fits as a tough frontline defender whose temper and pride can become his downfall.
- Sikh warrior: turbaned soldier-saint who carries a curved sword, steel bracelet, and strict code of discipline, fighting to protect the weak and uphold justice. Calm in prayer and ferocious in battle, he offers a disciplined, honour-bound fighter archetype who never abandons the helpless.
- Churail: witch ghost of South Asian folklore, the vengeful spirit of a woman who died in childbirth or by cruelty, with backward-turned feet and a long tangled mane. She lures men with a beautiful face before revealing her horror, making her a classic seductive ambush predator.
- Peer Baba: revered saint resting at a village shrine, whose green-draped tomb draws pilgrims seeking cures, children, and fortune. Devotees tie threads and light lamps for his blessings, so he can serve as a sanctuary guardian, a quest hub, or a miracle-working spirit with strict expectations.
- Mirza and Sahiban: doomed lovers of a legendary Punjabi romance who flee together on horseback from her angry brothers. Mirza's overconfidence and Sahiban's torn loyalties lead to tragic betrayal, giving a tale of fatal pride, split allegiance, and star-crossed pursuit scenes.
- Pakistani truck art: vibrant painter-artist who decorates trucks and buses with bold flowers, birds, chrome, and shimmering patterns, treating each vehicle as a rolling canvas. Cheerful and showy, this craftsman can supply charms, painted wards, and flamboyant vehicles to a travelling party.
### Nepali
- Kumari: living goddess of Nepal, a young girl chosen as the incarnation of divine power, dressed in red with a painted third eye and carried in a sacred chariot. Rarely allowed to touch the ground, she acts as a revered figure whose blessing grants kings legitimacy and whose displeasure foretells disaster.
- Gurkha: elite Nepali soldier famed for fearlessness and loyalty, armed with the curved kukri blade and trained in mountain warfare. Disciplined, cheerful under hardship, and relentless in the charge, he makes an ideal elite guardian, mercenary captain, or bodyguard companion.
- Yeti: legendary snow creature of the Himalayas, a towering shaggy ape-like beast that leaves enormous footprints and haunts high passes. Elusive and immensely strong, it is rarely seen except as shadow in blizzards, serving as a wilderness hazard, a feared guardian, or a rare reclusive ally.
- Sherpa guide: expert mountaineer who leads climbers up the highest peaks, acclimatised to thin air and skilled with ropes, ice, and weather reading. Quietly brave and deeply respectful of the mountain gods, he works as a trusted guide, porter leader, or rescuer in lethal terrain.
- Newari priest: temple priest of the Kathmandu Valley who tends ancient rites, festival processions, and carved pagoda shrines. Versed in Hindu and Buddhist ritual, he mediates between worshippers and gods, so he can serve as a ritual specialist, lore-keeper, or protector of sacred relics.
- Bhaktapur spirit: ancient guardian presence haunting the temples, courtyards, and old brick squares of Bhaktapur. It lingers near carved windows and shrines, whispering warnings to the respectful and tormenting vandals, making it a good local ghost with a protective yet unforgiving temperament.
- Mountain guardian: protective spirit of the snowy peaks who watches over passes, glaciers, and sacred summits. It rewards humble travellers with safe passage and punishes arrogant climbers with avalanches and storms, offering an environmental boss or a moral test for adventurers.
- Pashupati ascetic: ash-covered holy man devoted to Shiva, lord of beasts, with matted hair, trident, and a body smeared in sacred ash. Living at the temple complex by the river, he practises severe austerities, giving him mystic insight, fearless detachment, and unsettling powers over animals and death.
### Sri Lankan
- Yaksha: powerful nature spirit of Sri Lankan lore, ranging from guardian to malevolent demon, often living in forests, ruins, and hidden pools. Shapeshifters of great strength and cunning, they can bargain, possess, or terrorise, making them flexible antagonists, tricksters, or reluctant allies.
- Devil dancer: masked ritual performer who drives out sickness and demons through all-night dances of fire, drums, and ecstatic movement. Dressed in elaborate headdresses and colourful costumes, he confronts disease spirits directly, serving as a healer, exorcist, or spiritual combatant.
- Naga: serpent being of Sri Lankan and wider South Asian myth, a hooded cobra-like or half-human guardian of treasure, water, and underworld palaces. Proud and venomous, nagas honour oaths strictly, so they suit roles as keepers of hidden riches or dangerous but fair negotiators.
- Raksha: fearsome demon with fangs, bulging eyes, and a monstrous appetite, rooted in the epic tradition of ogres who plague the righteous. Brutish yet sometimes cunning, it hunts travellers at night, offering a classic man-eating foe that can also serve a dark sorcerer.
- Sinhalese king: island monarch ruling from an ancient capital of great stupas, reservoirs, and rock fortresses. Patron of Buddhism and master of irrigation, he balances war against invaders with sacred duty, making him a political centrepiece, a patron, or a tragic ruler besieged from within.
- Demon mask dancer: performer in grotesque painted masks that depict diseases, ghosts, and monsters for healing rites. Each carved wooden face represents a specific affliction, so the dancer acts as a ritual diagnostician and healer, using spectacle and fear to cure the sick.
- Elephant mahout: trainer who rides and commands a giant elephant, bonded to the animal for life through years of care and quiet command. Sitting on its neck with a hooked goad, he supplies a mount-and-rider combination for war, labour, and ceremonial processions.
- Kataragama deity: six-faced war god who wields a spear and rides a peacock, venerated at a famous jungle shrine by many faiths. Fire-walkers and pilgrims seek his protection and vengeance on enemies, which makes him a potent divine patron, judge, or terrifying champion.
## East and Southeast Asia (remaining)
### Chinese minority peoples
- Miao silver warrior: fighter decked in heavy ornate silver jewellery, with towering headdresses, collars, and bells that jingle as he moves. The silver is both wealth and ward against evil spirits, so he combines display, defence, and mountain-bred combat skill in a vivid, colourful frontline character.
- Yi shaman (bimo): ritual priest of the Yi people who reads sacred scripts, performs divination, and conducts funeral and healing ceremonies. Wearing a woven hat and carrying a book of ancient texts, the bimo wards off ghosts and keeps ancestral memory, serving as a scholar-priest and exorcist.
- Zhuang song master: folk singer who trades improvised verses in mountain song contests, courting, mocking, and telling stories through melody. Quick-witted and charismatic, he wins crowds and challenges alike with words, making him a bard, social negotiator, or duelling rival in a battle of verse.
- Qiang priest: ritual healer who uses drums, sheepskin garments, and chants in mountain rites to commune with the gods of cliff and field. Guardian of tradition in stone-tower villages, he performs protective ceremonies and cures, serving as a village shaman and spiritual defender.
- Naxi dongba priest: pictograph-reading priest who performs nature and ancestral rites using one of the world's last living picture scripts. He mediates between humans and nature spirits, restoring harmony after offences, which suits a lore-keeping scholar who can read hidden meaning and calm angry spirits.
- Dai water goddess: river spirit woman who blesses festivals and rice fields, graceful in flowing dress and linked to the Water-Splashing festival. Gentle but powerful, she grants fertility and cleansing to those who honour her, though drought and flood follow when she is insulted.
- Tibetan-Qiang mountain guardian: stone-tower dweller protecting a high valley, a spirit or watcher of ancient watchtowers perched on rugged slopes. Silent and enduring, it repels raiders and corrupting influences, serving as a landscape guardian whose favour must be earned with offerings and respect.
- Miao witch: village sorceress who brews poisons, casts curses, and is both feared and consulted by neighbours. Folk tales say she keeps poisonous insect charms and manipulates fortune, giving a morally ambiguous antagonist, suspicious healer, or scapegoat bound up in village politics.
### Taiwanese Indigenous
- Atayal facial-tattoo warrior: mountain fighter marked with ritual facial tattoos earned through courage and, for women, weaving skill. The marks identify him to ancestors in the afterlife and signal honour, making him a proud hunter and defender with fierce resolve in forested highlands.
- Rukai hundred-pace snake: venomous serpent ancestor sacred to the Rukai, said to kill within a hundred steps of its bite and linked to noble lineage. Revered in carvings and legend, it works as a deadly totem creature, a clan symbol, or a patient predator guarding sacred ground.
